                                          Totally 2-closed finite groups with trivial Fitting subgroup
                                          Majid Arezoomand1 , Mohammad A. Iranmanesh2 , Cheryl E Praeger3 and Gareth Tracey4
                                          1 University of Larestan, Larestan, 74317-16137, Iran; E-mail: arezoomand@lar.ac.ir.
                                          2 Yazd University, Yazd, 89195-741, Iran; E-mail: iranmanesh@yazd.ac.ir.
                                          3 University of Western Australia, 35 Stirling Highway, Crawley, WA 6009, Australia; E-mail: cheryl.praeger@uwa.edu.au.
                                          4 School of Mathematics, University of Birmingham, Edgbaston, Birmingham, B15 2TT, United Kingdom;

                                          E-mail: g.tracey@bham.ac.uk.
                                          Received xx xxx xxxx
                                          Keywords: 2-closed permutation groups, graph representations of groups, simple groups
                                          MSC Codes: Primary – 20B05, 20E42; Secondary – 05C20



                                          Abstract
                                          A group 𝐺 is said to be totally 2-closed if in each of its faithful permutation representations, say on a set Ω, 𝐺
                                          is the largest subgroup of Sym(Ω) which leaves invariant each of the 𝐺-orbits for the induced action on Ω × Ω.
                                          We prove that there are precisely 47 finite totally 2-closed groups with trivial Fitting subgroup. Each of these
                                          groups is a direct product of pairwise non-isomorphic sporadic simple groups, with the direct factors coming from
                                          the Janko groups J1 , J3 and J4 , together with Ly, Th and the Monster M. These are the first known examples of
                                          insoluble totally 2-closed groups. As a by-product of our methods, we develop several tools for studying 2-closures
                                          of transitive permutation groups – a vital tool in the study of representations of finite groups as automorphism
                                          groups of digraphs. We also prove a dual to a 1939 theorem of Frucht from Algebraic Graph Theory.


                                          1. Introduction
                                          In 1969, Wielandt [33, Definition 5.3] introduced the concept of 2-closure for a permutation group 𝐺
                                          on a set Ω. The 2-closure 𝐺 (2) of 𝐺 is the set of all 𝑔 ∈ Sym(Ω) such that 𝑔 leaves invariant each
                                          𝐺-orbit in the induced 𝐺-action on ordered pairs from Ω. The 2-closure 𝐺 (2) is a subgroup of Sym(Ω)
                                          containing 𝐺 [33, Theorem 5.4], and 𝐺 is said to be 2-closed if 𝐺 (2) = 𝐺.
                                              It is important to note that the 2-closure of a permutation group 𝐺 on Ω is not intrinsic to the group 𝐺.
                                          It can depend on the nature of the action on Ω. For example, the symmetric group Sym(3) acts faithfully
                                          and intransitively on {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} with orbits {1, 2, 3} and {4, 5}, and in this action its 2-closure is
                                          Sym(3) × 𝐶2 ; while Sym(3) is 2-closed in its natural action on {1, 2, 3}. In 2016, D. F. Holt1 suggested
                                          a stronger concept independent of the permutation representation. This was adopted and explored by the
                                          first author with Abdollahi in [1] where it was called total 2-closure. To explain the concept we first enrich
                                          the notation for 2-closure by writing 𝐺 (2),Ω for the 2-closure of a permutation group 𝐺 ≤ Sym(Ω). We
                                          then define a group 𝐺 to be totally 2-closed if 𝐺 (2),Ω = 𝐺 whenever 𝐺 is faithfully represented as a
                                          permutation group on Ω. It was proved in [1, Theorem 1] that a finite totally 2-closed group has cyclic
                                          centre, and moreover [1, Theorem 2] that a finite nilpotent group is totally 2-closed if and only if it is
                                          either cyclic or a direct product of a generalised quaternion group with a cyclic group of odd order.


                                            1mathoverflow.net/questions/235114/2-closure-of-a-permutation-group
2

   The first and fourth authors, with Abdollahi undertook a general study of total 2-closure in [2]. They
proved [2, Theorem B] that a finite soluble group is totally 2-closed if and only if it is nilpotent, and
hence is one of the groups identified in [1, Theorem 2]. Further they showed in [2, Theorem A] that the
Fitting subgroup of a totally 2-closed finite group is itself totally 2-closed (and hence lies in the family
just described). At the time of their writing of the paper [2], no examples of insoluble totally 2-closed
groups were known. They studied the structure of an insoluble example 𝐺 of smallest order, showing
that 𝐺 modulo its cyclic centre 𝑍 (𝐺) has a unique minimal normal subgroup which is nonabelian, [2,
Proposition 4.1].
   The purpose of this paper is to seek out finite insoluble totally 2-closed groups 𝐺. We focus on the
case where the Fitting subgroup 𝐹 (𝐺) is trivial, or equivalently, the case where 𝐺 has no nontrivial
abelian normal subgroup. We show first that such a group 𝐺 is a direct product of nonabelian simple
groups, each of which is itself totally 2-closed (see Theorem 2.5). In light of this result, we decided that
our next challenge should be to find all totally 2-closed finite simple groups. The 2-closure condition
seemed so strong that we initially believed that we would find no examples. Surprisingly (to us) such
groups do indeed exist, but they are rare, and the only examples are six of the sporadic simple groups.
Theorem 1.1. Let 𝑇 be a nonabelian finite simple group. Then 𝑇 is totally 2-closed if and only if 𝑇 is
one of the groups J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly, Th or M.
   Theorem 1.1 gives us the building blocks of finite totally 2-closed groups with trivial Fitting subgroup.
We were able to use this result as the basis of an inductive approach yielding the following complete
classification of all such groups.
Theorem 1.2. Let 𝐺 be a non-trivial finite group with trivial Fitting subgroup. Then 𝐺 is totally 2-closed
if and only if each of the following holds:
(1) 𝐺 = 𝑇1 × . . . × 𝑇𝑟 , where the 𝑇𝑖 are nonabelian finite simple groups and 𝑟 ≤ 5;
(2) 𝑇𝑖  𝑇 𝑗 for each 𝑖 ≠ 𝑗; and
(3) One of the following holds:
      (i) 𝑇𝑖 ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Th, Ly} for each 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟; or
     (ii) 𝑇𝑖 ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly, M} for each 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟.
Corollary 1.3. There are precisely 47 finite totally 2-closed groups with trivial Fitting subgroup.
   Proving these results involved a wide variety of methods, and we needed to develop several tools
which we hope will assist future analyses of finite totally 2-closed groups. More generally, we also
hope that our results will add significantly to the understanding of 2-closures of transitive permutation
groups. In particular, in Section 3, we prove that if 𝐺 is an imprimitive transitive permutation group,
and its action on a set of non-trivial blocks is faithful and 2-closed, then either 𝐺 is 2-closed, or the
2-closure of 𝐺 has a very particular structure (see Lemma 3.5 and Proposition 3.8).
   The study of 2-closures of transitive permutation groups has important applications in graph theory,
the basis of which we discuss in Subsection 1.1. Perhaps because of these applications, such as to the
Polycirculant conjecture (that each vertex-transitive graph has an automorphism of prime order with no
fixed vertices), the theory of 2-closures of transitive permutation groups has become a well-developed
branch of both group theory and graph theory over the past fifty years (see, for example, [8, Section
1.3.4] and the recent survey [3]). We hope that the general theory we develop through this paper, as well
as our main results, will play an important role in making further progress in this area.


1.1. Link between 2-closure and graphs, and an application
The concept of 2-closure is a very combinatorial notion, and there is indeed a close relationship between
2-closed permutation groups and digraphs: each subset 𝐴 ⊆ Ω × Ω may be viewed as the arc-set
of a digraph Γ = (Ω, 𝐴) with vertex-set Ω and with a directed edge (an arc) from 𝛼 to 𝛽 for each
(𝛼, 𝛽) ∈ 𝐴. The automorphism group Aut(Γ) of Γ is defined as the subgroup of all permutations of
                                                                                                          3

Ω which leave the arc-set 𝐴 invariant. In particular, each element of (Aut(Γ)) (2),Ω leaves 𝐴 invariant
and hence is an automorphism of Γ. Thus (Aut(Γ)) (2),Ω ⊆ Aut(Γ), and the reverse inclusion holds
by the definition of 2-closure. Therefore (Aut(Γ)) (2),Ω = Aut(Γ). The same argument also shows that
(Aut(Γ)) (2),Ω = Aut(Γ) when Γ is an undirected graph. Thus, to summarise, for each (di)graph Γ with
vertex set Ω, the automorphism group Aut(Γ) is a 2-closed subgroup of Sym(Ω). In fact, for each
permutation group 𝐺 ≤ Sym(Ω), the 2-closure 𝐺 (2),Ω is equal to the intersection of the groups Aut(Γ)
over all digraphs Γ = (Ω, 𝐴) for which the arc-set 𝐴 is a 𝐺-orbit in Ω × Ω.
   In particular, if 𝐺 ≤ Sym(Ω) is transitive on Ω and if 𝐴 is a 𝐺-orbit in Ω × Ω not equal to the
diagonal {(𝛼, 𝛼) | 𝛼 ∈ Ω}, then the digraph Γ = (Ω, 𝐴) is called a 𝐺-orbital digraph, and the group
𝐺 is admitted as a vertex-transitive and arc-transitive subgroup of Aut(Γ). Thus, in this case, the 2-
closure 𝐺 (2),Ω is the intersection of the automorphism groups of all the 𝐺-orbital digraphs. The study
of 𝐺-orbital digraphs goes back to the work of D. G. Higman [17] at approximately the same time as
Wielandt’s work on closures in the late 1960s.
   Before describing our approach to proving Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, we would like to draw attention
to a graph theoretic consequence of our results, which may be of independent interest. In 1939, Frucht
[14] confirmed a conjecture of König that every finite group 𝐺 can be written as the automorphism
group of a finite simple undirected graph Γ. We will say that a faithful permutation representation
𝐺 ↩→ 𝐺 Ω ≤ Sym(Ω) of 𝐺 on a finite set Ω is a Frucht representation of 𝐺 if there exists a set 𝐸 of
unordered pairs from Ω such that 𝐺 Ω is the automorphism group of the finite simple undirected graph
Γ = Γ(Ω, 𝐸). Since Aut(Γ) is 2-closed, Theorem 1.2 implies the following, which can be viewed as a
dual to Frucht’s theorem in the case where 𝐹 (𝐺) = 1.
Corollary 1.4. Let 𝐺 be a non-trivial finite group with trivial Fitting subgroup, and assume that every
faithful permutation representation of 𝐺 is a Frucht representation. Then 𝐺 = 𝑇1 × . . . × 𝑇𝑟 , where the
𝑇𝑖 are pairwise non-isomorphic finite simple groups; 𝑟 ≤ 5; and either
  (i) for each 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟, 𝑇𝑖 ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Th, Ly}; or
 (ii) for each 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟, 𝑇𝑖 ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly, M}.
   We mention a few open questions about total closure. Firstly, since we have considered only groups
with trivial Fitting subgroup in this paper, we ask:
Question 1. Are there any finite insoluble totally 2-closed groups with nontrivial Fitting subgroup? If
so, can we classify them?
One of the ultimate goals of this programme of work is to classify all finite totally 2-closed groups.
Given the results in the current paper, this goal would be realised with a complete answer to Question 1.
See Section 8 for some remarks on the obstacles involved in answering this question.
    The analogous concept of total 𝑘-closure may be defined for arbitrary positive integers 𝑘, namely 𝐺
is totally 𝑘-closed if, for every faithful representation 𝐺 ≤ Sym(Ω), 𝐺 is equal to the set of all elements
𝑔 ∈ Sym(Ω) such that 𝑔 leaves invariant each 𝐺-orbit in the induced 𝐺-action on ordered 𝑘-tuples
from Ω. This concept has been explored by Churikov and the third author in [12]. For each 𝑘 ≥ 2, it
follows from [33, Theorem 5.8] that, if 𝐺 is totally (𝑘 − 1)-closed then 𝐺 is also totally 𝑘-closed. On the
other hand, by [12, Theorem 1.2], there are infinitely many finite totally 𝑘-closed groups which are not
totally (𝑘 − 1)-closed, and this is true even for abelian 𝑝-groups for each prime 𝑝. The paper [12] gives
a discussion of the topic and poses three open problems about total 𝑘-closure (where 𝑘 ≥ 3) for finite
nilpotent groups, soluble groups, and sporadic simple groups – all problems which have been resolved
for 𝑘 = 2, in [1, 2] and the current paper. It follows from [33, Theorem 5.11] that an alternating group
𝐴𝑛 (with 𝑛 ≥ 5) is not totally 𝑘-closed for any 𝑘 ≤ 𝑛 − 2, so we further ask:
Question 2. Are there any finite simple groups of Lie type which are totally 3-closed? If so, find them all.
4

   Moreover, for any faithful representation of a finite simple group 𝐺, there is a 𝐺-orbit on which
𝐺 acts nontrivially and hence faithfully; applying [33, Theorem 5.12] to the 𝐺-action on this orbit we
deduce that 𝐺 is totally 𝑛-closed, where 𝑛 = |𝐺 |. Thus we ask:
Question 3. Is there a fixed integer 𝑘 such that all finite simple groups are totally 𝑘-closed? Indeed, for
a given finite simple group 𝐺, what is the least integer 𝑘 such that 𝐺 is totally 𝑘-closed?


1.2. Structure of the paper
In the remained of this section, we outline our approach to the proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, and
detail the structure of the paper. The fundamental starting point is Wielandt’s Dissection Theorem [33,
Dissection Theorem 6.5] which for convenience we state as Theorem 2.1. It is an invaluable tool, and
in particular it underpins our proof of Theorem 2.5, which we present in Section 2.
    As mentioned above, Theorem 2.5 reduces our classification of finite totally 2-closed groups 𝐺 with
trivial Fitting subgroup to the case where 𝐺 is a direct product of nonabelian simple groups, which are
‘independent’ of each other in the sense that each of the simple direct factors is not isomorphic to a
section of the direct product of the others. (We comment on this condition in relation to the sporadic
simple groups in Remark 2.6.) Our next step is to reduce further: in Proposition 2.10, we show that such
a group 𝐺 is totally 2-closed if and only if no simple direct factor of 𝐺 admits a non-trivial factorisation,
and each (not necessarily faithful) transitive permutation representation of 𝐺 is 2-closed.
    This suggests two natural avenues to pursue. The first is to use the classification of the maximal
factorisations of the nonabelian simple groups in [24] to eliminate many families of simple groups from
being direct factors of 𝐺. We do this in Section 2.3, where we show, in particular, that the simple direct
factors of 𝐺 are either sporadic groups or exceptional groups of Lie type.
    Our second natural avenue to pursue concerns transitive actions of such groups 𝐺. Strong restrictions
on the 2-closures of primitive almost simple groups were obtained in [23]. With these restrictions in
mind for the case where 𝐺 is simple, we develop powerful reduction theorems in Section 3 for general
transitive imprimitive permutation groups 𝐺 which induce a faithful 2-closed action on a set of non-
trivial blocks of imprimitivity: we show that either 𝐺 itself is 2-closed, or the 2-closure of 𝐺 has a very
particular structure. This provides further criteria to determine whether or not such permutation groups
are 2-closed (see, in particular, Proposition 3.10).
    The tools developed in Sections 2 and 3 are sufficient to begin our analysis of the 2-closures of
permutation representations of the finite simple groups. In Sections 4, and 6, we deal with the sporadic
groups other than J4 , and the exceptional groups of Lie type, respectively. The case of 𝐺 = J4 is delicate,
and requires a nuanced approach, see Section 5. These three sections complete the proof of Theorem 1.1.
    Section 7 is reserved for the study of 2-closures of direct products of finite simple groups, and the
proof of Theorem 1.2.
    Finally, in Section 8, we make some concluding remarks on the question of classifying the finite
insoluble totally 2-closed groups with non-trivial Fitting subgroup. We also prove a useful reduction
theorem for this problem.

Notation: Most of our notation is standard. For a finite group 𝐺, we write 𝑍 (𝐺), 𝐹 (𝐺), Φ(𝐺) and
[𝐺, 𝐺] for the centre, Fitting subgroup, Frattini subgroup, and derived subgroup of 𝐺, respectively.
    For a set Ω, we write Sym(Ω) and Alt(Ω) for the symmetric and alternating group on Ω respectively.
If a finite group 𝐺 acts on Ω, we write 𝐺 Ω for the image of the induced action of 𝐺 on Ω.
    For group names, we use conventions from the Atlas [11, especially page xx], except that we write
Alt(𝑛) and Sym(𝑛) for the alternating and symmetric groups of degree 𝑛.

2. Applying Wielandt’s Dissection Theorem
As we mentioned in Section 1, Wielandt’s Dissection Theorem [33, Dissection Theorem 6.5] is a
fundamental tool for studying 2-closure. For convenience we state it here. Note that, for 𝐺 ≤ Sym(Ω)
and 𝛿 ∈ Ω, we denote by 𝐺 𝛿 the stabiliser of 𝛿 in 𝐺, and by 𝛿 𝐺 the 𝐺-orbit in Ω containing 𝛿. Also if
Γ ⊆ Ω and Γ is 𝐺-invariant, then 𝐺 Γ denotes the permutation group on Γ induced by 𝐺.
Theorem 2.1. [Wielandt’s Dissection Theorem] Let 𝐺 ≤ Sym(Ω), and suppose that Ω is the disjoint
union Ω = Γ ∪ Δ such that both Γ and Δ are 𝐺-invariant. Then the following are equivalent.
(a) 𝐺 Γ × 𝐺 Δ ≤ 𝐺 (2),Ω ;
(b) 𝐺 = 𝐺 𝛾 𝐺 𝛿 for all 𝛾 ∈ Γ, 𝛿 ∈ Δ;
(c) 𝐺 𝛿 is transitive on 𝛾 𝐺 for all 𝛾 ∈ Γ, 𝛿 ∈ Δ.
   In this section we discuss some ways in which this result can be applied. To begin, we state the
following helpful application given in [2]. Here, for a subgroup 𝐻 of a group 𝐺, we denote by Core𝐺 (𝐻)
the core of 𝐻 in 𝐺, that is, Core𝐺 (𝐻) = ∩𝑔 ∈𝐺 𝐻 𝑔 , the largest normal subgroup of 𝐺 contained in 𝐻. By
a nontrivial factorisation of 𝐺 we mean a factorisation 𝐺 = 𝐻𝐾 with both 𝐻 and 𝐾 proper subgroups
of 𝐺.
Lemma 2.2. [2, Lemma 3.1]         Let 𝐺 be a finite totally 2-closed group such that 𝐺 admits a nontrivial
factorisation 𝐺 = 𝐻𝐾 with
                                       Core𝐺 (𝐻) ∩ Core𝐺 (𝐾) = 1.

Then 𝐺 = Core𝐺 (𝐻) ×Core𝐺 (𝐾) and both Core𝐺 (𝐻) and Core𝐺 (𝐾) are totally 2-closed. In particular,
if 𝐻 ∩ 𝐾 = 1, then 𝐺 = 𝐻 × 𝐾 and both 𝐻 and 𝐾 are totally 2-closed.
   Lemma 2.2 has the following important consequence for simple groups.
Corollary 2.3. Let 𝑇 be a finite nonabelian simple group. If 𝑇 is totally 2-closed, then 𝑇 admits no
nontrivial factorisation.
Proof. Suppose that 𝑇 is totally 2-closed. If 𝑇 = 𝐻𝐾 is a nontrivial factorisation, then the cores
Core𝑇 (𝐻) = Core𝑇 (𝐾) = 1 since 𝑇 is simple, and this contradicts Lemma 2.2. Hence 𝑇 has no
nontrivial factorisations.                                                                      

   The following result from Wielandt [33] is also useful when making a detailed analysis of 2-closures.
Theorem 2.4. [33, Theorem 5.6] Let 𝐺 ≤ Sym(Ω) and 𝑥 ∈ Sym(Ω). Then 𝑥 ∈ 𝐺 (2),Ω if and only if,
for all 𝛼, 𝛽 ∈ Ω, there exists 𝑔 ∈ 𝐺 such that 𝛼 𝑥 = 𝛼 𝑔 and 𝛽 𝑥 = 𝛽𝑔 .


2.1. Reduction to direct products of nonabelian finite simple groups
In this section, we reduce our proof of Theorem 1.2 to particular direct products of finite simple groups.
Before we state our main result, we remind the reader of some standard terminology: a nontrivial group
𝑋 is said to be a section of a group 𝐺 if there are subgroups 𝐿  𝐻 ≤ 𝐺 such that 𝐻/𝐿  𝑋. Our
reduction theorem can now be stated as follows.
6

Theorem 2.5. Let 𝐺 be a non-trivial finite totally 2-closed group such that 𝐹 (𝐺) = 1. Then 𝐺 =
𝑇1 × · · · × 𝑇𝑟 for some 𝑟 ≥ 1, where for each 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟, 𝑇𝑖 is a finite nonabelian simple group which is totally
                                      Î
2-closed, and 𝑇𝑖 is not a section of 𝑗≠𝑖 𝑇 𝑗 .
Proof. Since 𝐺 is finite, nontrivial, and 𝐹 (𝐺) = 1, a minimal normal subgroup 𝑀 of 𝐺 is a direct
product of nonabelian finite simple groups. If 𝑀 = 𝐺 then, as 𝑀 is minimal normal, the group 𝐺 would
itself be a nonabelian simple group which is totally 2-closed, and the conclusion holds with 𝑟 = 1. Thus
we may assume that 𝑀 ≠ 𝐺, and 𝑀 = 𝑆1 × · · · × 𝑆 𝑠 with each 𝑆𝑖 a finite nonabelian simple group. We
note that the minimal normal subgroups of 𝑀 are precisely the subgroups

                         𝑆b𝑖 = {(𝑥 1 , . . . , 𝑥 𝑠 ) | 𝑥 𝑗 = 1 for 𝑗 ≠ 𝑖, and 𝑥𝑖 ∈ 𝑆𝑖 }  𝑆𝑖 ,

for 𝑖 = 1, . . . , 𝑠 (see, for example, [27, Theorem4.16(iv)]). By the ‘Odd Order Theorem’, since each of
the 𝑆b𝑖 is a finite nonabelian simple group, each 𝑆b𝑖 has a nontrivial Sylow 2-subgroup, 𝑃𝑖 say, and hence
𝑃 = 𝑃1 × · · · × 𝑃𝑠 is a (nontrivial) Sylow 2-subgroup of 𝑀. By the Frattini argument (see, for example,
[29, 5.2.14]), 𝐺 = 𝑁𝐺 (𝑃) 𝑀. Now 𝑁 𝑀 (𝑃) = 𝑁 𝑆b1 (𝑃1 ) × · · · × 𝑁 𝑆b𝑠 (𝑃𝑠 ), and 𝑁 𝑀 (𝑃) projects to a proper
subgroup 𝑁 𝑆b𝑖 (𝑃𝑖 ) of 𝑆b𝑖 , for each 𝑖. In particular 𝑀  𝑁𝐺 (𝑃). Hence the core 𝑋 = Core𝐺 (𝑁𝐺 (𝑃)) does
not contain 𝑀, and so 𝑋 ∩ 𝑀 = 1 since 𝑀 is a minimal normal subgroup of 𝐺. Also since 𝑀 is normal
in 𝐺, Core𝐺 (𝑀) = ∩𝑔 ∈𝐺 𝑀 𝑔 = 𝑀. Then, since 𝐺 is totally 2-closed, it follows from Lemma 2.2 that
𝐺 = 𝑋 × 𝑀 and both 𝑋 and 𝑀 are totally 2-closed. Since 𝑀 ≠ 𝐺 it follows that 𝑋 ≠ 1 and since 𝑀 is a
minimal normal subgroup of 𝐺 we conclude that 𝑀 = 𝑆b1 is a finite nonabelian simple group.
    Thus each minimal normal subgroup of 𝐺 is a totally 2-closed, finite nonabelian simple group and
is a direct factor of 𝐺. Applying this argument recursively we conclude that 𝐺 = 𝑇1 × 𝑇2 × · · · × 𝑇𝑟 for
some 𝑟 ≥ 2, where each 𝑇𝑖 is a totally 2-closed, finite nonabelian simple group. For 1 ≤ 𝑗 ≤ 𝑟 let 𝜋 𝑗
denote the projection 𝜋 𝑗 : 𝐺 → 𝑇 𝑗 given by (𝑡 1 , . . . , 𝑡𝑟 ) → 𝑡 𝑗 , and let 𝑇b𝑗 denote the minimal normal
subgroup of 𝐺 defined similarly to the 𝑆b𝑖 above.
    Let 𝑖, 𝑗 be distinct integers between 1 and 𝑟. We show next that 𝑇𝑖 is not a section of 𝑇 𝑗 . Suppose
that this is false, so there exist subgroups 𝐿  𝐻 ≤ 𝑇 𝑗 such that 𝐻/𝐿  𝑇𝑖 , or equivalently, there
exists an epimorphism 𝜑 : 𝐻 → 𝑇𝑖 with kernel 𝐿. Without loss of generality assume that 𝑖 = 1 and
𝑗 = 2, and let 𝐽 = {(𝜑(ℎ), ℎ, 1, . . . , 1) | ℎ ∈ 𝐻} and 𝐾 = 1 × 𝑇2 × · · · × 𝑇𝑟 . Clearly both 𝐽 and 𝐾 are
proper subgroups of 𝐺. Moreover, since 𝜑 is an epimorphism it follows that 𝐺 = 𝐽𝐾 is a nontrivial
factorisation, and since 𝐾 is normal in 𝐺 we have Core𝐺 (𝐾) = 𝐾. We claim that Core𝐺 (𝐽) = 1. Now
Core𝐺 (𝐽) ≤ 𝐽 < 𝑇b1 × 𝑇b2 × 1 · · · × 1, and if Core𝐺 (𝐽) ≠ 1 then Core𝐺 (𝐽) would contain at least one
of the minimal normal subgroups of 𝐺, namely one of 𝑇b1 , . . . , 𝑇b𝑟 , so Core𝐺 (𝐽) would contain 𝑇b1 or 𝑇b2 .
Let 𝑥 = (𝜑(ℎ), ℎ, 1, . . . , 1) ∈ Core𝐺 (𝐽). If 𝑥1 = 𝜑(ℎ) ≠ 1 then ℎ ≠ 1, so Core𝐺 (𝐽) ∩ 𝑇b1 = 1. Also
if 𝑥 ∈ 𝑇b2 , then 𝑥1 = 𝜑(ℎ) = 1 so ℎ ∈ Ker(𝜑) = 𝐿. Since 𝐿 is a proper subgroup of 𝑇2 it follows that
Core𝐺 (𝐽) does not contain 𝑇b2 either. Hence Core𝐺 (𝐽) = 1 as claimed. It now follows from Lemma 2.2
that 𝐺 = 1 × 𝐾, which is a contradiction. Thus none of the 𝑇𝑖 is a section of any of the other 𝑇 𝑗 (and in
particular the 𝑇𝑖 are pairwise non-isomorphic).                            Î
    Finally, suppose that, for some 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟, 𝑇𝑖 is a section of 𝐾 := 𝑗≠𝑖 𝑇 𝑗 . Then there are subgroups
𝐿  𝐻 ≤ 𝐾 such that 𝐻/𝐿  𝑇𝑖 . Let 𝐻, 𝐿 be subgroups            Îof 𝐾 with this property such that |𝐻| is as
small as possible. Identify 𝐾 with the normal subgroup 𝑗≠𝑖 𝑇b𝑗 of 𝐺. Let 1 ≤ 𝑗 ≤ 𝑟 with 𝑗 ≠ 𝑖, and
                            Î
consider 𝐻 𝑗 := 𝐻 ∩ ( 𝑘≠ 𝑗 𝑇b𝑘 ), the kernel of the restriction 𝜋 𝑗 | 𝐻 to 𝐻 of the projection 𝜋 𝑗 . We will
identify 𝜋 𝑗 (𝐻) with the quotient 𝐻/𝐻 𝑗 so that, for each subgroup 𝐽 ≤ 𝐻, the image 𝜋 𝑗 (𝐽) is identified
with 𝐽𝐻 𝑗 /𝐻 𝑗 . In particular 𝜋 𝑗 (𝐿) = 𝐿𝐻 𝑗 /𝐻 𝑗 . Then

              𝑄 := 𝜋 𝑗 (𝐻)/𝜋 𝑗 (𝐿) = (𝐻/𝐻 𝑗 )/(𝐿𝐻 𝑗 /𝐻 𝑗 )  𝐻/(𝐿𝐻 𝑗 )  (𝐻/𝐿)/(𝐿𝐻 𝑗 /𝐿),

a quotient of the simple group 𝐻/𝐿  𝑇𝑖 . Thus 𝑄  𝑇𝑖 or 1. Now 𝜋 𝑗 (𝐿)  𝜋 𝑗 (𝐻) ≤ 𝑇 𝑗 , and by the
previous paragraph 𝑇𝑖 is not a section of 𝑇 𝑗 , and hence the quotient 𝜋 𝑗 (𝐻)/𝜋 𝑗 (𝐿)  𝑇𝑖 . Thus 𝑄 must
be trivial, and hence 𝐻 = 𝐿𝐻 𝑗 . This, however, implies that 𝑇𝑖  𝐻/𝐿 = (𝐿𝐻 𝑗 )/𝐿  𝐻 𝑗 /(𝐿 ∩ 𝐻 𝑗 ), and
                                                                                                             7

so, by the minimality of |𝐻|, we conclude that 𝐻 = 𝐻 𝑗 , that is to say, 𝜋 𝑗 (𝐻) = 1. Since this holds for
                          Î
each 𝑗 ≠ 𝑖, and since 𝐻 ≤ 𝑗≠𝑖 𝑇b𝑗 = 𝐾, it follows that 𝐻 = 1, which is a contradiction. Thus 𝑇𝑖 is not a
section of 𝐾, and the proof is complete.                                                                
Remark 2.6. We make some      Î comments about the condition in Theorem 2.5 that each 𝑇𝑖 is not isomorphic
to a section of the product 𝑗≠𝑖 𝑇 𝑗 . Since the 𝑇𝑖 are simple groups, this condition is equivalent to requiring
that, for all distinct 𝑖, 𝑗, the group 𝑇𝑖 is not isomorphic to a section of 𝑇 𝑗 . Deciding precisely when this
condition holds was not easy, but in the case where both 𝑇𝑖 and 𝑇 𝑗 are sporadic simple groups (which is
the case with the examples in Theorem 1.2), an almost complete answer is given in [11, p. 238], which
provides a beautiful diagram showing exactly which sporadic simple groups are involved in this way
in other sporadic simple groups. The only unresolved case in this diagram is whether or not the small
Janko group 𝐽1 occurs as a section of the Monster M, but it is now known that 𝐽1 is not a section of the
Monster, see [34, Section 5.8] for a discussion. Considering this diagram (and the situation for 𝐽1 , M)
we see that, for 𝑇𝑖 , 𝑇 𝑗 any distinct pair of sporadic groups occurring in the statement of Theorem 1.2, if
𝑇𝑖 is a section of 𝑇 𝑗 then 𝑇𝑖 = 𝑇 ℎ and 𝑇 𝑗 = M (which explains the need for two parts in Theorem 1.2(3)).


2.2. Totally 2-closed direct products of simple groups
By Theorem 2.5, we need to analyse direct products of totally 2-closed simple groups. With this in mind
we introduce the following hypothesis and notation.
Hypothesis 2.7. Let 𝐺 = 𝑇1 × 𝑇2 × · · · × 𝑇𝑟 for some 𝑟 ≥ 1, where each 𝑇𝑖 is a finite nonabelian simple
                                                                      Î
group, and suppose that, for 1 ≤ 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟, 𝑇𝑖 is not a section of 𝑗≠𝑖 𝑇 𝑗 . For 1 ≤ 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟, let 𝜋𝑖 : 𝐺 → 𝑇𝑖
denote the projection map 𝜋𝑖 : (𝑡 1 , . . . , 𝑡𝑟 ) → 𝑡 𝑖 , and define

                               𝑇b𝑖 = {𝑔 ∈ 𝐺 | 𝜋 𝑗 (𝑔) = 1 for all 𝑗 ≠ 𝑖}  𝑇𝑖 .

As mentioned earlier, (see, for example, [27, Theorem 4.16(iv)]), {𝑇b1 , . . . , 𝑇b𝑟 } is the complete set of
minimal normal subgroups of 𝐺.
   This notation helps avoid possible confusion by distinguishing between the abstract group 𝑇𝑖 and
the simple normal subgroup 𝑇b𝑖 of 𝐺. Note that Hypothesis 2.7 holds, by Theorem 2.5, if 𝐺 is totally
2-closed with 𝐹 (𝐺) = 1. We extend the argument in the last paragraph of the proof of Theorem 2.5 to
obtain the following characterisation of certain subgroups of 𝐺.
Lemma 2.8. Let 𝐺, 𝑟 be as in Hypothesis 2.7, and let 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟. If 𝐻 ≤ 𝐺 has 𝑇𝑖 as a section, then 𝐻
contains 𝑇b𝑖 .
Proof. Suppose that 𝐻 ≤ 𝐺 and 𝐻 has a section 𝑇𝑖 , that is to say, there exist 𝐿  𝐾 ≤ 𝐻 such that
 𝐾/𝐿  𝑇𝑖 . We need to show that 𝑇b𝑖 ≤ 𝐻. Without loss of generality we may assume      Î      that no proper
subgroup of 𝐾 has 𝑇𝑖 as a section. Let 1 ≤ 𝑗 ≤ 𝑟 with 𝑗 ≠ 𝑖, and let 𝐽 = 𝐾 ∩ ( 𝑘≠ 𝑗 𝑇b𝑘 ), the kernel
of the restriction 𝜋 𝑗 | 𝐾 of 𝜋 𝑗 to 𝐾. Then 𝜋 𝑗 (𝐿)  𝜋 𝑗 (𝐾) ≤ 𝑇 𝑗 and 𝜋 𝑗 (𝐾)/𝜋 𝑗 (𝐿)  (𝐾/𝐽)/(𝐿𝐽/𝐽) 
 𝐾/(𝐿𝐽)  (𝐾/𝐿)/(𝐿𝐽/𝐿), a quotient of the simple group 𝐾/𝐿  𝑇𝑖 . By Hypothesis 2.7, 𝑇𝑖 is not a
            Î
section of 𝑘≠𝑖 𝑇𝑘 , and in particular, 𝑇𝑖 is not a section of 𝑇 𝑗 . Hence 𝜋 𝑗 (𝐾)/𝜋 𝑗 (𝐿)  𝑇𝑖 . This implies
that 𝜋 𝑗 (𝐾) = 𝜋 𝑗 (𝐿), or equivalently, 𝐾 = 𝐿𝐽. Thus 𝑇𝑖  𝐾/𝐿 = (𝐿𝐽)/𝐿  𝐽/(𝐿 ∩ 𝐽), and since 𝑇𝑖
is not a section of any proper subgroup of 𝐾, we conclude that 𝐾 = 𝐽, that is, 𝜋 𝑗 (𝐾) = 1. Since this
holds for each 𝑗 ≠ 𝑖, it follows that 𝐾 ≤ 𝑇b𝑖 , and since 𝑇𝑖 is a section of 𝐾 this means that 𝐾 = 𝑇b𝑖 . Hence
𝑇b𝑖 ≤ 𝐻.                                                                                                     
    Lemma 2.8 has an important consequence for factorisations of groups satisfying Hypothesis 2.7. The
proof uses the notion of a strip. For 𝐺 = 𝑇1 × 𝑇2 × · · · × 𝑇𝑟 as in Hypothesis 2.7, a subgroup 𝐷 is called
a strip if 𝐷 ≠ 1, and for each 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟, either 𝜋𝑖 (𝐷) = 1 or 𝐷 ∩ Ker(𝜋𝑖 ) = 1. Note that 𝐷 ∩ Ker(𝜋𝑖 ) = 1 if
and only if the restriction 𝜋𝑖 | 𝐷 of 𝜋𝑖 to 𝐷 is an isomorphism from 𝐷 to 𝜋𝑖 (𝐷). The support of a strip
is the set {𝑖 | 𝜋𝑖 (𝐷) ≠ 1}, and two strips are said to be disjoint if their supports are disjoint. A strip
8

𝐷 is full if 𝜋𝑖 (𝐷) = 𝑇𝑖 for all 𝑖 in the support of 𝐷. A subgroup 𝐻 of a group 𝐺 with a given direct
decomposition 𝐺 = 𝑇1 × 𝑇2 × · · · × 𝑇𝑟 is called a subdirect subgroup if 𝜋𝑖 (𝐻) = 𝑇𝑖 for each 𝑖 = 1, . . . , 𝑟.
Lemma 2.9. Let 𝐺 be as in Hypothesis 2.7, and such that each 𝑇𝑖 admits no nontrivial factorisation. If
𝐺 = 𝐻𝐾 is a nontrivial factorisation, then Core𝐺 (𝐻) ≠ 1 and Core𝐺 (𝐾) ≠ 1.
Proof. Suppose that 𝐺 = 𝐻𝐾 with proper subgroups 𝐻, 𝐾, and suppose that one of 𝐻, 𝐾 is core-free,
say Core𝐺 (𝐻) = 1. By the assumption on the 𝑇𝑖 , we must have 𝑟 ≥ 2. Let 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟. If 𝜋𝑖 (𝐻) = 𝑇𝑖 , then 𝑇𝑖
is a quotient of 𝐻, and hence by Lemma 2.8, 𝐻 contains 𝑇b𝑖 , contradicting the fact that Core𝐺 (𝐻) = 1.
Thus 𝜋𝑖 (𝐻) < 𝑇𝑖 . Now the factorisation 𝐺 = 𝐻𝐾 implies that 𝑇𝑖 = 𝜋𝑖 (𝐻)𝜋𝑖 (𝐾), and since 𝜋𝑖 (𝐻) < 𝑇𝑖 ,
and by assumption the group 𝑇𝑖 has no nontrivial factorisation, it follows that 𝜋𝑖 (𝐾) = 𝑇𝑖 . Thus 𝐾 is a
subdirect subgroup of 𝐺 = 𝑇1 × 𝑇2 × · · · × 𝑇𝑟 . By ‘Scott’s Lemma’ [27, Theorem 4.16(iii)], 𝐾 is a direct
product of pairwise disjoint full strips of 𝐺. Since 𝐾 is a proper subgroup of 𝐺, at least one of these
strips, say 𝐷, has support of size greater than 1. Let 𝑖, 𝑗 be distinct elements of the support of 𝐷. By
the definition of a strip, 𝐷 ∩ Ker(𝜋𝑖 ) = 1 and 𝐷 ∩ Ker(𝜋 𝑗 ) = 1, and as we noted above, this implies
that 𝐷  𝜋𝑖 (𝐷) = 𝑇𝑖 and 𝐷  𝜋 𝑗 (𝐷) = 𝑇 𝑗 . This implies that 𝑇𝑖 is a section of 𝑇 𝑗 , and hence also of
Î
   𝑘≠𝑖 𝑇𝑘 , contradicting Hypothesis 2.7.                                                               


   The next proposition assists us to decide which groups satisfying Hypothesis 2.7 are in fact totally
2-closed by reducing consideration to transitive (not necessarily faithful) permutation representations.
Proposition 2.10. Let 𝐺 be as in Hypothesis 2.7. Then 𝐺 is totally 2-closed if and only if, the following
two conditions hold.
(a) For 𝑖 = 1, . . . , 𝑟, the group 𝑇𝑖 admits no nontrivial factorisation; and
(b) for each permutation representation 𝜑 : 𝐺 → Sym(Ω) with |Ω| > 1 and 𝜑(𝐺) transitive, we have
    𝜑(𝐺) (2),Ω = 𝜑(𝐺).
Proof. Suppose first that 𝐺 is totally 2-closed. Then condition (a) holds by Theorem 2.5. Let 𝜑 :
𝐺 → Sym(Ω) with |Ω| > 1 and 𝜑(𝐺) transitive. By [27, Theorem 4.16(iv)], there is a proper
                                                  Î                                             Î
subset 𝐼 ⊆ {1, . . . , 𝑟 } such that Ker(𝜑) = 𝑖 ∈𝐼 𝑇b𝑖 , and so 𝜑(𝐺)  𝐺 0 where 𝐺 0 := 𝑗 ∈𝐽 𝑇b𝑗 with
𝐽 = {1, . . . , 𝑟 } \ 𝐼. Hence 𝐺 = Ker(𝜑) × 𝐺 0 and by Lemma 2.2, 𝐺 0 is totally 2-closed, whence
𝜑(𝐺) (2),Ω = 𝜑(𝐺) holds. Thus condition (b) holds also.
    Conversely suppose that conditions (a) and (b) hold for 𝐺. In particular each nontrivial transitive
permutation representation of 𝐺 is 2-closed. In order to prove that 𝐺 is totally 2-closed we must therefore
show that each faithful intransitive permutation representation of 𝐺 is also 2-closed. Suppose that this
is not true. Then we may suppose that 𝐺 ≤ Sym(Ω) with orbits Ω1 , . . . , Ω𝑚 and 𝑚 ≥ 2, such that
𝑋 := 𝐺 (2) ,Ω contains 𝐺 as a proper subgroup. Suppose moreover that 𝑚 is minimal, over all faithful non-
2-closed intransitive representations of all groups 𝐺 satisfying Hypothesis 2.7 and satisfying conditions
(a) and (b).
    For each 𝑖 ≤ 𝑚, let 𝐺 𝑖 = 𝐺 Ω𝑖 , the transitive permutation group on Ω𝑖 induced by 𝐺. It follows
from the minimality of 𝑚 that each of the |Ω𝑖 | ≥ 2 and hence each of the 𝐺 𝑖 is a nontrivial transitive
permutation representation of 𝐺. Thus by condition (b), each 𝐺 𝑖 is 2-closed, that is 𝐺 𝑖(2),Ω𝑖 = 𝐺 𝑖 . Let
Δ = ∪𝑖=2𝑚 Ω , and let 𝑌 = 𝐺 Δ , the permutation group on Δ induced by 𝐺. Then, arguing as in the first
             𝑖       Î                  Î
paragraph, 𝐺 1  𝑖 ∈𝐼 𝑇𝑖 and 𝑌  𝑗 ∈𝐽 𝑇 𝑗 for some non-empty subsets 𝐼, 𝐽 ⊆ {1, . . . , 𝑟 }, and since 𝐺
is faithful on Ω, 𝐼 ∪ 𝐽 = {1, . . . , 𝑟 }. Further, Hypothesis 2.7 holds for 𝑌 , as does condition (a) since it

by Theorem 2.4, 𝑋 = 𝐺 (2),Ω ≤ 𝐺 1(2),Ω1 × 𝑌 (2),Δ = 𝐺 1 × 𝑌  ( 𝑖 ∈𝐼 𝑇𝑖 ) × ( 𝑗 ∈𝐽 𝑇 𝑗 ). If 𝐼 ∩ 𝐽 = ∅, then

 𝛼𝑖 = 𝛿𝑖 = 2. Such an 𝑖 must lie in 𝐼 ∩ 𝐽, and without loss of generality, we may assume that 𝑖 = 1 so
1 ∈ 𝐼 ∩ 𝐽. Hence 𝑇b1 acts nontrivially on both Ω1 and Δ, and 𝑋 contains 𝑇b1Ω1 × 𝑇b1Δ  𝑇12 . Again, without

    Let 𝐾 = 𝑗≠1 𝑇b𝑗 , so that 𝐺 = 𝑇b1 × 𝐾. If 𝐾 is transitive on Ω1 then 𝐺 = 𝐾𝐺 𝜔 , where 𝜔 ∈ Ω1 , and
𝐺 𝜔 /(𝐾 ∩ 𝐺 𝜔 )  𝐺 𝜔 𝐾/𝐾 = 𝐺/𝐾  𝑇1 . Then, by Lemma 2.8, 𝑇b1 ≤ 𝐺 𝜔 , which implies that 𝑇b1 fixes
Ω1 pointwise, a contradiction. Hence 𝐾 is intransitive on Ω1 , and the same argument shows that 𝐾 is
also intransitive on Ω2 . Let Σ𝑖 denote the set of 𝐾-orbits in Ω𝑖 , for 𝑖 = 1, 2. Since 𝐺 = 𝑇b1 × 𝐾, the group
𝑇b1 is transitive on both Σ1 and Σ2 , and since 𝑋 contains 𝑇b1Ω1 × 𝑇b1Δ  𝑇12 , it follows that 𝑋 is transitive on
Σ1 × Σ2 in product action, that is, 𝑥 : (𝜎1 , 𝜎2 ) → (𝜎1𝑥 , 𝜎2𝑥 ) for 𝜎1 ∈ Σ1 , 𝜎2 ∈ Σ2 , 𝑥 ∈ 𝑋.
    We claim that the subgroup 𝑇b1 is also transitive on Σ1 × Σ2 . Choose (𝜎1 , 𝜎2 ) ∈ Σ1 × Σ2 , and let
 𝛽1 ∈ 𝜎1 , 𝛽2 ∈ 𝜎2 . Since 𝑋 = 𝐺 (2),Ω , the 𝐺-orbit (𝛽1 , 𝛽2 ) 𝐺 is equal to the 𝑋-orbit (𝛽1 , 𝛽2 ) 𝑋 . First we
note that, since 𝑋 is transitive on Σ1 × Σ2 , the stabiliser 𝑋 𝜎1 is transitive on Σ2 . Now 𝜎1 is a 𝐾-orbit
in Ω1 and so 𝑋 𝜎1 = 𝐾 𝑋𝛽1 . It follows that the 𝑋𝛽1 -orbit containing 𝛽2 must contain points from each
element of Σ2 . On the other hand, (𝛽1 , 𝛽2 ) 𝐺 = (𝛽1 , 𝛽2 ) 𝑋 implies that the 𝑋𝛽1 -orbit containing 𝛽2 is the
same as the 𝐺 𝛽1 -orbit containing 𝛽2 , and therefore this 𝐺 𝛽1 -orbit contains points from each element of
Σ2 , and hence 𝐺 𝛽1 is transitive on Σ2 . Since 𝐺 𝛽1 < 𝐺 𝜎1 , also 𝐺 𝜎1 is transitive on Σ2 and hence 𝐺 is
transitive on Σ1 × Σ2 . Since 𝐺 = 𝑇b1 × 𝐾 and 𝐾 acts trivially on Σ1 × Σ2 , we conclude that 𝑇b1 is transitive
on Σ1 × Σ2 , proving the claim.
    Finally, for 𝑖 = 1, 2, let 𝑆𝑖 = (𝑇b1 ) 𝜎𝑖 . Then since 𝑇b1 is transitive on Σ1 × Σ2 , 𝑆1 is transitive on Σ2 and
hence 𝑇b1 = 𝑆1 𝑆2 , a nontrivial factorisation, which is a contradiction to condition (a).                         

   For proving that a simple group is totally 2-closed, the following immediate corollary of
Proposition 2.10 gives a reduction to consideration of transitive actions.
Corollary 2.11. Let 𝑇 be a finite nonabelian simple group. Then 𝑇 is totally 2-closed if and only if 𝑇
admits no nontrivial factorisations and, for each permutation representation 𝜑 : 𝐺 → Sym(Ω) with
|Ω| > 1 and 𝜑(𝐺) transitive, we have 𝜑(𝐺) (2),Ω = 𝜑(𝐺).


2.3. Simple groups, factorisations, and rank
In Proposition 2.12, we consider the totally 2-closed simple groups 𝐺 in the light of Corollary 2.11,
applying the classification of their maximal factorisations [24], and considering their low rank permu-
tation representations. For example, if a simple group 𝐺 is 2-transitive on Ω then 𝐺 (2),Ω = Sym(Ω), by
[33, Theorem 5.11], and hence 𝐺 is not totally 2-closed.
    We denote the socle of 𝐺 by soc(𝐺), that is, the product of the minimal normal subgroups of 𝐺.
We denote the set of right cosets of a subgroup 𝐻 in 𝐺 by [𝐺 : 𝐻] = {𝐻𝑔 | 𝑔 ∈ 𝐺}, and note that 𝐺
induces by right multiplication a transitive action on [𝐺 : 𝐻] with kernel Core𝐺 (𝐾), and such that 𝐻
is the stabiliser of the ‘point’ 𝐻.
Proposition 2.12. Let 𝐺 be a finite nonabelian simple group that is totally 2-closed. Then one of the
following is true.
(a) 𝐺 lies in one of the following infinite families: 3 𝐷 4 (𝑞), 𝐸 6 (𝑞), 2 𝐸 6 (𝑞), 𝐸 7 (𝑞), 𝐸 8 (𝑞), 𝐹4 (𝑞) (with
    𝑞 odd), 2 𝐹4 (𝑞) 0 (with 𝑞 = 22𝑐+1 ); or
(b) 𝐺 is one of J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly, ON, Co2 , Fi23 , HN, Th, B, M.
10

Proof. By Corollary 2.11, 𝐺 admits no nontrivial factorisation. We treat the simple groups by families.
First, if 𝐺 = 𝐴𝑛 , then 𝐺 is 2-transitive of degree 𝑛 and so, as we observed above, 𝐺 is not totally
2-closed, a contradiction. Thus 𝐺  𝐴𝑛 .
   If 𝐺 is a totally 2-closed sporadic simple group, then this implies, by [24, Theorem C], that either
                                          0
𝐺 is as in part (b), or 𝐺 ∈ {Co3 , McL, Fi24 }. Now 𝐺 ≠ Co3 since Co3 has a 2-transitive representation
                                                                           0
of degree 276 (see, for example [13, Section 7.7]). If 𝐺 is McL or Fi24      , then 𝐴 = Aut(𝐺) = 𝐺.2,
and the coset action of 𝐴 on the set Ω = [ 𝐴 : 𝐻] of right cosets of 𝐻 = 𝑃𝑆𝑈 (4, 3) : 23 or Fi23 × 2,
respectively, is such that both 𝐴 and 𝐺 have rank 3 (see [11, Pages 100, 207]). It follows that 𝐴 ≤ 𝐺 (2),Ω
by Theorem 2.4, so that 𝐺 ≠ 𝐺 (2),Ω , which is a contradiction.
   Thus we may assume that 𝐺 is a totally 2-closed simple group of Lie type. Suppose first that 𝐺
is a classical simple group. Then 𝐺 ≠ PSL𝑛 (𝑞) or PSU3 (𝑞) since these groups have a 2-transitive
representation, (see, for example [13, Section 7.7]). Among the other simple classical groups, the only
ones which have no nontrivial factorisations are, by [24, Theorem A],
• 𝐺 = PSU𝑛 (𝑞) with 𝑛 odd, 𝑛 ≥ 5, and (𝑛, 𝑞) ≠ (9, 2); and
• 𝐺 = PΩ−2𝑚 (𝑞) with 𝑚 even, 𝑚 ≥ 4, 𝑞 ≠ 2, 4.
For 𝐺 one of these groups, it follows from [21, Theorem 1.1 and Table IV on page 45], that 𝐺 has a
rank 3 action on the set Ω of totally singular (or isotropic) 1-spaces of the natural module, of degree
                           (𝑞 𝑛 +1) (𝑞 𝑛−1 −1)        (𝑞 𝑚 +1) (𝑞 𝑚−1 −1)
                                  𝑞 2 −1
                                                 or          𝑞−1          ,   respectively.

However the group 𝐴 = PΓU𝑛 (𝑞) or PΓO−2𝑚 (𝑞), respectively, contains 𝐺 as a proper subgroup (see [24,
Table 2.1]), and also acts on Ω with rank 3. Hence 𝐴 ≤ 𝐺 (2),Ω by Theorem 2.4, and so 𝐺 ≠ 𝐺 (2),Ω ,
which is a contradiction.
   Finally suppose that 𝐺 is an exceptional simple group of Lie type. Then 𝐺 ≠ Sz(𝑞) or Ree(𝑞)
since each of these groups has a 2-transitive representation, (see, for example [13, Section 7.7]).
Among the other exceptional simple groups of Lie type, the only ones which do not appear in part
(a), and which have no nontrivial factorisations are, by [24, Theorem B], the groups 𝐺 = 𝐺 2 (𝑞) (with
𝑞 > 2, 𝑞 ≠ 4, 3𝑐 ). However it follows from [23, Theorem 1], that such a group 𝐺 has a primitive
permutation representation on a set Ω of size 𝑞 3 (𝑞 3 − 1)/2 such that 𝐺 (2),Ω has socle Ω7 (𝑞), so
𝐺 ≠ 𝐺 (2),Ω , which is a contradiction.                                                              
   To summarise this section, we have proved that to determine the finite totally 2-closed groups 𝐺
with 𝐹 (𝐺) = 1, we need only consider the groups 𝐺 which are a direct product of a subset of the
nonabelian finite simple groups listed in Proposition 2.12. Furthermore, the direct factors must satisfy
the conditions listed in Theorem 2.5. Finally, by Corollary 2.11, such a group is totally 2-closed if and
only if it is 2-closed in each of its (not necessarily faithful) transitive permutation representations. We
investigate the transitive representations of these, and other more general, groups in Section 3.


3. Tools for analysing imprimitive actions
In this section we introduce some group theoretic and combinatorial tools for studying 2-closures of
transitive group actions.
    Let Ω be a finite set, and let 𝐺 be a subgroup of Sym(Ω). A partition Σ of Ω is 𝐺-invariant if each
element of 𝐺 permutes the parts of Σ among themselves. A partition is said to be trivial either if it
consists of a single part, namely Ω, or if each of its parts consists of a single point. All other partitions
are nontrivial. Each transitive permutation group 𝐺 leaves invariant these two trivial partitions, and 𝐺
is called primitive if the only 𝐺-invariant partitions are the two trivial partitions; otherwise 𝐺 is said to
be imprimitive.
    Higman’s landmark result [17, (1.12)] in this area (which we will use) is that a finite transitive
permutation group 𝐺 is primitive if and only if all the nondiagonal 𝐺-orbital digraphs are connected.
                                                                                                            11

   For a more general example of inequality in part (a), suppose that 𝐺 is a finite transitive permutation
group on a set Σ such that 𝐺 is not 2-closed, that is, 𝐺 (2),Σ ≠ 𝐺. Let 𝐵 ∈ Σ and let 𝐻 = 𝐺 𝐵 , so that
we may identify Σ with [𝐺 : 𝐻] = {𝐻𝑔 | 𝑔 ∈ 𝐺} and 𝐺 acts by right multiplication. Consider the

   By Theorem 2.5 and Proposition 2.10, the classification of finite totally 2-closed groups with trivial
Fitting subgroup is reduced to the study of nontrivial transitive permutation representations of groups 𝐺
satisfying Hypothesis 2.7 such that the simple direct factors 𝑇𝑖 of 𝐺 admit no nontrivial factorisations.
Although it would be desirable to reduce further to primitive actions, this seems difficult (and perhaps
not possible). Loosely speaking, our goal in this section is to prove that if such groups 𝐺 are 2-closed
in all of their primitive permutation representations, then it is ‘likely’ that they are totally 2-closed.
   More precisely, we will explicitly construct the 2-closure of a finite group 𝐺 acting imprimitively on
a set Ω, with the property that its induced action on a nontrivial 𝐺-invariant partition Σ of Ω is faithful
and 2-closed. To state our results, we require some notation.

  closed. We will see that this seems like quite an unusual phenomenon. We begin with a straightforward
  lemma from representation theory.
  Lemma 3.4. Let 𝐺, Σ, 𝑀, 𝑠 be as in Notation 3.3, let 𝑝 be a prime, and let

                                             𝑉 = {(𝑦 1 , . . . , 𝑦 𝑠 ) : 𝑦 𝑖 ∈ F 𝑝 },
                                                                                                               13

be the permutation module for 𝐺 on Σ over the field F 𝑝 . Suppose that 𝑀 is not contained in a proper
normal subgroup of 𝐺. Then the only 1-dimensional F 𝑝 [𝐺]-submodule of 𝑉 is the trivial submodule
{(𝑦, . . . , 𝑦) : 𝑦 ∈ F 𝑝 }.
Proof. Let 𝑈 be a 1-dimensional F 𝑝 [𝐺]-submodule of 𝑉. Then there is an injective homomorphism
from 𝑈 to 𝑉, that is, the F 𝑝 -space Hom𝐺 (𝑈, 𝑉) of F 𝑝 [𝐺]-homomorphisms from 𝑈 to 𝑉 is non-zero.
Since 𝑉 is the induced module (1 𝑀 ) ↑𝐺 , where 1 𝑀 denotes the trivial F 𝑝 [𝑀]-module, it follows from
Frobenius reciprocity [4, Proposition 3.3.1] that Hom 𝑀 (𝑈 ↓ 𝑀 , 1 𝑀 ) is also non-zero. Thus 𝑈 has a non-
zero quotient F 𝑝 [𝑀]-module acted upon trivially by 𝑀, and since dim(𝑈) = 1, it follows that 𝑀 acts
trivially on 𝑈. Thus 𝑀 is contained in the kernel of the action of 𝐺 on 𝑈. Since 𝑀 is not contained in
a proper normal subgroup of 𝐺, we deduce that 𝐺 acts trivially on 𝑈. It is then an elementary exercise
to prove that {(𝑦, . . . , 𝑦) : 𝑦 ∈ F 𝑝 } is the only non-zero trivial F 𝑝 [𝐺]-submodule of 𝑉. This completes
the proof.                                                                                                 

  The next lemma is a crucial tool in our treatment of imprimitive groups 𝐺 as in Notation 3.3. It
makes use of Lemma 3.1. Recall in particular the definition of base groups in Notation 3.3.7.
Lemma 3.5. Let 𝐺, Ω, Σ, Δ, 𝐿, 𝑅, 𝑀, 𝑀𝑖 , 𝑠, 𝜌𝑖, 𝑗 be as in Notation 3.3, let 𝑋 := 𝐺 (2),Ω , and 𝑌 := 𝑋ΔΔ .
Suppose that 𝐺 ≠ 𝑋 but 𝐿 = 𝐿 (2),Σ . Then the following hold.
  1. 𝑋 ≤ 𝑌 o 𝐿 = 𝐵𝑌 o 𝐿, and 𝑅 ≤ 𝑌 ≤ 𝑅 (2),Δ ;
  2. 𝑋 = 𝑁 o 𝐺, where 𝑁 = 𝐵𝑌 ∩ 𝑋 > 1, and 𝑁 consists precisely of all the elements (𝑦 1 , . . . , 𝑦 𝑠 ) ∈ 𝐵𝑌
     such that

     First we derive a useful consequence of Lemma 3.5.
Lemma 3.6. Let 𝐺, Ω, Σ, 𝑀, 𝑅, 𝐿, Δ, etc. be as in Notation 3.3, and let 𝑋 := 𝐺 (2),Ω and 𝑌 = 𝑋ΔΔ .
Suppose also that 𝐺 ≠ 𝑋, that 𝐿 = 𝐿 (2),Σ , that 𝑝 := |𝑅| is prime, and that 𝑀 is not contained in a
proper normal subgroup of 𝐺. Let 𝐽 consist of representative elements 𝑗 ∈ {2, 3, . . . , 𝑠}, where 𝑠 = |Σ|,
such that
                                         (𝜌1, 𝑗 (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 )) Δ1 ×Δ 𝑗  𝐶 𝑝 ,

and such that, for distinct 𝑗, 𝑗 0 ∈ 𝐽, the parts Δ 𝑗 , Δ 𝑗 0 ∈ Σ lie in distinct 𝑀-orbits in Σ \ {Δ}. If 𝑗 ∈𝐽 |𝑀 :
                                                                                                         Í
𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 | ≥ 𝑠/2, then the subgroup 𝑁 from Lemma 3.5 is the diagonal subgroup {(𝑥, . . . , 𝑥) : 𝑥 ∈ 𝑅} of
𝐵 𝑅 = 𝑅 𝑠  𝐶 𝑠𝑝 .
Proof. Write the cyclic group 𝑅  𝐶 𝑝 additively, and let 𝑁 be the normal subgroup of 𝑋 from
Lemma 3.5. By Lemma 3.5 parts (b) and (c), 𝑋 = 𝑁 o 𝐺, 𝑁 is an elementary abelian 𝑝-subgroup of
𝐵𝑌 = 𝐵 𝑅 = 𝑅 𝑠 = 𝐶 𝑠𝑝 , and by Notation 3.3.10, 𝐺  𝐺 Σ = 𝐿. Thus 𝐵 𝑅 may be viewed as the permutation
module 𝑉 for the 𝐺-action on Σ over the field F 𝑝 , and 𝑁 as a non-zero 𝐺-submodule. Note that 𝑉 is the
induced module 1↑𝐺     𝑀 , and by assumption 𝑀 is not contained in a proper normal subgroup of 𝐺. Hence,
by Lemma 3.4, it suffices to prove that |𝑁 | = 𝑝.
    Assume to the contrary that |𝑁 | ≥ 𝑝 2 . Then there exists a nontrivial element 𝑦 = (𝑦 1 , . . . , 𝑦 𝑠 ) ∈ 𝑁
with the property that 𝑦 𝑒 = 0 for some 𝑒 ≤ 𝑠. Since 𝐺 Σ is transitive, we may assume, without loss of
generality, that 𝑦 1 = 1. Let O be the union of those 𝑀-orbits in Σ containing some Δ 𝑗 with 𝑗 ∈ 𝐽. Since
                                                                    Í
𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 is the setwise stabiliser in 𝑀 of Δ 𝑗 , the set O has length 𝑗 ∈𝐽 |𝑀 : 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 | ≥ 𝑠/2. By Lemma
3.5(c) and the definition of 𝐽, 𝜌1,𝑖 (𝑁) is a full diagonal subgroup of 𝑅 × 𝑅  𝐶 2𝑝 , for all 𝑖 ∈ O. Thus,
there exist automorphisms 𝜃 𝑖 ∈ Aut(𝑅) for 𝑖 ∈ O such that, if 𝑧 = (𝑧1 , . . . , 𝑧 𝑠 ) ∈ 𝑁, then 𝑧𝑖 = 𝑧1𝜃𝑖 for all
𝑖 ∈ O.
    Since 𝑦 1 ≠ 0, the number of nonzero entries in 𝑦 is therefore at least 1 + |O| > 𝑠/2, that is, strictly
more than half the entries of 𝑦 are non-zero. On the other hand, since 𝑦 also contains zero entries, and
𝐺 Σ is transitive, it follows that, for some 𝑔 ∈ 𝐺, the conjugate 𝑦 𝑔 has first entry (𝑦 𝑔 )1 = 0. Then, since
𝑦 𝑔 ∈ 𝑁, it follows from the previous paragraph that (𝑦 𝑔 )𝑖 = 0 for all 𝑖 ∈ O, that is, strictly more than
half the entries of 𝑦 𝑔 are zero. However, since 𝑦 𝑔 is conjugate to 𝑦, this implies that strictly more than
half the entries of 𝑦 are zero. This is a contradiction. Hence |𝑁 | = 𝑝 and the result follows.                 

  𝑗 ∈𝐽 |𝑀 : 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 | > 𝑠/2.

    Our next result is useful for reducing consideration of all transitive actions of a given group to the
consideration of primitive ones. We summarise some concepts used in the statement and proof: For a
finite group 𝐸 and a positive integer 𝑓 , a subgroup 𝐷 ≤ 𝐸 𝑓 is called a diagonal subgroup if 𝐷 is of the
form 𝐷 = {(𝑒, 𝑒 𝜃2 , . . . , 𝑒 𝜃 𝑓 ) : 𝑒 ∈ 𝐹} for some subgroup 𝐹 of 𝐸 and automorphisms 𝜃 𝑖 of 𝐹; 𝐷 is called
a full diagonal subgroup if 𝐹 = 𝐸. If 𝑓 = 2 and 𝐷 is a subdirect subgroup of 𝐸 1 × 𝐸 2 , for finite groups
𝐸 1 , 𝐸 2 , then by [27, Theorem 4.8] (sometimes called ‘Goursat’s Lemma’), 𝐾𝑖 := 𝐷 ∩ Ker(𝜋3−𝑖 )  𝐸 𝑖
for 𝑖 = 1, 2, and there is a well defined homomorphism 𝜑 𝐷 : 𝐸 1 → 𝐸 2 /𝐾2 with kernel 𝐾1 such that
𝐷 = {(𝑒 1 , 𝑒 2 ) : 𝑒 1 ∈ 𝐸 1 , 𝑒 2 ∈ 𝜑 𝐷 (𝑒 1 )}. In particular 𝐷 contains 𝐾1 × 𝐾2 as a normal subgroup and
𝐷/(𝐾1 × 𝐾2 )  𝐸 1 /𝐾1  𝐸 2 /𝐾2 ; and moreover 𝐷 is a full diagonal subgroup if and only if 𝐾1 × 𝐾2 = 1.
    Finally, we will write Ω (2) for the set of ordered pairs of distinct points of a set Ω, and, for a finite
group 𝑌 , we will write S(𝑌 ) for the intersection of all nontrivial subnormal subgroups of 𝑌 . Note that
S(𝑌 ) is nontrivial only if 𝑌 has a unique minimal normal subgroup, which is simple.
Proposition 3.8. Let 𝐺, Ω, Σ, 𝑀, 𝑅, 𝐿, Δ, 𝑠, 𝜌𝑖, 𝑗 , etc. be as in Notation 3.3, and let 𝑋 := 𝐺 (2),Ω and
𝑌 = 𝑋ΔΔ . Suppose that 𝐺 ≠ 𝑋 but 𝐿 = 𝐿 (2) ,Σ .
(a) Then 𝑋 = 𝑁 o 𝐺 with 𝑁 = 𝑋 ∩ 𝐵𝑌 ≠ 1 as in Lemma 3.5, and 𝑁 is a subdirect subgroup of a base
    group 𝐵 𝐴 = 𝐴𝑠 for some 𝐴  𝑌 (see Notation 3.3.7).

           𝑁 contains the base group 𝐵 S (𝑌 ) , or 𝑌 has a unique minimal normal subgroup which is
           isomorphic to 𝐶 𝑝 , for some prime 𝑝.

    holds, then 𝑌 = 𝑅 and 𝑁 is the diagonal subgroup {(𝑥, . . . , 𝑥) : 𝑥 ∈ 𝑅} of 𝐵 𝑅 = 𝑅 𝑠  𝐶 𝑠𝑝 .
Proof. (a) Since 𝑁 is a subgroup of the base group 𝐵𝑌 of 𝑌 o 𝐿 and 𝑁 is normalised by 𝑋, it follows
that 𝑁 is a subdirect subgroup of a base subgroup 𝐵 𝐴 = 𝐴𝑠 for some subgroup 𝐴  𝑌 , as in part (a).
Note that each element 𝑦 ∈ 𝑌 acting by conjugation induces an automorphism of 𝐴, and we denote this
automorphism by 𝜄(𝑦). For the rest of the proof assume that 𝑀 is maximal in 𝐺, or equivalently, 𝐿 = 𝐺 Σ
is primitive. This means, by Higman’s theorem [17, (1.12)] discussed above, that every nondiagonal
𝐿-orbital digraph is connected.

with 𝑦 ∈ 𝐵𝑌 , 𝜎 ∈ 𝐿 and ( 𝑗, 𝑗 0) = (𝑖, 𝑖 0) 𝜎 , and if 𝑧 ∈ 𝑁 such that 𝜌𝑖,𝑖0 (𝑧) = (𝑥, 𝑥 𝜃 ), then 𝑧 𝑔 ∈ 𝑁 (since
𝐺 normalises 𝑁) and

               𝜌 𝑗, 𝑗 0 (𝑧 𝑔 ) = (𝑥 𝑦𝑖 , (𝑥 𝜃 ) 𝑦𝑖0 ) = (𝑢, 𝑢 𝜃 ) where 𝑢 = 𝑥 𝑦𝑖 and 𝜃 0 = 𝜄(𝑦 −1

some 𝜃 ∈ Aut( 𝐴), and by induction, 𝜌1,𝑘 (𝑁) = {(𝑥, 𝑥 𝜃 ) : 𝑥 ∈ 𝐴} for some 𝜃 0 ∈ Aut( 𝐴), and it follows

that 𝜌1, 𝑗 (𝑁) = {(𝑥, 𝑥 ) : 𝑥 ∈ 𝐴}. Thus the claim is proved by induction. It now follows that there exist
                          𝜃 𝜃

automorphisms 𝜃 2 , . . . , 𝜃 𝑠 ∈ Aut( 𝐴) such that 𝑁 = {(𝑥, 𝑥 𝜃2 , . . . , 𝑥 𝜃𝑠 ) : 𝑥 ∈ 𝐴} and (b)(i) holds.
    Thus we may assume that, for all distinct 𝑖, 𝑗, the subdirect subgroup 𝜌𝑖, 𝑗 (𝑁) of 𝐴 × 𝐴 is not a full
diagonal subgroup. This is the first assertion of part (b)(ii). As mentioned before the statement of the
proposition, S(𝑌 ) is trivial unless 𝑌 has a unique minimal normal subgroup, which is simple. Thus, to
complete the proof of (b)(ii), we may assume that 𝑌 is almost simple with simple socle S(𝑌 ). Hence
also 𝐴 is almost simple with socle S(𝑌 ). If S(𝑌 ) = 𝐶 𝑝 , for some prime 𝑝, then part (b)(ii) holds, so we
may assume further that S(𝑌 ) is a nonabelian simple group. Let 𝑁1 := 𝑋 ∩ 𝐵 S (𝑌 ) = 𝑁 ∩ 𝐵 S (𝑌 ) . Then
𝑁1 is normalised by 𝑋, and as in the proof of part (a), 𝑁1 is a subdirect subgroup of 𝐵 𝐴1 = 𝐴1𝑠 for some
𝐴1  𝑌 . By the definition of 𝑁1 , 𝐴1 ⊆ S(𝑌 ), so either 𝐴1 = 1 or 𝐴1 = S(𝑌 ). If 𝐴1 = 1 then 𝑁1 = 1, and
so the insoluble group 𝑁  𝑁/𝑁1 is isomorphic to a subgroup of 𝐵 𝐴/𝐵 S (𝑌 ) ≤ Out(S(𝑌 )) 𝑠 , which by
the ‘Schreier Conjecture’ is soluble, a contradiction. Thus 𝐴1 = S(𝑌 ). Then for distinct 𝑖, 𝑗, the image
𝜌𝑖, 𝑗 (𝑁1 ) = 𝐴1 × 𝐴1 (since 𝜌𝑖, 𝑗 (𝑁) is not a diagonal subgroup of 𝐴 × 𝐴). Further, the subdirect subgroup
𝑁1 of 𝐵 𝐴1 is, by ‘Scott’s Lemma’ [27, Theorem 4.16(iii)], a direct product of pairwise disjoint full strips
of 𝐵 𝐴1 ; and by our observation about the 𝜌𝑖, 𝑗 (𝑁1 ) it follows that each of the strips has support of size
1, that is, it is one of the simple direct factors of 𝐵 𝐴1 . Thus in this case 𝑁1 = 𝐵 𝐴1 , and part (b)(ii) holds.
    (c) Finally suppose that 𝑀 is maximal but not normal in 𝐺, that |𝑅| = 𝑝 is prime, and (a)(i) holds.
Then 𝑌 = 𝑅 since 𝑅 ≤ 𝑌 ≤ 𝑅 (2),Δ = 𝑅. Also 𝑀 is not contained in a proper normal subgroup of 𝐺, and
so the stated assertion follows from Lemma 3.4.                                                                    

     The next result is needed to prove some important consequences of Proposition 3.8.
Lemma 3.9. For 𝑖 = 1, 2, let Δ𝑖 be a finite set and 𝐸 𝑖 a transitive subgroup of Sym(Δ𝑖 ). Let Ω = Δ1 × Δ2 ,
and consider the product action of 𝐸 1 ×𝐸 2 on Ω. Suppose that 𝐾, a finite group, acts on Δ𝑖 with 𝐾 Δ𝑖 ≤ 𝐸 𝑖 ,
for each 𝑖, such that the induced 𝐾-action on Ω is faithful. Let Γ𝑖 be the set of 𝐾-orbits in Δ𝑖 , and let 𝐹𝑖
be the (largest) subgroup of 𝐸 𝑖 fixing setwise each 𝐾-orbit in Γ𝑖 . Then

                                        (𝐸 1 × 𝐸 2 ) ∩ 𝐾 (1),Ω ≤ 𝐹1 × 𝐹2 ,

and moreover, if 𝐾 Δ𝑖 = 𝐹𝑖 , for 𝑖 = 1, 2, then 𝐾 (1),Ω is a subdirect subgroup of 𝐹𝑖 × 𝐹2 .
Proof. Write Γ1 := {Λ1 , . . . , Λ𝑟 } and Γ2 := {Π1 , . . . , Π𝑠 }. Then the orbits of 𝐾 Δ1 ×𝐾 Δ2 in its action on Ω
are the sets Λ𝑖 ×Π 𝑗 , for 1 ≤ 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟, 1 ≤ 𝑗 ≤ 𝑠. Since the 1-closure of a permutation group is the stabiliser of
each of its orbits in the associated symmetric group, it follows that (𝐸 1 ×𝐸 2 )∩(𝐾 Δ1 ×𝐾 Δ2 ) (1),Ω = 𝐹1 ×𝐹2 .
Then since 𝐾 Ω ≤ (𝐾 Δ1 × 𝐾 Δ2 ) Ω , we deduce that (𝐸 1 × 𝐸 2 ) ∩ 𝐾 (1),Ω ≤ 𝐹1 × 𝐹2 . Finally, if 𝐾 Δ𝑖 = 𝐹𝑖 , for
𝑖 = 1, 2, then clearly (𝐸 1 × 𝐸 2 ) ∩ 𝐾 (1),Ω is a subdirect subgroup of 𝐹1 × 𝐹2 .                                 

includes the assumption that 𝐺  𝐺 Σ = 𝐿. The base size of a fnite transitive permutation group 𝐿 is the
minimum size of a subset 𝑆 of points such that ∩𝑖 ∈𝑆 𝐿 𝑖 = 1.

and suppose that 𝐿 = 𝐿 (2),Σ .

    𝐴  𝑌 , and all 𝐴-orbits in Δ have the same length, say 𝑎, where 𝑎 divides |𝐿 𝑖 𝑗 | for all distinct
    𝑖, 𝑗 ≤ 𝑠 (where 𝐿 𝑖 𝑗 is the stabiliser in 𝐿 of Δ𝑖 and Δ 𝑗 ).

Δ𝑖 . Moreover, since 𝐺 is transitive on Σ, we may assume that 𝑖 = 1. By Lemma 3.5(c), there exists

4. Total 2-closure of sporadic simple groups
A major objective for the remainder of the paper is to determine precisely which sporadic simple groups
are totally 2-closed. In the next few sections we will complete the proof that Theorem 1.1 holds if 𝑇 is a
sporadic simple group. In Proposition 2.12(b), we reduced the list of possible candidates to just eleven
sporadic groups. In this section we will eliminate the groups 𝑂𝑁, Co2 , Fi23 , HN, B, and we will show
that five of the remaining six groups, namely J1 , J3 , Ly, Th, M, are totally 2-closed. The remaining
group, namely the fourth Janko group J4 , requires additional effort and will be treated in Section 5.
   Our broad strategy is to apply Proposition 3.10 to the eleven sporadic groups listed in Proposition
2.12(b). To do this, we require detailed information, firstly, on the greatest common divisors of the
orders of the two-point stabilisers in transitive actions of these groups; and secondly, on the base sizes
of these transitive actions. Our main technical result is the following.
Proposition 4.1. Let 𝑇 be one of the following simple groups: J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly, Th, or M. Further, let 𝑀
be a proper subgroup of 𝑇, so that 𝑇 acts faithfully and transitively by right multiplication on the right
coset space [𝑇 : 𝑀]. Then
(a) either 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has base size at most 2, or (𝑇, 𝑀) is as in Table 1, (where the last two subgroups in
    the J4 -line may possibly have base size 2).
(b) Further, for each (𝑇, 𝑀) in Table 1, let 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝑀) be the greatest common divisor of the orders of the
    stabilisers in 𝑀 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] of points of [𝑇 : 𝑀] \ {𝑀 }. Then 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝑀) divides 𝑔(𝑇, 𝑀), where 𝑔(𝑇, 𝑀)
    is as in the third column of Table 1. Moreover, if 𝑇 = J4 and 𝑀 = 210 : L5 (2), then 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝑀) ≤ 30.
     The proof of Proposition 4.1 is spread over six propositions: one for each of the groups 𝑇 =
J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly, Th, and M. Most of these propositions will prove that the relevant group 𝑇 is totally 2-
closed, and also that Proposition 4.1 holds for 𝑇, namely Propositions 4.8, 4.9, 4.13, and 4.17 for J1 , J3 , Ly
and Th, respectively. For the monster however, we give the proof of Proposition 4.1 in Proposition 4.10,
and prove total 2-closure in Proposition 4.11. For the fourth Janko group J4 , we give the proof of
                                                                                                          19

Proposition 4.1 in Proposition 5.6, and prove total 2-closure in Proposition 5.8. Proposition 4.1 will be
applied in Section 7 where we study the total 2-closure of direct products of sporadic simple groups.
   The group 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has base size 1 if and only if 𝑀 = 1, so we will always assume that 1 < 𝑀 < 𝑇.
For the base sizes of the sporadic groups in their primitive actions, our main reference is [9, Tables 1
and 2]. However, the subgroup 𝑀 occurring in Notation 3.3.4 is not always maximal in the finite group
under investigation, and so we need also to study base sizes of imprimitive actions of sporadic simple
groups. The following preliminary result from [9] allows us to do this.
Proposition 4.2. [9, Corollary 2.4] Let 𝐺 be a transitive permutation group with point stabiliser 𝐻,
and for a positive integer 𝑐 let

                                                     ∑︁ |𝑥 𝐺 ∩ 𝐻| 𝑐
                                                           𝑖
                                     𝑄(𝐺,
                                     b    𝐻, 𝑐) :=
                                                     𝑖=1
                                                           |𝑥𝑖𝐺 | 𝑐−1

where 𝑥 1 , . . ., 𝑥 𝑚 are representatives for the conjugacy classes of elements of 𝐺 of prime order. If
𝑄(𝐺,
b    𝐻, 𝑐) < 1, then 𝐺 has base size at most 𝑐.
    Lemma 4.1 and Proposition 4.2 allow us to apply Proposition 3.10 parts (2) and (3) to the relevant
sporadic simple groups, to determine whether or not certain of their imprimitive actions are 2-closed.
Studying their primitive actions needs a different approach, and for this we use the following lemma.
Recall that, for a group 𝐺 acting on a set Ω, we denote by 𝐺 Ω the subgroup of Sym(Ω) induced by
𝐺. Also, we say that permutation groups 𝐺 Ω1 and 𝐻 Ω2 on finite sets Ω1 and Ω2 are permutationally
isomorphic if there exists a bĳection 𝑓 : Ω1 → Ω2 and a group isomorphism 𝜑 : 𝐺 Ω1 → 𝐻 Ω2 such that
 𝑓 (𝛼 𝑔 ) = 𝑓 (𝛼) 𝑔 𝜑 for all 𝛼 ∈ Ω1 , 𝑔 ∈ 𝐺 Ω1 .
Lemma 4.3. Let 𝑇 be a finite simple group with proper subgroup 𝑀, and let Ω = [𝑇 : 𝑀] so that
𝑇 ≤ Sym(Ω), acting by right multiplication, and 𝑀 = 𝑇𝛼 for the point 𝛼 = 𝑀 ∈ Ω.
(a) If also 𝑇 < 𝐺 ≤ Aut(𝑇), and 𝑀 = 𝑇 ∩ 𝐾 for some 𝐾 ≤ 𝐺 such that 𝑇 𝐾 = 𝐺 and 𝐺 [𝐺:𝐾 ]
    has base size 2, then the actions of 𝑇 on Ω and on [𝐺 : 𝐾] are permutationally isomorphic, and
    𝐺 [𝐺:𝐾 ]  𝑇 (2), [𝐺:𝐾 ] .
(b) Suppose now that 𝑀 is maximal in 𝑇, that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] is not 2-transitive, and that (𝑇, |𝑇 : 𝑀 |) is not
    one of the following:
    • 𝑇 = M11 , M12 , M23 , M24 , or Alt(9), with |𝑇 : 𝑀 | = 55, 66, 253, 276, or 120, respectively; or
    • 𝑇 = 𝐺 2 (𝑞) with 𝑞 ≥ 3 a prime power and |𝑇 : 𝑀 | = 21 𝑞 3 (𝑞 3 − 1); or
    • 𝑇 = Ω7 (𝑞) with 𝑞 a prime power and |𝑇 : 𝑀 | = (2,𝑞−1)1
                                                                𝑞 3 (𝑞 4 − 1).
    Then the following hold:
      (i) if 𝑇 = Aut(𝑇), then 𝑇 = 𝑇 (2),Ω ;
     (ii) if 𝑀 ≠ 𝑇 ∩ 𝐾 for any 𝐾 ≤ Aut(𝑇) such that 𝐾 ≠ 𝑀, then 𝑇 = 𝑇 (2),Ω ;
    (iii) if, for all 𝐾 ≤ Aut(𝑇) such that 𝑀 = 𝑇 ∩ 𝐾 ≠ 𝐾, the group (𝑇 𝐾) [𝑇 𝐾 :𝐾 ] has base size 2, then
          𝑇 = 𝑇 (2),Ω .
Proof. (a) Let 𝑀, 𝑇, 𝐾, 𝐺 be as in part (a). Since 𝐺 [𝐺:𝐾 ] is transitive with base size 2, there exists a
base {𝐾, 𝐾𝑥} containing the ‘point’ 𝐾, for some 𝑥 ∈ 𝐺, and hence the stabiliser in 𝐺 of these two
points, namely 𝐾 ∩ 𝐾 𝑥 , is trivial. Further, since 𝐺 = 𝑇 𝐾 = 𝐾𝑇, we may assume that 𝑥 ∈ 𝑇. The equality
𝐺 = 𝑇 𝐾 also implies that 𝑇 is transitive on [𝐺 : 𝐾] and the stabiliser in 𝑇 of the ‘point’ 𝐾 ∈ [𝐺 : 𝐾]
is 𝑇 ∩ 𝐾 = 𝑀. Thus the actions of 𝑇 on Ω and on [𝐺 : 𝐾] are permutationally isomorphic. Since
𝑀 = 𝑇 ∩ 𝐾, we have also 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑥 = 𝑇 ∩ 𝐾 ∩ (𝑇 ∩ 𝐾) 𝑥 = 𝑇 ∩ 𝐾 ∩ 𝐾 𝑥 = 1, that is, the stabiliser in 𝑀
of the point 𝐾𝑥 ∈ [𝐺 : 𝐾] is trivial, so the 𝑀-orbit containing 𝐾𝑥 has size |𝑀 : 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑥 | = |𝑀 |, while
the 𝐾-orbit containing 𝐾𝑥 has size |𝐾 : 𝐾 ∩ 𝐾 𝑥 | = |𝐾 |. Since |𝐾 : 𝑀 | = |𝑇 𝐾 : 𝑇 | = |𝐺 : 𝑇 | > 1, it
follows that 𝐾 does not leave invariant the 𝑀-orbit containing 𝐾𝑥, and hence 𝐺 does not leave invariant
the 2-relation (𝐾, 𝐾𝑥)𝑇 of 𝑇. Hence 𝐺 [𝐺:𝐾 ]  𝑇 (2), [𝐺:𝐾 ] .
20

   (b) From now on assume that 𝑀 is maximal in 𝑇, and that 𝑇 is as in part (b), so 𝑇 Ω is primitive but
not 2-transitive. Then by [23, Theorem 1], the group 𝑇 (2),Ω is contained in 𝑁 := 𝑁Sym(Ω) (𝑇 Ω ). Since
𝑇 Ω is primitive, 𝑁 is almost simple with socle 𝑇 Ω . In particular 𝑇 Ω ≤ 𝑁 ≤ Aut(𝑇 Ω ), and part (b)(i)
follows. If 𝑇 (2),Ω properly contains 𝑇 Ω then, taking 𝐾 = (𝑇 (2),Ω ) 𝛼 , we have 𝑇 (2),Ω = 𝑇 Ω 𝐾 since 𝑇 Ω is
transitive, 𝐾 ≤ Aut(𝑇 Ω ) since 𝑁 has socle 𝑇 Ω , and 𝑀  𝑀 Ω = 𝑇 Ω ∩ 𝐾 = 𝑇𝛼Ω ≠ 𝐾. Thus in part (b)(ii)
we conclude that 𝑇 (2),Ω = 𝑇.
   Finally, suppose that the assumptions of part (b)(iii) hold, and that 𝑇 (2),Ω ≠ 𝑇 Ω . The previous
paragraph shows that 𝐾 = (𝑇 (2),Ω ) 𝛼 satisfies 𝐾 ≤ Aut(𝑇 Ω ) and 𝑀  𝑀 Ω = 𝑇 Ω ∩ 𝐾 ≠ 𝐾. Further,
since 𝑇 Ω is transitive we have 𝑇 (2),Ω = 𝑇 Ω 𝐾, and so, by the assumptions in (b)(iii), 𝑇 (2),Ω has base size
2. However part (a), applied with 𝐺 = 𝑇 (2),Ω , then gives a contradiction.                                  


   Before proceeding further with the general analysis, we illustrate how to use Lemma 4.3 by proving
the following useful corollary.
Corollary 4.4. Each primitive permutation group isomorphic to J3 or ON is 2-closed.
Proof. Let 𝑇 be J3 or ON, let 𝑀 be a maximal subgroup of 𝑇, and consider 𝑇 as a primitive permutation
group on Ω = [𝑇 : 𝑀] acting by right multiplication. Up to permutational isomorphism, each primitive
representation of 𝑇 arises in this way. We need to prove that 𝑇 is equal to 𝑋 := 𝑇 (2),Ω . By [23, Theorem
1], 𝑋 is almost simple with socle 𝑇. In each case 𝐺 := Aut(𝑇)  𝑇 .2, so 𝑋 is equal to either 𝑇 or
𝐺. Note that 𝑇 has no 2-transitive representations. If 𝑀 cannot be written as 𝑀 = 𝐾 ∩ 𝑇 for any
𝐾 ≤ 𝐺 with 𝐾 ≠ 𝑀, then 𝑋 = 𝑇 by Lemma 4.3(b)(ii). So assume that such a 𝐾 exists, and note that
𝑇 𝐾 = 𝐺. By Lemma 4.3(b)(iii), we may assume further that 𝐺 has base size larger than 2 in its action
on Σ := [𝐺 : 𝐾]. Using [9, Tables 1 and 2], the possibilities are as follows.
    If 𝐺 = J3 : 2, then 𝐾 ∈ {𝐿 2 (16) : 4, (3 × 𝑀10 ) : 2}. In these cases, we use GAP [15]. If 𝐾 = 𝐿 2 (16),
then 𝐺 Σ has rank 7, while 𝑇 Σ has rank 8. If 𝐾 = (3 × 𝑀10 ) : 2, then 𝐺 Σ has rank 18, while 𝑇 Σ has rank
28. Thus, 𝑇 Σ = 𝑇 (2),Σ in each case.
    If 𝐺 = 𝑂𝑁 : 2, then 𝐾 = 4.L3 (4).2.2. Here, we check using GAP [15] that 𝐺 Σ has rank 34, while
𝑇 has rank 48. So 𝑇 Σ = 𝑇 (2),Σ .
  Σ                                                                                                        


   We are now ready to outline our strategy to prove Theorem 1.1. Our analysis uses the notion of the
depth ℓ𝐺 (𝐻) of a proper subgroup 𝐻 of a finite group 𝐺, namely the least positive integer ℓ such that
there exists a subgroup chain 𝐻 = 𝐺 ℓ < · · · < 𝐺 1 < 𝐺 0 = 𝐺 with 𝐺 𝑖 maximal in 𝐺 𝑖−1 for 𝑖 = 1, . . . , ℓ.
The maximum value of ℓ𝐺 (𝐻) over all proper subgroups 𝐻 of 𝐺 is the depth of the trivial subgroup,
and this is at most the length of the longest subgroup chain in 𝐺 but may be smaller. For example,
1 < 𝐶2 < 𝐶22 < Alt(4) < Sym(4) is a subgroup chain for Sym(4) of maximum length four, while
ℓSym(4) (1) = 3 in view of the chain 1 < 𝐶3 < Sym(3) < Sym(4).
Strategy 4.5. Assume that 𝑇 is one of the sporadic simple groups in Proposition 2.12(b) so, in
particular, 𝑇 admits no non-trivial factorizations. By Corollary 2.11, 𝑇 is totally 2-closed if and only if
𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] = 𝑇 (2) , [𝑇 :𝐻 ] for all proper subgroups 𝐻 of 𝐺. It follows from Theorem 2.4 that this holds for
𝐻 = 1, so we need to consider proper nontrivial subgroups 𝐻, and in these cases we note that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ]
has base size at least 2.
    We proceed in a series of steps. At Step ℓ we will have remaining a non-empty set Sℓ of proper
nontrivial subgroups of 𝑇 to consider, where S1 is the set of all proper nontrivial subgroups of 𝑇. Either
(a) we complete the analysis at Step ℓ by concluding with certainty that 𝑇 is, or is not, totally 2-closed,
or (b) we remove some subgroups from Sℓ leaving a set Sℓ+1 which, if non-empty, will be considered
in Step ℓ + 1. In particular, for each ℓ, Sℓ will have the following property:
  (∗)   If 𝐻 ∈ Sℓ , then ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) ≥ ℓ, and if ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = ℓ and 𝐻 < 𝑀 < 𝑇, then 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] = 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝑀 ] and
                                     𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has base size at least 3.
                                                                                                              21

Note that S1 has property (∗) since if ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 1 then 𝐻 is maximal and the last condition holds
vacuously. Also the process will complete in a finite number of steps since 𝑇 is finite. Finally, we
describe what we do in Step ℓ (for an arbitrary value of ℓ).

Step ℓ: For each 𝐻 ∈ Sℓ with ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = ℓ, we determine 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝐻 ] . To do this when ℓ = 1 (that is,
when 𝐻 is maximal in 𝑇), we use Lemma 4.3 together with some known results about the subdegrees
of the primitive almost simple groups. If ℓ ≥ 2 then 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is imprimitive, and by property (∗),
𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] = 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝑀 ] for all 𝑀 such that 𝐻 < 𝑀 < 𝑇. We can therefore use Proposition 3.10 in our
analysis. (This of course is the most difficult part of the procedure.)
(1) Thus for each 𝐻 ∈ Sℓ with ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = ℓ, we determine 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝐻 ] .
    (a) If 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] < 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝐻 ] , for some such 𝐻, then we conclude that 𝑇 is not totally 2-closed, and
        the analysis is completed.
    (b) Else we have 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] = 𝑇 (2) , [𝑇 :𝐻 ] for every 𝐻 ∈ Sℓ with ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = ℓ.
(2) Next we check the base size of 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] for each 𝐻 ∈ Sℓ with ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = ℓ, and construct the new set
    Sℓ+1 .
    (a) If, 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 2, then it follows from Proposition 3.10(3) that, for each 𝐾 < 𝐻, we
        have 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐾 ] = 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝐾 ] . Thus proper subgroups of 𝐻 need no further testing.
    (b) We remove from Sℓ each 𝐻 ∈ Sℓ with ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = ℓ and, in addition, if 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 2,
        we also remove all proper subgroups of 𝐻. Let Sℓ+1 denote the resulting set of subgroups.
    (c) If Sℓ+1 = ∅ then we have successfully shown that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] = 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝐻 ] for every proper subgroup
        𝐻 of 𝑇, we conclude that 𝑇 is totally 2-closed, and the analysis is completed.
    (d) On the other hand if Sℓ+1 ≠ ∅, then by its construction it is not difficult to check that Sℓ+1 has
        property (∗) with ℓ + 1 in place of ℓ.
   We begin by applying this strategy to the group HN, and here we do not need to proceed past stage
(1) of Step 1 in Strategy 4.5.
Proposition 4.6. The Harada Norton group HN is not totally 2-closed.
Proof. Let 𝑇 = HN, the Harada Norton group. One of the groups 𝐻 ∈ S1 in Strategy 4.5 is 𝐻 = 4.HS,
and Aut(𝑇) = 𝑇 .2 has a primitive permutation representation on a set of size 1, 539, 000, with point
stabiliser 𝐻.2. For the normal subgroup 𝑇, this representation is permutationally isomorphic to its
transitive action on [𝑇 : 𝐻], which has rank 9, with all subdegrees distinct, see [19, Lemma 2.18.1].
Thus, in particular, 𝐻.2 must leave invariant each 𝐻-orbit in [𝑇 : 𝐻]. Hence Aut(𝑇) also has rank 9 on
[𝑇 : 𝐻]. We conclude that 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝐻 ] contains 𝑇 .2, so 𝑇 is not totally 2-closed.                


   We now move on to the group J1 , where we must use both stages of Steps 1 and 2 of Strategy 4.5.
Remark 4.7. At various stages in the remainder of the paper, we will us the following fact: if 𝐾 is a
proper nontrivial subgroup of a group 𝑇 and 𝐾 is contained in a core-free subgroup 𝐻 of 𝑇 such that
𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 2, then also 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐾 ] has base size 2. (This follows from the fact that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] having
a base of size 2 means that, for some 𝑔 ∈ 𝑇, 𝐻 ∩ 𝐻 𝑔 acts trivially on [𝑇 : 𝐻] and hence 𝐻 ∩ 𝐻 𝑔 = 1
since 𝐻 is core-free in 𝑇, whence also its subgroup 𝐾 ∩ 𝐾 𝑔 is trivial.)
Proposition 4.8. The Janko group J1 is totally 2-closed. Also Proposition 4.1, and in particular Table
1, holds for J1 .
Proof. Let 𝑇 = J1 . According to Strategy 4.5 our task is to prove that 𝑇 Ω = 𝑇 (2),Ω , where Ω = [𝑇 : 𝐻],
for each proper nontrivial subgroup 𝐻 of 𝑇. In Step 1 of Strategy 4.5, for each maximal subgroup 𝐻,
we conclude that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] = 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝐻 ] by Lemma 4.3(b)(i), since Aut(𝑇) = 𝑇 and 𝑇 has no 2-transitive
representations. Proceeding to stage (2) of Step 1, we find by [9, Table 1] that, for a maximal subgroup
𝐻, 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 2 unless 𝐻 is conjugate to 𝐿 2 (11). Thus the new subset S2 consists, up to
conjugacy, of all proper nontrivial subgroups of a maximal subgroup 𝑀 := 𝐿 2 (11).
22

   We proceed to stage (1) of Step 2 in Strategy 4.5. Let 𝐻 be a maximal subgroup of 𝑀. Then the
group 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ]  𝑇 is imprimitive, and we use the notation in Notation 3.3 with 𝐺 = 𝑇 and Ω = [𝑇 : 𝐻].
So 𝐻 = 𝐺 𝜔 , for a point 𝜔 contained in a part Δ in a 𝐺-invariant partition Σ of Ω, 𝑋 = 𝐺 (2),Ω ,
𝑌 = 𝑋ΔΔ , 𝐿 = 𝐺 Σ , and we may assume that 𝐺 Δ (setwise stabiliser) is the subgroup 𝑀 = 𝐿 2 (11). Thus
𝐿 = 𝐿 (2),Σ by the previous paragraph. Using the Web Atlas [35], we see that the 𝑀-orbits in Σ have
lengths 1, 11, 12, 110, 132. Thus since |𝑀 |/110 = 6 and |𝑀 |/132 = 5, the greatest common divisor of
the point-stabiliser orders in 𝑀 Σ is 1. Thus the first line of Table 1 holds, and it follows from Proposition
3.10(2) that 𝑋 = 𝐺, that is, 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] = 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝐻 ] . Next, for each maximal subgroup 𝐻 of 𝑀, we use
Magma [5] to compute the expression 𝑄(𝑇,  b 𝐻, 2) of Proposition 4.2 and find that the value is less than
1, and hence that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 2. Thus the subset S3 constructed in stage (2) of Step 2 is the
emptyset, and we conclude that 𝑇 is totally 2-closed.
   To complete the proof that Proposition 4.1 holds for 𝑇 = J1 , note that our argument has so far shown
that each proper nontrivial subgroup 𝐾 of 𝑇 is either conjugate to 𝑀 = 𝐿 2 (11), or is contained in a
subgroup 𝐻 such that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 2. In the latter case, as we observed above, 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐾 ] also has
base size 2. This completes the proof.                                                                       


     Next, we deal with the group J3 , where three steps of Strategy 4.5 are required.
Proposition 4.9. The Janko group J3 is totally 2-closed. Moreover, Proposition 4.1, and in particular
Table 1 holds for J3 .
Proof. Let 𝑇 := J3 . According to Strategy 4.5 our task is to prove that 𝑇 Ω = 𝑇 (2),Ω , where Ω = [𝑇 : 𝐻],
for each proper nontrivial subgroup 𝐻 of 𝑇.
    In Step 1 of Strategy 4.5, S1 is the set of all proper nontrivial subgroups. If 𝐻 ∈ S1 is maximal in 𝑇
then, by Corollary 4.4, 𝑇 Ω = 𝑇 (2),Ω , and by [9, Table 1], 𝐻  𝐿 2 (16) : 2 is the only maximal subgroup
such that 𝑇 Ω has base size greater than 2 (and in fact has base size 3). Thus the set S2 constructed in
Strategy 4.5 consists of all nontrivial, non-maximal subgroups 𝐻 such that, if 𝐻 < 𝑀 < 𝑇 with 𝑀
maximal, then 𝑀 is conjugate to 𝐿 2 (16) : 2.
    We see from the Web Atlas [35] that the 𝑀-orbits in [𝑇 : 𝑀] have lengths
1, 85, 120, 510, 680, 1360, 1360, 2040. Thus, since |𝑀 |/1360 = 6 and |𝑀 |/120 = 68, it is easily checked
that the greatest common divisor of the point stabiliser orders in 𝑀 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] is 2. The second line of Table
1 then follows for 𝑀 = 𝐿 2 (16) : 2. From now on the subgroups 𝐻 we consider are not maximal, and
we use Notation 3.3 with 𝐺 = 𝑇, Ω = [𝑇 : 𝐻], 𝑋 = 𝑇 (2),Ω , 𝐻 = 𝐺 𝜔 , with 𝜔 in a part Δ of a 𝐺-invariant
partition Σ of Ω such that 𝑀 = 𝐺 Δ (setwise stabiliser), so Σ = [𝑇 : 𝑀] and for 𝐿 = 𝐺 Σ , we will always
have 𝐿 = 𝐿 (2),Σ by Strategy 4.5.
    In Step 2, we consider all maximal subgroups 𝐻 of 𝑀 = 𝐿 2 (16).2. Thus 𝑀 Δ is primitive. First
we claim that, for each such 𝐻, 𝑇 Ω = 𝑇 (2),Ω . Suppose that this is false, so that, for some 𝐻, we have
𝑋 ≠ 𝐺. Then, by Proposition 3.10(2), 𝑋 = 𝑁 o 𝐺 with 𝑁 = 𝑋 (Σ) ≠ 1 (kernel of the 𝑋-action on Σ),
and the 𝑁 Δ -orbits have constant length 𝑎, where 𝑎 divides the greatest common divisor of the 2-point
stabilisers of 𝐿. By the previous paragraph 𝑎 divides 2. Since 1 ≠ 𝑁 Δ  𝑋ΔΔ and 𝑀 Δ ≤ 𝑋 Δ is primitive,
it follows that 𝑁 Δ is transitive, so 𝑎 = |Δ| = 2. This implies that |𝑀 : 𝐻| = 2 so 𝐻 is equal to the derived
subgroup 𝑀 0 = 𝐿 2 (16). We check, using Magma [5], that the stabiliser (a subgroup of order 6) in 𝑀 of
a part Δ 𝑗 in one of the two 𝑀-orbits of length 1360 in Σ lies in 𝐻, while the stabiliser of a part Δ 𝑘 in
the other 𝑀-orbit of length 1360 is not contained in 𝐻. Firstly we note that, for 𝜔 𝑘 ∈ Δ 𝑘 , this implies
that the two-point stabiliser 𝐺 𝜔, 𝜔𝑘 = 𝐻 𝜔𝑘  𝐶3 , and it follows that the greatest common divisor of the
point stabiliser orders in 𝐻 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 1, and hence Line 2 of Table 1 holds also for the subgroup 𝐿 2 (16).
Secondly, this means that, in the notation of Proposition 3.10, (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 )𝐺 𝜔 = 𝐻 ≠ 𝑀 so that property
(ii) in Proposition 3.10(1) fails, and hence 𝑋 = 𝐺, which is a contradiction. Thus 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] = 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝐻 ]
for all maximal subgroups 𝐻 of 𝑀. For those subgroups 𝐻 ≠ 𝐿 2 (16), we use Magma [5] and compute
that the value of the expression 𝑄(𝑇, b 𝐻, 𝑐) of Proposition 4.2, with 𝑐 = 2, is strictly less than 1, and
hence 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 2.
                                                                                                                 23

    Suppose now that 𝐻 = 𝐿 2 (16). We compute as follows using GAP [15] to prove that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has
base size 3. The generators for 𝑇 = J3 viewed as the primitive group 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] acting on Σ = [𝑇 : 𝑀] are
given in the ATLAS [11, 35] and using these we compute with [15] that the point stabilisers of 𝐻 Σ have
orders 8, 6, 6, 6, 6, 2, 48, 6, 34. This implies in particular that 𝐻 is transitive on the 𝑀 Σ -orbit Σ0 of length
2040 = |𝐻|/2. Let 𝐾 = 𝐻 ∩ 𝑀 𝑔  𝐶2 , the stabiliser in 𝐻 of a block Δ0 ∈ Σ0 . If 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] were to have
base size 2, then 𝐻 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] would have an orbit Ω0 of length |𝐻| = 4080 in Ω = [𝑇 : 𝐻], which would
have to be the union of the 2040 blocks of Σ in Σ0 . If this were the case then the stabiliser 𝐽 := 𝐻 ∩ 𝐻 𝑔
in 𝐻 of a point of Ω0 would be trivial. Thus we (only) need to check that 𝐽 ≠ 1, and we do this using
GAP. Now 𝐾 = 𝐻Δ0 , the stabiliser in 𝐻 of Δ 0 ∈ Σ0 . In GAP we construct 𝑇Δ0 (which is 𝑀 𝑔 ) and then the
derived subgroup of 𝑇Δ0 (which is 𝐻 𝑔 ). Finally we check (using the ‘IsSubgroup’ command in GAP)
that 𝐾 is a subgroup of 𝐻 𝑔 . Since 𝐾 by definition lies in 𝐻 we conclude that 𝐾 ≤ 𝐻 ∩ 𝐻 𝑔 = 𝐽, and
hence 𝐽 ≠ 1, as claimed. Thus 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 3. To complete stage (2) of Step 2 for Strategy 4.5
we remove various subgroups from S2 to form S3 : which consists, up to conjugacy, of those proper
nontrivial subgroups 𝐻 of 𝑀 0 = 𝐿 2 (16) such that the only maximal subgroup of 𝑀 containing 𝐻 is 𝑀 0.

   Next, we will deal with the case where 𝑇 is the monster. First, we prove Proposition 4.1 for this group.
Proposition 4.10. Let 𝑇 := M (the monster), and let 𝐾 < 𝑇 be such that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐾 ] has base size at least 3.
Then 𝐾 = 2.B, a maximal subgroup of 𝑇, and the greatest common divisor of the point-stabiliser orders
in 𝐾 [𝑇 :𝐾 ] is 209, 018, 880. In particular, Proposition 4.1 (expecially the final row of Table 1) holds for
M.
Proof. Let 𝐾 ≤ 𝑀 < 𝑇 with 𝑀 maximal in 𝑇. Then also 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has base size at least 3. Hence by [9,
Table 2], 𝑀 = 2.B. Suppose that 𝐾 < 𝑀, and let 𝐻 be a maximal subgroup of 𝑀 containing 𝐾. Then
also 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size at least 3. For all maximal subgroups 𝐻 of 𝑀, we use the GAP Character Table
Library [7] (together with the available class fusions) and compute, using GAP [15], that the value of
                  b 𝐻, 2) of Proposition 4.2 is strictly less than 1, and hence that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size
the expression 𝑄(𝑇,
