𝐾-orbits in [𝑇 : 𝐾] are given in [18, top of p. 101] and we compute that the greatest common divisor
of the point-stabiliser orders in 𝐾 [𝑇 :𝐾 ] is 209, 018, 880, completing the proof.                        
   We are now ready to prove that the monster is totally 2-closed.
Proposition 4.11. The monster M is totally 2-closed.
Proof. Let 𝑇 = M. As usual our task, using Strategy 4.5, is to prove that 𝑇 Ω = 𝑇 (2),Ω , where Ω = [𝑇 : 𝐻],
for each proper nontrivial subgroup 𝐻 of 𝑇. Since 𝑇 = Aut(𝑇) and 𝑇 has no 2-transitive representations,
it follows from Lemma 4.3(b)(i) that this holds for all maximal subgroups 𝐻. Thus we proceed to stage
(2) of Step 1 in Strategy 4.5, and here, by Proposition 4.10, the only maximal subgroup 𝑀 such that
𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has base size at least 3 is 𝑀 = 2.B. Hence the set S2 formed in Step 1 consists, up to conjugacy,
of all proper nontrivial subgroups of 𝑀.
24

   In Step 2 of Strategy 4.5, we examine the maximal subgroups 𝐻 of 𝑀. We again use Notation 3.3
with 𝐺 = 𝑇, Ω = [𝑇 : 𝐻], 𝑋 = 𝑇 (2),Ω , 𝐻 = 𝐺 𝜔 , with 𝜔 in a part Δ of a 𝑇-invariant partition Σ of
Ω such that 𝑀 = 𝐺 Δ , so Σ = [𝑇 : 𝑀] and 𝐿 = 𝐺 Σ satisfies 𝐿 = 𝐿 (2),Σ , and we set 𝑌 = 𝑋ΔΔ . Since
𝐻 is maximal in 𝑀 and 𝑍 (𝑀) = Φ(𝑀)  𝐶2 , we have 𝑍 (𝑀) = Core 𝑀 (𝐻) = Φ(𝑀) and 𝑀 Δ  B.
This implies that 𝑀 Δ = 𝑀 (2),Δ , by Lemma 4.3(b)(i), since Aut(B) = B and B has no 2-transitive
representations. It now follows from Lemma 3.1(b) that 𝑌 = B = 𝑀 Δ . Suppose now that 𝑋 ≠ 𝐺. Then
by Proposition 3.8(a), 𝑋 = 𝑁 o 𝐺 with 𝑁 Δ a nontrivial normal subgroup of 𝑌 , and hence 𝑁 Δ = 𝑌 . By the
definition of the subgroup 𝑁 from Lemma 3.5(b), this would imply that, for 1 < 𝑗 ≤ 𝑠 = |Σ|, the group
(𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 ) Δ is transitive. Since 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 is a proper subgroup of 𝑀 and 𝑍 (𝑀) = Core 𝑀 (𝐻) ≤ 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 ,
the induced group (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 ) Δ is a proper subgroup of 𝑀 Δ = 𝑌 , so we have a proper factorisation
𝑌 = 𝑌 𝜔 (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 ) Δ . This is a contradiction since 𝑌 has no such factorizations, by [24]. Thus 𝑋 = 𝐺,
that is, 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] = 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝐻 ] . We now move to stage (2) of Step 2 for Strategy 4.5. By Proposition 4.10,
each of the groups 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] just examined has base size 2. Hence the set S3 formed in Step 2 is empty,
and we conclude that 𝑇 is totally 2-closed.                                                                  

     The next two groups we deal with are the O’Nan group and the Lyons group.
Proposition 4.12. The O’Nan group ON is not totally 2-closed.
Proof. Let 𝑇 = ON and let 𝑀 be a maximal subgroup of 𝑇 with 𝑀 = 𝐿 3 (7) : 2. Also let 𝐻 = 𝑀 0 (the
derived subgroup), so |𝑀 : 𝐻| = 2. By Corollary 4.4, 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] = 𝑇 (2) , [𝑇 :𝑀 ] . We check, using GAP [15],
that no two-point stabiliser in 𝑀 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] is contained in 𝐻. Hence, (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑡 )𝐻 = 𝑀 for all 𝑡 ∈ 𝑇, that
is to say, condition (ii) of Proposition 3.10(1) holds. Since 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] = 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝑀 ] , Proposition 3.10(1)
applies, and we conclude that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is not 2-closed. Thus, 𝑇 is not totally 2-closed.                   

Proposition 4.13. The Lyons group Ly is totally 2-closed. Moreover, Proposition 4.1, and in particular
Table 1 holds for 𝑇 = Ly.
Proof. Let 𝑇 = Ly. As in the other cases, our task is to prove, using Strategy 4.5, that 𝑇 Ω = 𝑇 (2),Ω ,
where Ω = [𝑇 : 𝐻], for each proper nontrivial subgroup 𝐻 of 𝑇. Since 𝑇 = Aut(𝑇) and 𝑇 has no 2-
transitive representations, it follows from Lemma 4.3(b)(i) that this holds for all maximal subgroups 𝐻.
Thus we proceed to stage (2) of Step 1 in Strategy 4.5: constructing the set S2 . By [9, Table 2], there
are only two conjugacy classes of maximal subgroups 𝑀 of 𝑇 such that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has base size at least 3,
with representatives 𝑀1 = 𝐺 2 (5) and 𝑀2 = 3.McL : 2. Therefore according to Strategy 4.5, the set S2
consists of all non-maximal subgroups 𝐻 such that the only maximal subgroups of 𝑇 containing 𝐻 are
conjugate to 𝑀1 or 𝑀2 .
   We now move on to Strategy 4.5, Step 2, stage (1). Here, we need to prove that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 2-closed
for all 𝐻 ∈ S2 with ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 2. Let 𝐻 ∈ S2 with ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 2, and assume that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] ≠ 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝐻 ] .
Let 𝑀 be a maximal subgroup of 𝑇 containing 𝐻, so 𝐻 is maximal in 𝑀. Without loss of generality
we may assume that 𝑀 = 𝑀𝑖 for 𝑖 = 1 or 2. We adopt the rest of the notation in Notation 3.3, with
𝑇 = 𝐺. So Ω = [𝑇 : 𝐻], Σ = [𝑇 : 𝑀], 𝐿 = 𝑇 Σ , 𝑀 = 𝑇Δ (with Δ ∈ Σ), 𝐻 = 𝑇𝜔 (with 𝜔 ∈ Δ), etc. Note
that 𝐿 (2),Σ = 𝐿, by the previous paragraph, and 𝑀 Δ is primitive since 𝐻 is maximal in 𝑀. We also set
𝑋 = 𝑇 (2),Ω , so 𝑋 > 𝑇, and 𝑌 = 𝑋ΔΔ ≤ 𝑀 (2),Δ .
   We begin with the case 𝑀 = 𝑀1 = 𝐺 2 (5). We note that, by [19, Lemma 2.19.1], it follows that the
greatest common divisor of the orders of the 2-point stabilisers in 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] is 48, and hence the entry
in Table 1 for 𝑀 = 𝐺 2 (5) is correct. Suppose first that |𝑀 : 𝐻| ≠ 53 (53 − 1)/2. Then 𝑀  𝑀 Δ , so
[23, Theorem 1] implies that 𝑌 ≤ 𝑀 (2),Δ is almost simple with socle 𝐺 2 (5). Since Out(𝐺 2 (5)) = 1
and 𝐺 2 (5) has no 2-transitive representations, it follows from Lemma 4.3(b)(i) that 𝑀 Δ = 𝑀 (2),Δ .
Therefore 𝑌  𝐺 2 (5) and so the nontrivial normal subgroup 𝐴 of 𝑌 in Proposition 3.10(2) is equal
to 𝑌 . In particular, 𝐴Δ is transitive. However this means, by Proposition 3.10(2), that |𝑀 : 𝐻| = |Δ|
divides the greatest common divisor of the orders of the 2-point stabilisers in 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] , that is, |𝑀 : 𝐻|
divides 48. This is a contradiction since the smallest degree of a transitive permutation representation
of 𝐺 2 (5) is 3906, [11, page 114]. Thus |𝑀 : 𝐻| = 53 (53 − 1)/2, and [23, Theorem 1] implies that
                                                                                                         25

𝑌 ≤ 𝑀 (2),Δ ≤ Aut(Ω7 (5)) = Ω7 (5).2. Since 𝑀 ≤ 𝑌 and the only maximal overgroups of 𝐺 2 (5) in
Ω7 (5).2 are 𝐺 2 (5), Ω7 (5), and Ω7 (5).2, we have 𝑌 ∈ {𝐺 2 (5), Ω7 (5), Ω7 (5).2}. Hence the nontrivial
normal subgroup 𝐴 of 𝑌 in Proposition 3.10(2) satisfies 𝐴 ∈ {𝐺 2 (5), Ω7 (5), Ω7 (5).2}. In all cases
𝐴 ≥ 𝐺 2 (5), so 𝐴Δ is transitive since 𝑀 Δ is primitive. Then the same argument as in the previous shows
that |Δ| divides 48 and we get the same contradiction. Thus, we have shown that 𝑇 = 𝑇 (2) , [𝑇 :𝐻 ] for all
maximal subgroups 𝐻 of 𝑀 = 𝑀1 , completing Step 2 stage (1) for 𝑀 = 𝑀1 .
    Now we consider the case 𝑀 = 𝑀2 = 3.McL : 2. We note that, by [19, Lemma 2.19.1], it follows
that the greatest common divisor of the orders of the 2-point stabilisers in 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] is 30, and hence the
entry in Table 1 for 𝑀 = 3.McL : 2 is correct. Let 𝑍 = 𝑍 (𝑀 0), where 𝑀 0 = 3.McL is the derived
subgroup of 𝑀, so |𝑍 | = 3. Since 𝑍 ≤ Φ(𝑀) and 𝐻 is maximal in 𝑀, we have 𝑍 ≤ Core 𝑀 (𝐻). Suppose
first that 𝐻 = 𝑀 0, so |Δ| = 2. We will use Proposition 3.10(1): by [19, Lemma 2.19.1], 𝑀 Σ has an
orbit such that the stabiliser 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 in 𝑀 of a point in this orbit has shape 2.Sym(7). A computation
using MAGMA shows that (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 )𝐻 ≠ 𝑀. Thus the condition in Proposition 3.10(1)(ii) fails, and
hence 𝑋 = 𝑇, which is a contradiction. Therefore 𝐻 ≠ 𝑀 0, and hence Core 𝑀 (𝐻) = 𝑍  𝐶3 and
𝑀 Δ  McL : 2. Then 𝑀 Δ = 𝑀 (2),Δ , by [23, Theorem 1], and since 𝑀 Δ ≤ 𝑌 ≤ 𝑀 (2),Δ , this means
that 𝑌 = 𝑀 (2),Δ  McL : 2. Thus, the nontrivial normal subgroup 𝐴 of 𝑌 in Proposition 3.10(2) is
either McL or McL : 2. In particular, 𝐴Δ is transitive, and hence, by Proposition 3.10(2), |𝑀 : 𝐻| = |Δ|
divides the greatest common divisor of the orders of the 2-point stabilisers in 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] , that is, |𝑀 : 𝐻|
divides 30. This is a contradiction since the smallest degree of a transitive permutation representation
of McL : 2 is 275, [11, page 100].
    This completes stage (1) of Step 2. We now proceed to stage (2) of Step 2: constructing the set S3 .
To do this we prove the following claim.
Claim: If 𝐻 ≤ 𝑇 and either (i) ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 2 but 𝐻  𝑀20 = 3.McL, or (ii) 𝐻 < 𝑀20 with 𝐻 conjugate to
3.M22 or 3.24 .𝐴7 , then 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 2.
Proof of Claim: Let 𝑀 be a maximal subgroup of 𝑇 containing 𝐻. If 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has base size 2 then
so does 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] , so we may assume that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has base size greater than 2. As we saw above, this
means (replacing 𝐻, 𝑀 by some 𝑇-conjugate if necessary) that 𝑀 = 𝑀𝑖 for 𝑖 = 1 or 2. Suppose first
that ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 2, that is, 𝐻 is maximal in 𝑀, but 𝐻 ≠ 𝑀20 . Then 𝐻 is either a maximal subgroup
of 𝑀1 = 𝐺 2 (5), or 𝑀 = 𝑀2 , 𝐻 contains 𝑍 := 𝑍 (𝑀 0)  𝐶3 , and 𝐻/𝑍 is a maximal subgroup of
𝑀/𝑍  McL : 2 of index greater than 2. Such subgroups 𝐻 can be read off using the Web Atlas [35].
As in Proposition 4.11, an upper bound for the base size of 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] can be computed using Proposition
4.2. Using the character table library (together with the available class fusions), we check using GAP
          ˆ
[15] that 𝑄(𝑇,  𝐻, 2) < 1 for each choice of 𝐻. Hence by Proposition 4.2, 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 2. This
proves part (i). Finally suppose that 𝐻 < 𝑀20 with 𝐻 conjugate to 3.M22 or 3.24 .𝐴7 . The same method,
using GAP, shows that 𝑄(𝑇,ˆ     𝐻, 2) < 1, and hence that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 2, proving part (ii).
    It follows from part (i) of the claim, and the definition of S3 , that S3 consists of those subgroups
conjugate to a proper nontrivial subgroup 𝐻 of 𝑀20 = 3.McL such that the only subgroup 𝐾 containing
𝐻 with ℓ𝑇 (𝐾) = 2 is 𝐾 = 𝑀20 . Examining the Atlas [11, page 100], we see that 𝐻 must be conjugate to
a subgroup of 𝑁1 := 3.M22 or 𝑁2 := 3.24 : 𝐴7 , since all other proper subgroups of 𝑀20 are contained in
a subgroup 𝐾 of 𝑀2 with ℓ𝑇 (𝐾) = 2 and 𝐾 ≠ 𝑀20 .
    Now we move on to Strategy 4.5, Step 3, stage (1). We need to prove that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 2-closed for
all 𝐻 ∈ S3 with ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 3. By the previous paragraph each such subgroup 𝐻 is conjugate to 𝑁1 or
𝑁2 (both maximal subgroups of 3.McL). The argument showing that in these two cases 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 2-
closed is almost identical to that given in Step 2, stage (1) for maximal subgroups of 𝑀2 other than
𝑀20 . We assume that 𝐻 = 𝑁𝑖 and 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is not 2-closed. We have Core 𝑀20 (𝐻) = 𝑍  𝐶3 and (using
Notation 3.3) (𝑀20 ) Δ  McL where Δ = [𝑀20 : 𝐻]. We again apply [23, Theorem 1] to deduce that
𝑌 = (𝑀20 ) (2),Δ = McL. This implies that the subgroup 𝐴 in Proposition 3.10(2) is transitive on Δ and
hence that |Δ| = |𝑀20 : 𝐻| divides the greatest common divisor of the orders of the 2-point stabilisers in
        0
𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀2 ] . Hence |𝑀20 : 𝐻| divides 30, which is a contradiction. This completes Step 3, stage (1).

    Finally to complete Step 3, stage (2), we construct S4 . A subgroup 𝐻 ∈ S4 must satisfy 𝐻 ∈ S3 and
ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) ≥ 4, and further, if ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 4 and 𝐻 < 𝐾 < 𝑇, then in particular 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐾 ] has base size at least 3.
Now 𝐻 ∈ S3 and ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) ≥ 4 imply that 𝐻 is conjugate to a proper subgroup of 𝑁𝑖 for some 𝑖, and the
second condition implies that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑁𝑖 ] has base size at least 3. This however contradicts part (ii) of the
claim, and we conclude that S4 is empty. We have therefore shown that 𝑇 is totally 2-closed.
    Finally we prove Proposition 4.1 for 𝑇 = Ly. The information deduced above implies that, if 𝐻 is a
proper nontrivial subgroup of 𝑇 with 𝐻 ∉ {𝐺 2 (5), 3.McL, 3.McL : 2}, then 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 2. We
know from [9, Table 2] that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 3 when 𝐻 ∈ {𝐺 2 (5), 3.McL : 2}, and in these cases
the entries in Table 1 is correct. Suppose then that 𝐻 = 3.McL < 𝑀2 = 3.McL : 2. Then, for each 𝑔 ∈ 𝑇,
           𝑔                                                                    𝑔
|𝑀2 ∩ 𝑀2 : 𝐻 ∩ 𝐻 𝑔 | divides 4. However, by [19, Lemma 2.19.1], |𝑀2 ∩ 𝑀2 | > 4 for all 𝑔 ∈ 𝑇. Thus
𝐻 ∩ 𝐻 𝑔 ≠ 1 for each 𝑔 ∈ 𝑇, and hence 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size greater than 2. Finally, the greatest common
divisor of the orders of the 2-point stabilisers in 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] divides the analogous number for the action
𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀2 ] which, as we showed above, is 30. Thus the entry in Table 1 is correct also for 3.McL.          

     Now we deal with the Conway and Fischer groups Co2 and Fi23 , and then the baby monster B.
Proposition 4.14. Neither the second Conway group Co2 nor the Fischer group Fi23 is totally 2-closed.
Proof. Let 𝑇 ∈ {Co2 , Fi23 }. Consider the following maximal subgroup 𝑀 of 𝑇, namely 𝑀 = 𝑈6 (2) : 2
if 𝑇 = Co2 , and 𝑀 = 𝑂 +8 (3) : Sym(3) if 𝑇 = Fi23 . In each case, 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has rank 3. Set 𝐻 := 𝑀 0,
the derived subgroup, so that |𝑀 : 𝐻| = 2, and adopt the notation in Notation 3.3, with 𝑇 = 𝐺. We
argue as in the case of 𝑇 = ON in Proposition 4.12: we check, using GAP [15], that each of the 2-point
stabilisers 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 in the 𝑇-action on [𝑇 : 𝑀] satisfies (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 )𝐻 = 𝑀, that is to say, condition (ii) of
Proposition 3.10(1) holds. On the other hand 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] = 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝑀 ] by Lemma 4.3(b)(i) since 𝑇 = Aut(𝑇)
and 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] is not 2-transitive. Hence Proposition 3.10(1) applies, and we conclude that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is not
2-closed. Hence, 𝑇 is not totally 2-closed.                                                               

Proposition 4.15. Fischer’s baby monster B is not totally 2-closed.
Proof. Let 𝑇 = B, and consider the maximal subgroup 𝑀 = 2.2 𝐸 6 (2).2. Then 𝑀/𝑍 (𝑀) is an extension
of 2 𝐸 6 (2) by a graph automorphism. Let 𝐻 = 𝑀 0  2.2 𝐸 6 (2), of index 2 in 𝑀. The stabilisers in 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ]
of two distinct points are given in [19, Lemma 2.25.1], namely

                     (2 × 21+20 .𝑈6 (2)).2,   22 × 𝐹4 (2),    Fi22 : 2,   21+20 .𝑈4 (3).22 .

We call these groups 𝐸 𝑖 = 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀𝑖 , for 𝑖 = 2, 3, 4, 5, respectively. We claim that 𝐻𝐸 𝑖 = 𝑀 for
𝑖 = 2, . . . , 5. All assertions in the next two paragraphs are from the short proof of the main theorem in
[22]. The groups 𝐸 𝑖 are the same as in [22], but there the group 𝑀 is denoted by 𝐸.
    First, |𝑀 : 𝐸 2 | is odd, so certainly 𝐸 2 𝐻 = 𝑀. The group 𝐸 3 contains 𝑍 (𝑀), and 𝐸 3 /𝑍 (𝑀) is the
centraliser in 2 𝐸 6 (2).2 of a graph automorphism. In particular, 𝐸 3 contains a graph automorphism,
so we also have 𝐸 3 𝐻 = 𝑀. Next, 𝑀 has precisely two conjugacy classes of subgroups isomorphic to
Fi22 : 2, and they are interchanged by an automorphism of 𝑀 which acts trivially on 𝐻 (see [22, top of
page 1040]). It follows, since 𝐸 4 is one of these groups, that 𝐸 4 6 ≤ 𝐻, and hence 𝐸 4 𝐻 = 𝑀.
    Finally, the group 𝐸 5 can be written as 𝐸 5 = 𝐾𝑄 as follows (see [22, page 1040]). We may take
𝐸 2 = 𝐶 𝑀 (𝑑2 ) with 𝑑2 ∈ 𝐸 4 being a 2𝐴-involution of 𝐸 4 = Fi22 : 2; and 𝐾 = 𝐶𝐸4 (𝑑2 ) ∩ 𝐶𝐸4 (𝑑20 ) with
𝑑20 a 2𝐵-involution of 𝐸 4 which does not commute with 𝑑2 (using ATLAS notation). Then 𝑄 is a unique
index 2 subgroup of 𝑂 2 (𝐸 2 ) = 2 × 21+20 which is normalised by 𝐾. A computation in GAP [15] shows
that 𝐾 𝐸 40 = 𝐸 4 . Hence, since 𝑄 ≤ 𝑀 0 = 𝐻, 𝐸 40 ≤ 𝑀 0 = 𝐻 and 𝐸 4 𝐻 = 𝑀, we deduce that

                  𝑀 = 𝐸 4 𝐻 = (𝐾 𝐸 40 )𝐻 = 𝐾 (𝐸 40 𝐻) = 𝐾 𝐻 = 𝐾 (𝑄𝐻) = (𝐾𝑄)𝐻 = 𝐸 5 𝐻.

Thus 𝐸 𝑖 𝐻 = 𝑀 for all 𝑖, proving the claim. Hence the condition of Proposition 3.10(1)(ii) holds for the
action 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] , and it follows from Proposition 3.10(1) that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is not 2-closed. The result follows. 

   We now move on to our second to last case: the Thompson group Th. We begin by showing that a
particular transitive action of Th is 2-closed.
Proposition 4.16. Suppose that 𝐻 = 3 𝐷 4 (2) is a subgroup of 𝑇 = Th with ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 2, with 𝐻 contained
in a maximal subgroup 𝑀 := 3 𝐷 4 (2).3. Then 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 2-closed.
Proof. Let 𝑇, 𝐻, and 𝑀 be as in the statement, and use the notation in Notation 3.3, with 𝑇 = 𝐺. So
Ω = [𝑇 : 𝐻], Σ = [𝑇 : 𝑀] with 𝑠 = |Σ|, 𝐿 = 𝑇 Σ , 𝑀 = 𝑇Δ (with Δ ∈ Σ), 𝐻 = 𝑇𝜔 (with 𝜔 ∈ Δ), etc. By
Lemma 4.3(b)(i), 𝐿 (2),Σ = 𝐿, since 𝑇 = Aut(𝑇) and 𝑇 has no 2-transitive representations. We also set
𝑋 = 𝑇 (2),Ω and 𝑌 = 𝑋ΔΔ ≤ 𝑀 (2),Δ . Since |Δ| = 3, we have 𝑅 = 𝑀 Δ = 𝑌 = 𝑀 (2),Δ  𝐶3 .
   Assume that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is not 2-closed. Then, by Lemma 3.5, 𝑋 = 𝑁 o 𝑇 with 𝑁 a nontrivial subdirect
subgroup of 𝐵𝑌 = 𝐶3𝑠 , and moreover, for each 𝑗 = 2, . . . , 𝑠, (𝜌1, 𝑗 (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 )) Δ×Δ 𝑗 is either equal to 𝑌 × 𝑌
or is a diagonal subgroup of 𝑌 × 𝑌 . By Proposition 3.7, this group is diagonal for strictly more than
𝑠/2 values of 𝑗, and hence by Lemma 3.6, 𝑁 is a diagonal subgroup of 𝐵𝑌 . Thus 𝑁  𝐶3 and, since
𝑋 = 𝑁 o 𝑇 with 𝑇 a nonabelian simple group, the group 𝑇 centralises 𝑁.
   We now examine a part Δ2 ∈ Σ such that 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2 = 22 .[29 ].(Sym(3) × 3). As in the proof of
Proposition 3.7, (𝜌1,2 (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2 )) Δ×Δ2 is a diagonal subgroup of 𝑌 ×𝑌 . Further, the subdegrees of 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ]
are pairwise distinct, so each 𝑇-orbit in Σ (2) = {(𝛼, 𝛽) : 𝛼, 𝛽 ∈ Σ, 𝛼 ≠ 𝛽} is self-paired. It follows
that the setwise stabiliser 𝑇{Δ∪Δ2 } in 𝑇 of Δ ∪ Δ2 contains an element, say 𝑔, which interchanges Δ
and Δ2 . Thus the permutation group induced by 𝑇{Δ∪Δ2 } on Δ ∪ Δ2 is regular of order 6, so is either
𝐶6 or Sym(3). Moreover, since 𝑔 ∈ 𝑇{Δ∪Δ2 } and 𝑇 centralises 𝑁, it follows from Lemma 3.5(b) that 𝑔
centralises 𝜌1,2 (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2 )) Δ×Δ2 , and hence the permutation group induced by 𝑇{Δ∪Δ2 } on Δ∪Δ2 is 𝐶6 , and

                                          𝑇{Δ∪Δ2 } /(𝐻 ∩ 𝐻 𝑔 )  𝐶6 .                                      (4.1)

    Let 𝑃 := 𝑂 2 (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2 ) = 22 .[29 ], and 𝑄 := 𝑁𝑇 (𝑃). Since |𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2 : 𝐻 ∩ 𝐻 𝑔 | = 3 it follows
that 𝑃 < 𝐻 ∩ 𝐻 𝑔 < 𝐻 < 𝑄. Also, since 𝑃 is characteristic in 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2 and 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2  𝑇{Δ∪Δ2 } ,
we have 𝑃 < 𝑇{Δ∪Δ2 } < 𝑄. By [25, Section 2.2], 𝑄 has shape 25 .(26 : Sym(3) × 𝐿 3 (2)) and 𝑄
is contained in a maximal subgroup 𝐾 := 25 .L5 (2) of 𝑇. More precisely, 𝑄 contains 𝑂 2 (𝐾)  25 ,
and 𝑄/𝑂 2 (𝐾) is a maximal parabolic subgroup of L5 (2) of shape 26 : Sym(3) × 𝐿 3 (2). Further,
𝑂 2 (𝑄) = 𝑂 2 (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2 ) = 𝑃 and (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2 )/𝑃 has shape Sym(3) × 3. Hence, since 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2 has
index 2 in 𝑇{Δ∪Δ2 } , it follows that 𝑇{Δ∪Δ2 } /𝑃 is isomorphic to a subgroup of Sym(3) × 𝐿 3 (2) of shape
(Sym(3) × 3).2. The only such subgroups of Sym(3) × 𝐿 3 (2) are the Sylow 3-normalisers, and they are
isomorphic to Sym(3) × Sym(3). However, since 𝐻 ∩ 𝐻 𝑔 contains 𝑃, 𝑇{Δ∪Δ2 } /(𝐻 ∩ 𝐻 𝑔 ) is isomorphic
to a quotient of 𝑇{Δ∪Δ2 } /𝑃  Sym(3) × Sym(3). This contradicts (4.1), since Sym(3) × Sym(3) has no
cyclic quotients of order 6. Thus 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 2-closed.                                                 
Proposition 4.17. The Thompson group Th is totally 2-closed. Furthermore, Proposition 4.1, and in
particular Table 1, holds for 𝑇 = Th.
Proof. Let 𝑇 = Th. Our task is to prove, using Strategy 4.5, that 𝑇 Ω = 𝑇 (2),Ω , where Ω = [𝑇 : 𝐻], for
each proper nontrivial subgroup 𝐻 of 𝑇. Since 𝑇 = Aut(𝑇) and 𝑇 has no 2-transitive representations, it
follows from Lemma 4.3(b)(i) that this holds for all maximal subgroups 𝐻. Thus we proceed to stage
(2) of Step 1 in Strategy 4.5: constructing the set S2 . By [9, Table 2], there are only two conjugacy
classes of maximal subgroups 𝑀 of 𝑇 such that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has base size at least 3, with representatives
𝑀1 = 3 𝐷 4 (2) : 3 and 𝑀2 = 25 .L5 (2). Therefore according to Strategy 4.5, the set S2 consists of all
non-maximal subgroups 𝐻 such that the only maximal subgroups of 𝑇 containing 𝐻 are conjugate to
𝑀1 or 𝑀2 .
    We now move on to Strategy 4.5, Step 2, stage (1). We need to prove that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 2-closed for
all 𝐻 ∈ S2 with 𝑙𝑇 (𝐻) = 2. Let 𝐻 ∈ S2 , and assume that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] ≠ 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝐻 ] . Let 𝑀 be a maximal
subgroup of 𝑇 containing 𝐻, so without loss of generality we may assume that 𝑀 ∈ {𝑀1 , 𝑀2 }. We use
the rest of the notation in Notation 3.3, with 𝑇 = 𝐺. So Ω = [𝑇 : 𝐻], Σ = [𝑇 : 𝑀], 𝐿 = 𝑇 Σ , 𝑀 = 𝑇Δ
(with Δ ∈ Σ), 𝐻 = 𝑇𝜔 (with 𝜔 ∈ Δ), etc. Note that 𝐿 (2),Σ = 𝐿, by Step 1. We also set 𝑋 = 𝑇 (2),Ω , so
28

𝑋 > 𝑇, and 𝑌 = 𝑋ΔΔ ≤ 𝑀 (2),Δ . Suppose first that 𝑀 = 𝑀2 . We note that, by [19, Lemma 2.20.1(ii)], it
follows that the greatest common divisor of the orders of the two-point stabilisers in 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] is 1, and
hence the entry in Table 1 for 𝑀 = 25 .L5 (2) is correct. This implies, by Proposition 3.10(2), that 𝑋 = 𝑇,
which is a contradiction. We note here that this argument is valid for all proper subgroups 𝐻 of 𝑀2
(without the condition ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 2).
    Thus 𝑀 = 𝑀1 . At this point, we note that it follows from [19, Lemma 2.20.1(i)] that the greatest
common divisor of the orders of the 2-point stabilisers in 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] is 6, and hence the entry in Table 1
for 𝑀 = 3 𝐷 4 (2) : 3 is correct. Further this also implies correctness of the entry in that table for the
                                                                      0
derived subgroup 𝑀 0 = 3 𝐷 4 (2) (we show below that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has base size at least 3). If 𝐻 = 𝑀 0 then
𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 2-closed by Proposition 4.16. Thus we may assume that 𝐻 ≠ 𝑀 0, and we assume also that
ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 2. Then, by [23, Theorem 1], 𝑀 (2),Δ , and hence also its subgroup 𝑌 , is almost simple with
socle 3 𝐷 4 (2). Since 𝑋 > 𝑇, the nontrivial normal subgroup 𝐴 of 𝑌 in Proposition 3.10(2) must contain
3 𝐷 (2). In particular, 𝐴Δ is transitive, and so by Proposition 3.10(2), |𝑀 : 𝐻| = |Δ| divides the greatest

common divisor of the orders of the 2-point stabilisers in 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] , which as noted above is 6. This is a
contradiction, and hence 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 2-closed, completing Step 2, stage (1).
    We now proceed to stage (2) of Step 2: constructing the set S3 . Given the results of Step 1 above,
the set S3 will consist of all conjugates of proper nontrivial subgroups 𝐻 of 𝑀 = 𝑀1 or 𝑀 = 𝑀2 such
that ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) ≥ 3, and if ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 3 then, for any maximal subgroup 𝐽 of 𝑀 containing 𝐻, 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐽 ] has
base size at least 3. If 𝑀 = 𝑀1 , then one such subgroup 𝐽 is 𝑀 0 = 3 𝐷 4 (2). However if 𝐻 < 𝑀 0 is
maximal then, by the Atlas [11, p.89], 𝐻 < 𝑁 𝑀 (𝐻) < 𝑀, and 𝑁 𝑀 (𝐻) is another maximal subgroup
of 𝑀 containing 𝐻. Thus each subgroup 𝐻 < 𝑀 with ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 3 is contained in a maximal subgroup
𝐽 of 𝑀 with 𝐽 lying in the union C of the nine conjugacy classes of maximal subgroups of 𝑀 of index
greater than 3 (that is, maximal subgroups not equal to 𝑀 0). Thus if we can prove that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐽 ] has base
size 2 for all 𝐽 ∈ C, and also for all maximal subgroups 𝐽 of 𝑀2 = 25 .L5 (2), then the set S3 would be
empty, and we will have proven that 𝑇 is totally 2-closed.
    So let 𝐽 be either a maximal subgroup of 𝑀2 = 25 .L5 (2), or a member of C. We use Proposition 4.2
to show that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐽 ] has base size 2. So let 𝑥1 , . . . , 𝑥 𝑚 be representatives for the 𝑇-conjugacy classes of
elements of prime order. First we note the following crude upper bound:


                                 b 𝐽, 2) ≤
                                                 ∑︁     |{𝑔 ∈ 𝐽 : |𝑔| = 𝑝}| 2
                                 𝑄(𝑇,                                             .                        (4.2)
                                                𝑝 prime

We use Magma [5] to compute the right hand side of (4.2), and find that it is less than 1 for each subgroup
𝐽, and hence, by Proposition 4.2, 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐽 ] has base size 2 for each 𝐽. Thus, 𝑇 is totally 2-closed. (For
𝐽 a maximal subgroup of 𝑀2 = 3 𝐷 4 (2) : 3, we work with the degree 819 permutation representation
of 3 𝐷 4 (2) from the Web Atlas to construct 3 𝐷 4 (2) in Magma [5], and then we take its normaliser in
Sym(819) to get 3 𝐷 4 (2) : 3. For 𝐽 contained in the Dempwolff group 𝑀2 = 25 .L5 (2), we work with the
degree 7440 permutation representation of 𝑀2 given in the Web Atlas.)
    Finally we complete the proof of Proposition 4.1 for the group Th. Suppose that 𝐻 is a proper
subgroup of 𝑇 for which 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size at least 3. Let 𝑀 be a maximal subgroup of 𝑇 containing
𝐻, so also 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has base size at least 3. Then, as above, 𝑀 is conjugate to 𝑀1 or 𝑀2 , so we may assume
that 𝑀 ∈ {𝑀1 , 𝑀2 } and 𝐻 ≠ 𝑀. Let 𝐽 be a maximal subgroup of 𝑀 containing 𝐻. If either 𝑀 = 𝑀2
or 𝐽 ∈ C, then we showed above that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐽 ] has base size 2, and hence also 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 2,
which is a contradiction. Thus 𝑀 = 𝑀1 and 𝐽 = 𝑀 0 is the only maximal subgroup of 𝑀 containing 𝐻.
As discussed above, by [11, p.89], the only possibility is 𝐻 = 𝐽 = 𝑀 0. Now |𝑀 : 𝐻| = 3 and hence, for
each 𝑔 ∈ 𝑇, the index |𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑔 : 𝐻 ∩ 𝐻 𝑔 | divides 9. Moreover, it follows from [19, Lemma 2.20.1(i)]
that, for each 𝑔 ∈ 𝑇, gcd(|𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑔 |, 9) is strictly less than |𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑔 |, and hence 𝐻 ∩ 𝐻 𝑔 ≠ 1. Thus,
𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size at least 3. This proves Proposition 4.1(a), and the assertions of Proposition 4.1(b)
have been verified already in the course of the proof.                                                     

5. The case 𝑇 = J4
In this section, we prove that the fourth Janko group J4 is totally 2-closed, and in so-doing we prove
Proposition 4.1 for J4 . This will complete the proofs of Theorem 1.1 and Proposition 4.1. Our main
reference is Janko’s original paper [20], and wherever possible we try to be consistent with his notation,
or draw attention to it. See Remark 5.1 for more information.
   Throughout the section we set 𝑇 := J4 , and we adopt Strategy 4.5. To complete Step 1 of Strategy 4.5,
we need to know all maximal subgroups 𝑀 of 𝑇 such that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has base size at least 3. By [9, Table
2], each such subgroup 𝑀 is conjugate to one of the following three maximal subgroups 𝐷 1 , 𝐷 2 , 𝐷 3 ,
where 𝑧 is a representative of the 2𝐴 conjugacy class of involutions in 𝑇, and in fact 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has base
size 3 in each case.
• 𝐷 1 := 𝑁𝑇 (𝑉) = 𝑉 o 𝐹1  211 : M24 , where 𝑉 = 𝑂 2 (𝐷 1 ) lies in the unique conjugacy class of
  elementary abelian subgroups of 𝑇 of order 211 and 𝐹1  M24 , [20, Propositions 7 and 18].
• 𝐷 2 := 𝐶𝑇 (𝑧)  21+12 .3.M22 : 2. The subgroup 𝑂 2 (𝐷 2 ) is not complemented in 𝐷 2 , but has a
  supplement 𝐹2  6.M22 : 2 such that 𝐹2 ∩ 𝑂 2 (𝐷 2 ) = h𝑧i  𝐶2 , [20, Proposition 1].
• 𝐷 3 := 𝑁𝑇 ( 𝐴) = 𝐴 o 𝐹3  210 : L5 (2), where 𝐴 = 𝑂 2 (𝐷 3 ) is an elementary abelian self-centralizing
  subgroup of order 210 , contained in 𝐷 2 , and 𝐹3  L5 (2), [20, Propositions 20 and 21].
   Maximality of the subgroups 𝐷 1 , 𝐷 2 , and 𝐷 3 can also be checked from the Web Atlas [35]. For
Strategy 4.5 we also need to examine transitive actions 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] with base size at least 3 for non-maximal
subgroups 𝐻. For such a subgroup, if 𝐻 < 𝑀 < 𝑇 with 𝑀 maximal, then 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] also has base size at
least 3, and hence 𝑀 is conjugate to 𝐷 𝑖 for some 𝑖. In similar situations in Section 4, we determined
whether or not such an action 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 2 by finding crude upper bounds on |𝑥𝑇 ∩ 𝐻| for
each element 𝑥 ∈ 𝐻 of prime order, and then applying Proposition 4.2. For 𝑇 = J4 , we need to be much
more careful when finding upper bounds for |𝑥𝑇 ∩ 𝐻| in the case where 𝑥 is an involution. Thus the first
lemma in this section counts involutions in subgroups of the maximal subgroups 𝐷 1 , 𝐷 2 , and 𝐷 3 . Since
we make frequent reference to Janko’s paper [20], we summarise Janko’s notation in Remark 5.1.
Remark 5.1. The Janko group 𝑇 = J4 has precisely two classes of involutions, denoted class 2𝐴 and
2𝐵, and Janko uses 𝑧 and 𝑓 , respectively, to denote representatives of these classes, [20, Theorem A(5)].
He also uses the following notation for the subgroups 𝐷 1 , 𝐷 2 , and 𝐷 3 :
(1) Janko writes 𝑀 = 𝐷 1 , and 𝐾 = 𝐹1 , so 𝑀 = 𝑉 o 𝐾  211 o M24 with 𝑉 ∩ 𝐾 = 1, [20, Proposition 18].
(2) Janko writes 𝐻 = 𝐷 2 = 𝐶𝑇 (𝑧), 𝐸 = 𝑂 2 (𝐷 2 )  21+12 , and 𝐻0 = [𝐷 2 , 𝐷 2 ]  21+12 .3.M22 : 2 for the
(index 2) derived subgroup of 𝐻, [20, Section 3]. In [20, last 13 lines of Proposition 1], Janko describes
the 𝐷 2 -conjugacy classes of involutions in 𝐻0 : there are two classes in 𝐸 \ h𝑧i, with representatives 𝑒
and 𝑓 , and four classes in 𝐻0 \ 𝐸, with representatives 𝑡 0, 𝑡 0 𝑧, 𝑡1 , and 𝑡2 . Moreover all of 𝑡 0, 𝑡 0 𝑧, 𝑡1 , 𝑡2
lie in the same coset of 𝐸, [20, Page 570, line-11]. As noted above, 𝑓 ∈ 2𝐵; by [20, Proposition 9],
the elements 𝑒, 𝑡 0, 𝑡1 all lie in class 2𝐴, and 𝑡 0 𝑧 ∈ 2𝐵; while by [20, Proposition 15], 𝑡2 ∈ 2𝐵. Finally,
by [20, Propositions 6 and 10], there are three 𝐷 2 -conjugacy classes of involutions in 𝐻 \ 𝐻0 , with
representatives 𝑡e1 , 𝑡e1 𝑧, and 𝑡e2 , and by [20, Proposition 15], 𝑡e1 ∈ 2𝐴, and 𝑡e1 𝑧, 𝑡e2 ∈ 2𝐵.
(3) Janko writes 𝐷 3 = 𝑁𝑇 ( 𝐴) = 𝐴 o 𝐵, where 𝐴 = 210 is self-centralizing with 𝐴 < 𝐷 2 and
𝐵 = 𝐹3  L5 (2), [20, Propositions 20 and 21]. He notes that 𝑂 2 (𝐷 2 )  21+12 normalises 𝐴 = 𝑂 2 (𝐷 3 ),
and 𝑁 𝐷2 ( 𝐴)/𝐴 is isomorphic to the parabolic subgroup 26 : (Sym(3) × 𝐿 3 (2)) of 𝐷 3 /𝐴  𝐵  L5 (2),
[20, Page 587, lines 4–7].
   To help us find upper bounds for |𝑥𝑇 ∩ 𝐻| in the case where 𝑥 is an involution in 𝐻 < 𝑇, we introduce
the following (non-standard) notation for counting involutions in finite groups.
Notation 5.2. For a subset 𝑆 of a finite group 𝐺, define

                                               Inv(𝑆 : P1 , . . . , P𝑟 )
30

to be the number of involutions in 𝑆 with properties P1 , . . . , P𝑟 . For example, if 𝐻 is a subgroup of 𝐷 𝑗 ,
for some 𝑗, then
                                    Inv(𝐻\[𝐷 𝑗 , 𝐷 𝑗 ] : 2-central in 𝐷 𝑗 )

is the number of involutions in 𝐻\[𝐷 𝑗 , 𝐷 𝑗 ] which are centralised by a Sylow 2-subgroup of 𝐷 𝑗 . We
also define
                             Inv(𝑆) to be the total number of involutions in 𝑆,
and for 𝑆 ⊆ J4 , we denote by Inv(𝑆 : 2𝐴) and Inv(𝑆 : 2𝐵) the number of involutions in 𝑆 in the conjugacy
class 2𝐴 and 2𝐵 of J4 , respectively, so that

                                   Inv(𝑆) = Inv(𝑆 : 2𝐴) + Inv(𝑆 : 2𝐵).

Remark 5.3. In some of our proofs we use Magma [5] to compute certain quantities in 𝑇 = J4 .
More precisely, we use the 112-dimensional representation for 𝑇 over F2 . The Magma code for this
representation is available from the Web Atlas [35], and it conveniently includes constructions of the
subgroups 𝐷 1 , 𝐷 2 , 𝐷 3 , and 𝐹3 defined above.
Lemma 5.4. For 𝑗 = 1, 2, 3, let 𝐷 𝑗 be as described above, let 𝐸 𝑗 = 𝑂 2 (𝐷 𝑗 ) and consider a subgroup
𝐻 satisfying 𝐸 𝑗 ≤ 𝐻 ≤ 𝐷 𝑗 . For each such subgroup let 𝐻 = 𝐻/𝐸 𝑗 . Then the following assertions hold.
(1) If 𝑗 = 1, then

                           Inv(𝐻 : 2𝐴) =7.11.23 + 16 Inv(𝐻 : 2-central in M24 )+
                                           32 Inv(𝐻 : non 2-central in M24 ), and
                           Inv(𝐻 : 2𝐵) =4.3.23 + 7.16 Inv(𝐻 : 2-central in M24 )+
                                           32 Inv(𝐻 : non 2-central in M24 ).

(2) For 𝑗 = 2, and for 𝑘 ≥ 1, let P𝑘 be the condition on an involution ℎ ∈ 𝐻 that |𝐶𝐸2 (ℎ)| = 2 𝑘 for
    some preimage ℎ ∈ 𝐷 2 of ℎ, and set 𝐻0 := [𝐷 2 , 𝐷 2 ]. Then

                       Inv(𝐻 : 2𝐴) =1387 + 112 Inv(𝐻 0 ) + 64 Inv(𝐻 \ 𝐻 0 : P7 ), and
                       Inv(𝐻 : 2𝐵) =2772 + 208 Inv(𝐻 0 ) + 128 Inv(𝐻 \ 𝐻 0 : P6 )+
                                       64 Inv(𝐻 \ 𝐻 0 : P7 ).

(3) If 𝑗 = 3, then

                           Inv(𝐻 : 2𝐴) =5.31 + 64 Inv(𝐻 : 2-central in L5 (2))+
                                           16 Inv(𝐻 : non 2-central in L5 (2)), and
                           Inv(𝐻 : 2𝐵) =4.7.31 + 64 Inv(𝐻 : 2-central in L5 (2))+
                                           48 Inv(𝐻 : non 2-central in L5 (2)).

Proof. For 𝑖 ∈ {1, 2, 3}, and 𝑋 ∈ {𝐴, 𝐵}, let [𝐻 : 𝐸 𝑖 ] denote a set of representatives for the 𝐸 𝑖 -cosets
in 𝐻. Then we have
                                                 ∑︁
                                Inv(𝐻 : 2𝑋) =             Inv(𝐸 𝑖 ℎ : 2𝑋).                             (5.1)
                                                   ℎ ∈ [𝐻 :𝐸𝑖 ]

If ℎ1 and ℎ2 are conjugate in 𝐷 𝑖 , then Inv(𝐸 𝑖 ℎ1 : 2𝑋) and Inv(𝐸 𝑖 ℎ2 : 2𝑋) are equal. If ℎ ∈ 𝐷 𝑖 \ 𝐸 𝑖
and 𝐸 𝑖 ℎ contains an involution, then we may assume that ℎ is an involution, and also in this case ℎ is
                                                                                                                    31

an involution in 𝐷 𝑖 . On the other hand, if 𝑖 = 1 or 3, then 𝐷 𝑖 = 𝐸 𝑖 o 𝐹𝑖 , and in these cases if ℎ is an
involution then we may assume that ℎ ∈ 𝐹𝑖 and hence ℎ is also an involution. If 𝑖 = 2, then 𝐷 𝑖 = 𝐸 𝑖 𝐹𝑖
with 𝐸 𝑖 ∩ 𝐹𝑖 = 𝑍 (𝐸 𝑖 ) = h𝑧i of order 2. In this case, if 𝐸 2 ℎ is such that ℎ is an involution, then we have
checked using Magma (see Remark 5.3) that there is an involution 𝑥 ∈ 𝐷 2 such that 𝐸 2 ℎ = 𝐸 2 𝑥. Thus,
for all 𝑖, a nontrivial coset 𝐸 𝑖 ℎ contains an involution if and only if ℎ is an involution. We use these facts
frequently throughout the proof. We now prove parts (1), (2), and (3) separately.
(1) Here, we are counting involutions in 𝐷 1 = 211 : M24 with 𝐸 1  211 . By (5.1), we just need to compute
Inv(𝐸 1 ℎ) for each ℎ ∈ [𝐻 : 𝐸 2 ]. We first deal with the case ℎ = 1. Here Inv(𝐸 1 : 2𝐴) = 7.11.23 and
Inv(𝐸 1 : 2𝐵) = 4.3.23, by [20, Proposition 9] (see also Remark 5.1). Suppose now that 1 ≠ ℎ ∈ [𝐻 : 𝐸 1 ].
As mentioned above, we may assume that ℎ is an involution and also that ℎ is an involution. Since
𝐸 1 is an elementary abelian 2-group, the involutions in 𝐸 1 ℎ are precisely the elements of 𝐶𝐸1 (ℎ)ℎ.
Thus, Inv(𝐸 1 ℎ) = |𝐶𝐸1 (ℎ)|. We now use [20, Proposition 18]: if ℎ is 2-central in 𝐷 1  M24 , then
|𝐶𝐸1 (ℎ)| = 27 , and 24 of the 27 involutions in 𝐸 1 ℎ are of type 2𝐴, with the other 7.24 of type 2𝐵. If ℎ
is not 2-central in M24 , then |𝐶𝐸1 (ℎ)| = 26 , and 𝐸 1 ℎ contains 25 involutions of type 2𝐴 and 25 of type
2𝐵. The stated formulae in (1) then follow from (5.1).
(2) Here, we are counting involutions in 𝐷 2 = 21+12 .3.M22 : 2 with 𝐸 2  21+12 . As mentioned above, for
each coset 𝐸 2 ℎ in 𝐻 we may assume that ℎ ∈ 𝐹2 = 6.M22 : 2, where 𝐹2 ∩ 𝐸 2 = h𝑧i. By Remark 5.1(2),
there are two 𝐷 2 -conjugacy classes of involutions in 𝐸 2 \ h𝑧i, with representatives 𝑒 and 𝑓 , in 2𝐴 and 2𝐵
respectively, and from the information in [20, Proposition 1 (from line –13)] about |𝐶𝐷2 (𝑒)|, |𝐶𝐷2 ( 𝑓 )|,
we compute their class sizes as |𝑒 𝐷2 | = 1386 and | 𝑓 𝐷2 | = 2772. Thus we have the following, which will
also be important for part (3):

                The group 𝐸 2 contains 4159 involutions, with 1 + 1386 = 1387 of type 2𝐴
                 and 2772 of type 2𝐵.                                                                            (5.2)

Next, we count the involutions in 𝐻0 \ 𝐸 2 , where 𝐻0 = [𝐷 2 , 𝐷 2 ]. By Remark 5.1(2), there are four
𝐷 2 -conjugacy classes of involutions in 𝐻0 \ 𝐸 2 with representatives 𝑡 0, 𝑡1 (in class 2𝐴) and 𝑡 0 𝑧, 𝑡2 (in
class 2𝐵), and all four of these elements lie in the same coset 𝐸 2 𝑡 0. Thus, by our remarks above, the only
nontrivial 𝐸 2 -cosets containing involutions are 𝐸 2 ℎ with ℎ conjugate in 𝐷 2 to 𝑡 0. By [20, Page 569, line
-3], 𝐸 2 𝑡 0 contains 16 involutions conjugate to 𝑡 0 and 16 conjugate to 𝑡 0 𝑧, and by [20, Page 570, line -11,
-10], 𝐸 2 𝑡 0 contains 25 .3 involutions conjugate to 𝑡 1 and 26 .3 conjugate to 𝑡 2 . Hence, for each involution
ℎ in 𝐻 0 ,

                    𝐸 2 ℎ contains 26 .5 involutions, with 24 + 25 .3 = 112 of type 2𝐴, and
                    24 + 26 .3 = 208 of type 2𝐵.                                                                 (5.3)

Finally, we count the involutions in 𝐻 \ 𝐻0 . Again, as above, the only 𝐸 2 -cosets in 𝐻 \ 𝐻0 containing
involutions are those of the form 𝐸 2 ℎ for an involution ℎ ∈ 𝐻 \ 𝐻0 . By Remark 5.1(2), there are three
𝐷 2 -conjugacy classes of involutions in 𝐻 \ 𝐻0 with representatives 𝑡e1 (in class 2𝐴) and e           𝑡 2 (in class

2𝐵). By [20, Proposition 6], e          𝑡1 𝑧 have property P7 while e
                                𝑡 1 and e                            𝑡 2 has property P6 . Let 𝑠 ∈ {𝑡e1 , 𝑡e1 𝑧, 𝑡e2 },
so 𝑠 has property P𝑘 with 𝑘 = 6 or 7. An element 𝑥𝑠 ∈ 𝐸 2 𝑠 is an involution if and only if 𝑥 𝑠 = 𝑥 −1 and
this, in turn, is equivalent to either (i) 𝑥 ∈ 𝐶𝐸2 (𝑠) with 𝑥 2 = 1, or (ii) |𝑥| = 4 and 𝑠 inverts 𝑥. Now, for

contradicting the fact that 𝑡e1 and 𝑡e1 𝑧 = 𝑧𝑡e1 are not conjugate. Thus, for 𝑠 = 𝑡e1 , the involutions in 𝐸 2 𝑡e1 are
precisely the elements 𝑥 𝑡e1 , where 𝑥 ∈ 𝐶𝐸2 ( 𝑡e1 ) and 𝑥 2 = 1. Since 𝐶𝐸2 ( 𝑡e1 ) is elementary abelian of order

contains both 𝑡e1 and 𝑡e1 𝑧, exactly half (that is, 26 ) of these involutions are 𝐷 2 -conjugate to 𝑡e1 , and the
other 26 involutions are conjugate to 𝑡e1 𝑧.
      Finally consider 𝑠 = 𝑡e2 . The element 𝑡e2 inverts 26 elements of 𝐸 2 of order 4 (this can be checked using
Magma [5], see Remark 5.3 above). In particular, there exists 𝑥 ∈ 𝐸 2 of order 4 such that 𝑥 𝑡e2 = 𝑥𝑧. Also,
𝐶𝐸2 ( 𝑡e2 ) is elementary abelian of order 26 by [20, Propositions 6 and 10]. Thus, there are 26 + 26 = 27
involutions in 𝐸 2 𝑡e2 , consisting of the elements of the form 𝑥 𝑡e2 , where either 𝑥 ∈ 𝐶𝐸2 ( 𝑡e2 ), or |𝑥| = 4 and
𝑥 𝑡e2 = 𝑥𝑧. If 𝑥 ∈ 𝐶𝐸2 ( 𝑡e2 ), then 𝐶𝐸2 (𝑥 𝑡e2 ) = 𝐶𝐸2 ( 𝑡e2 )  26 , so 𝑥 𝑡e2 cannot be 𝐷 2 -conjugate to 𝑡e1 or 𝑡e1 𝑧 (since
these elements have centralisers of order 27 in 𝐸). If |𝑥| = 4 and 𝑥 𝑡e2 = 𝑥 −1 , then 𝑥 𝑡e2 inverts the element
𝑥 of order 4, so again 𝑥 𝑡e2 cannot be 𝐷 2 -conjugate to 𝑡e1 or 𝑡e1 𝑧. Hence all of the 27 involutions in 𝐸 2 𝑡e2 are
𝐷 2 -conjugate to 𝑡e2 .
      It follows from the last two paragraphs above that if ℎ ∈ 𝐷 2 \ 𝐻0 and ℎ is an involution, then
• Inv(𝐸 ℎ : 2𝐴) = Inv(𝐸 ℎ : 2𝐵) = 26 if |𝐶𝐸2 (ℎ)| = 27 ; and
• Inv(𝐸 ℎ : 2𝐴) = 0 and Inv(𝐸 ℎ : 2𝐵) = 27 if |𝐶𝐸2 (ℎ)| = 26 .
Putting all these counts together and applying (5.1) yields part (2).
(3) Here, we are counting involutions in 𝐷 3 = 210 : L5 (2) (so 𝐸 3  210 ). Recall that 𝐷 3 = 𝐸 3 o 𝐹3 with

have

is normalised by 𝐸 2 . Furthermore, |𝐸 2 𝐸 3 | = 216 , and 𝑁 𝐷2 (𝐸 3 ) = 𝐸 3 𝑄, where 𝑄 is a subgroup of

non 2-central. Note that |𝐸 2 𝐸 3 : 𝐸 2 | = 23 , and 𝐸 2 𝐸 3 ≤ [𝐷 2 , 𝐷 2 ]. Let {ℎ1 = 1, ℎ2 , . . . , ℎ8 } ⊆ [𝐷 2 , 𝐷 2 ]

   Finally, we use Magma [5] to compute the J4 -conjugacy classes of involutions in which the involutions
in 𝐷 3 lie (see Remark 5.3 above). We find that the group 𝐷 3 contains 134705 involutions in the class

                     465 Inv(𝐸 3 𝑥 : 2𝐴) + 6510 Inv(𝐸 3 𝑦 : 2𝐴) + 5.31 = 134705, and

The system of equations given by (5.5) and (5.6) can be solved to give Inv(𝐸 3 𝑥 : 2𝐴) =

Inv(𝐸 3 𝑦 : 2𝐵) = 48. Part (3) then follows from (5.1).                                

Corollary 5.5. Let 𝐷 1 , 𝐷 2 , 𝐷 3 be as described above, and let 𝐻 be a subgroup of 𝑇 = J4 . Then 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ]
has base size 2 for each of the following subgroups 𝐻.
(1) 𝑂 2 (𝐷 1 ) < 𝐻 < 𝐷 1 , with 𝐻/𝑂 2 (𝐷 1 ) maximal in 𝐷 1 /𝑂 2 (𝐷 1 )  M24 ;
(2) 𝑂 2 (𝐷 2 ) < 𝐻 < 𝐷 2 such that one of the following holds:
    (a) 𝐻/𝑂 2 (𝐷 2 ) is maximal in 𝐷 2 /𝑂 2 (𝐷 2 )  3.M22 : 2, and 𝐻/𝑂 2 (𝐷 2 ) is not of shape 3.L3 (4).2
         or 3.M22 ;
    (b) 𝐻/𝑂 2 (𝐷 2 ) is a maximal subgroup of 3.L3 (4).2 < 3.M22 : 2, and 𝐻/𝑂 2 (𝐷 2 ) ≠ 3.L3 (4);
    (c) 𝐻/𝑂 2 (𝐷 2 ) is a maximal subgroup of 3.M22 < 3.M22 : 2 isomorphic to 3.Alt(7);
(3) 𝑂 2 (𝐷 3 ) < 𝐻 < 𝐷 3 , with 𝐻/𝑂 2 (𝐷 3 ) maximal in 𝐷 3 /𝑂 2 (𝐷 3 )  L5 (2);
(4) 𝐻 conjugate to a maximal subgroup M24 of 𝐷 1 (in one of two 𝐷 1 -conjugacy classes); or the maximal
    𝐹2  6.M22 : 2 in 𝐷 2 ; or the maximal 𝐹3  L5 (2) in 𝐷 3 ;
(5) 𝐻 maximal of shape [27 ].3.L3 (4).2 in the maximal subgroup of the form 21+12 .3.L3 (4).2 of 𝐷 2 .

   We now have the tools needed to prove Lemma 4.1 for J4 . Recall the notion of the depth ℓ𝐺 (𝐻) of a
subgroup 𝐻 of a group 𝐺 introduced just before Strategy 4.5.
Proposition 5.6. Let 𝐻 be a proper subgroup of 𝑇 = J4 .
(1) If 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size at least 3, then one of the following holds:
    (a) ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 1 and 𝐻 is 𝑇-conjugate to one of 𝐷 1 , 𝐷 2 , or 𝐷 3 ;
    (b) ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 2 and either 𝐻 is 𝑇-conjugate to [𝐷 2 , 𝐷 2 ]  21+12 .3.M22 ; or 𝐻 is 𝑇-conjugate to a
          maximal subgroup of 𝐷 2 containing 𝑂 2 (𝐷 2 ) of shape 21+12 .3.L3 (4) : 2.
    (c) ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 3 and 𝐻 is 𝑇-conjugate to a second maximal subgroup of 𝐷 2 containing 𝑂 2 (𝐷 2 ) of
          shape 21+12 .3.L3 (4).
(2) If ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) ≥ 4, then 𝐻 is properly contained in a subgroup 𝐾 of 𝑇 such that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐾 ] has base size 2.
(3) Proposition 4.1, and in particular Table 1 holds for 𝑇 = J4 .
   Since it is not necessary for our purposes, we have not attempted to resolve whether or not the
permutation group 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size 2 in the cases where 𝐻 has shape 21+12 .3.L3 (4) : 2 (in Part
(1)(b)), or 21+12 .3.L3 (4) (in Part (1)(c)).
Proof. We first prove part (1) for subgroups 𝐻 with ℓ(𝐻) ≤ 3. Let 𝐻 be a proper subgroup of 𝑇 such
that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size larger than 2. Then by [9], and as noted at the beginning of the section, 𝐻 is
conjugate to a subgroup of 𝐷 1 , 𝐷 2 , or 𝐷 3 . Thus if ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 1 then Part (1)(a) holds. Therefore we may
assume both that ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) ≥ 2, and that 𝐻 < 𝐷 𝑖 for some 𝑖 = 1, 2, 3. Recall that, if 𝐻 < 𝐾 < 𝑇 then also
𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐾 ] has base size larger than 2. Also 𝐷 𝑖 = 𝐸 𝑖 𝐹𝑖 , where 𝐸 𝑖 = 𝑂 2 (𝐷 𝑖 ), and 𝐸 𝑖 ∩ 𝐹𝑖 is trivial with 𝐸 𝑖
elementary abelian and 𝐹𝑖 acting irreducibly on it, if 𝑖 = 1 or 3, and 𝐸 2 ∩ 𝐹2 = 𝑍 (𝐸 2 ) = h𝑧i of order
2 with 𝐹2 irreducble on 𝐸 2 /𝑍 (𝐸 2 ), (see Remark 5.1). Also using Magma [5], we find that there are two
𝐷 1 -conjugacy classes of complements to 𝐸 1 , with representatives 𝐹1 and 𝐹11 , and we obtain, for each 𝑖,
a complete set M (𝐷 𝑖 ) of representatives for the 𝐷 𝑖 -conjugacy classes of maximal subgroups of 𝐷 𝑖 , as:

               M (𝐷 1 ) = {𝐹1 , 𝐹11 } ∪ {𝐸 1 𝐼 : 𝐼 < 𝐹1 maximal} ∪ {𝐸 1 𝐼 : 𝐼 < 𝐹11 maximal},
               M (𝐷 2 ) = {𝐹2 } ∪ {𝐸 2 𝐼 : 𝐼 < 𝐹2 maximal},
               M (𝐷 3 ) = {𝐹3 } ∪ {𝐸 3 𝐼 : 𝐼 < 𝐹3 maximal}.


Assume now that ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 2 so that 𝐻 ∈ M (𝐷 𝑖 ) for some 𝑖. It then follows from Corollary 5.5 that
𝑖 = 2 and, up to 𝑇-conjugacy, 𝐻 = 𝐸 2 𝐼 with 𝐼/h𝑧i maximal in 𝐹2 /h𝑧i  3.M22 .2 of shape 3.L3 (4).2 or
3.M22 . This proves (1)(b).

   Next we complete the proof of (1) in the case of subgroups 𝐻 with ℓ(𝐻) ≥ 4, and prove (2). Note
that, if (2) holds then, for any subgroup 𝐻 with ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) ≥ 4, the base size of 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is at most 2, and
hence Part (1) lists all possibilities for 𝐻 where the base size of 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] could possibly be greater than
2. So assume that 𝐻 is a subgroup of 𝑇, ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) ≥ 4, and 𝐻 is not properly contained in a subgroup 𝐾
of 𝑇 with 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐾 ] having base size 2. Then, by our arguments up to this point, 𝐻 is 𝑇-conjugate to a
subgroup of 𝐾1 := 𝐸 2 𝐼1 , where 𝐼1  3.L3 (4). Since ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) ≥ 4, we may assume that 𝐻 < 𝐾1 = 𝐸 2 𝐼1 .
Using Magma, we find that
                                     {𝐸 0 𝐼1 } ∪ {𝐸 2 𝐼2 : 𝐼2 < 𝐼1 maximal}

is a complete set of representatives for the 𝐾1 -conjugacy classes of maximal subgroups of 𝐾1 , where
𝐸 0 is as defined in the previous paragraph. Consider 𝑀 = 𝐸 2 𝐼2 , for some maximal subgroup 𝐼2 of 𝐼1 .
We can check using Magma that, for every subgroup 𝐼2 < 𝐼1 < [𝐹2 , 𝐹2 ]  3.M22 , 𝐼2 is contained in
either a maximal subgroup of 𝐹2 which is not isomorphic to 3.M22 or 3.L3 (4).2; or a maximal 3.Alt(7)
subgroup of 3.M22 . Thus 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has base size 2 by Corollary 5.5, and hence 𝐻 is not contained in any
such subgroup 𝑀. Thus we may assume that 𝐻 ≤ 𝐸 0 𝐼1 and 𝐻 projects onto 𝐼1 . Now 𝐸 0 𝐼1 is an index 2
subgroup of 𝐸 0 𝐼, with 𝐼 = 3.L3 (4).2 as above, and by Corollary 5.5(5), the permutation group 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐸0 𝐼 ]
has base size 2. Hence also 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐽 ] has base size 2, for all subgroups 𝐽 of 𝐸 0 𝐼1 . This is a contradiction
to our assumption that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has base size larger than 2, and hence Part (2) is proved.
    Finally, we complete the proof of Part (3). If 𝑀 = 𝐷 1  211 : M24 , then the subdegrees of 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] are
given in [19, Lemma 2.23.1]. Thus, we can compute 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝑀) precisely (the greatest common divisor
of the orders of the stabilisers in 𝑀 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] of points in [𝑇 : 𝑀] \ {𝑀 }): we get 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝑀) = 24. The first
entry in the final column of the third row of Table 1 follows.
    Next, suppose that 𝑀 = 𝐷 3 = 𝐸 3 𝐹3 = 210 : L5 (2). As noted above, the maximal subgroups of 𝑀 are
𝑇-conjugate to either 𝐹3 , or 𝐸 3 𝐼, where 𝐼 is a maximal subgroup of 𝐹3 . Now, since (|𝑀 |, |𝑇 : 𝑀 | −1) = 1,
there exists, for each prime 𝑝 dividing |𝑀 |, a point stabiliser 𝑀 ( 𝑝) := 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑡 𝑝 in 𝑀 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] containing
a Sylow 𝑝-subgroup of 𝑀. If 𝐿 is a maximal subgroup of 𝑀 containing a Sylow 31-subgroup of 𝑀,
then either 𝐿 is 𝑇-conjugate to 𝐹3 , or 𝐿 contains 𝐸 3 and |𝐿/𝐸 3 | = 5.31 (one can see this by inspection
of the maximal subgroups of L5 (2)  𝑀/𝑂 2 (𝑀)). Thus, |𝑀 (31) | divides 210 .32 .5.7.31. Similarly, 𝑀 (2)
has order dividing 220 .32 .5.7. Thus, the greatest common divisor of the orders of the point stabilisers in
𝑀 [𝑀 :𝑇 ] divides 210 .32 .5.7. On the other hand, we can compute the rank of 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] using the permutation
character and GAP [15] – it is 27. Thus, at least one of the 𝑀-orbits in [𝑇 : 𝑀] must be of size greater
than or equal to (|𝑇 : 𝑀 | − 1)/26. It follows that at least one point stabiliser in 𝑀 has order less than
26|𝑀 |/(|𝑇 : 𝑀 | − 1) < 32. Thus, 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝑀) divides 210 .32 .5.7 and is less than 32. It follows that 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝑀)
divides 24 .32 .5.7 and 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝑀) ≤ 30, as required.
    To prove Part (3), suppose that

                          𝑀 ∈ {𝐷 2 , [𝐷 2 , 𝐷 2 ], 21+12 .3.L3 (4) : 2, 21+12 .3.L3 (4)}.

Then 𝑀 is 𝑇-conjugate to a subgroup of 𝐷 2 . Thus, 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝑀) divides 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝐷 2 ). The subdegrees of
𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐷2 ] are given in [6, Table 2], and the number 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝐷 2 ) can then be computed immediately: we get
𝑑 (𝑇, 𝐷 2 ) = 2. The remaining entries in the third column of the J4 -row of Table 1 follow. In the case
where 𝑀 = 𝐷 2 , the base size of 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] is 3, by [9, Table 2]. This action is equivalent to the conjugation
action of 𝑇 on the class of 2𝐴-involutions of 𝑇. The orders of the 2-point stabilisers in this action have
36

been computed by Bray et al in [6] and are listed in the column headed 𝑠2 in [6, Table 2]. The smallest
order is 16. If now 𝐻 = [𝐷 2 , 𝐷 2 ], of index 2 in 𝑀, then each 2-point stabiliser 𝐻 ∩ 𝐻 𝑥 in the permutation
group 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] has index at most 4 in 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑥 , and since |𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑥 | ≥ 16, it follows that 𝐻 ∩ 𝐻 𝑥 ≠ 1.
Thus 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] also has base size greater than 2.                                                            


   We remark that by proving Proposition 5.6(3), we have completed the proof of Proposition 4.1. As
final preparation for proving that 𝑇 = J4 is totally 2-closed, we deal separately with a specific coset
action.
Proposition 5.7. Let 𝑇 = J4 and 𝐷 1 = 𝐸 1 o 𝐹1 = 211 : M24 as above, and consider 𝐻 = 𝐸 1 o M23 < 𝐷 1
(so ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 2). Then 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 2-closed.
Proof. We use the notation in Notation 3.3, with 𝐺 = 𝑇 and 𝑀 = 𝐷 1 . So Ω = [𝑇 : 𝐻], Σ = [𝑇 : 𝑀]
with 𝑠 = |Σ|, 𝐿 = 𝑇 Σ , 𝑀 = 𝑇Δ (with Δ ∈ Σ), 𝐻 = 𝑇𝜔 (with 𝜔 ∈ Δ), etc. By Lemma 4.3(b)(i),
𝐿 (2),Σ = 𝐿, since 𝑇 = Aut(𝑇) and 𝑇 has no 2-transitive representations. We also set 𝑋 = 𝑇 (2),Ω
and 𝑌 = 𝑋ΔΔ ≤ 𝑀 (2),Δ . The group 𝑅 = 𝑀 Δ  M24 is 2-transitive of degree 24. Hence, we have
M24  𝑅 = 𝑀 Δ ≤ 𝑌 ≤ 𝑀 (2),Δ  Sym(24). The only overgroups of M24 in Sym(24) are M24 , Alt(24),
and Sym(24). Thus, 𝑌 ∈ {M24 , Alt(24), Sym(24)}.
    Assume that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is not 2-closed. Then, by Lemma 3.5, 𝑋 = 𝑁 o 𝑇 with 𝑁 a nontrivial subdirect
subgroup of 𝐵 𝐴, for some non-trivial normal subgroup 𝐴 of 𝑌 . Hence, 𝐴 ∈ {M24 , Alt(24), Sym(24)}.
    We now examine a part Δ2 ∈ Σ such that 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2 = 𝐿 2 (23) (the groups 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑗 are listed in [18,
Lemma 2.23.1]). Suppose that the subdirect subgroup 𝜌1,2 (𝑁) ≤ 𝐴 × 𝐴 is not a full diagonal subgroup
of 𝐴 × 𝐴. Then since 𝐴 is almost simple, 𝜌1,2 (𝑁) must contain soc( 𝐴) × soc( 𝐴). Since soc( 𝐴) acts
transitively on Δ, it follows that 𝜌1,2 (𝑁) Δ×Δ2 is transitive. On the other hand, by Lemma 3.5(b), the group
𝜌1,2 (𝑁) Δ×Δ2 leaves invariant each (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2 ) Δ×Δ2 -orbit. Since 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2  𝐿 2 (23) cannot act transitively
on a set of size 242 , we have a contradiction. Thus 𝜌1,2 (𝑁) ≤ 𝐴 × 𝐴 is a full diagonal subgroup of
𝐴 × 𝐴. It then follows from Proposition 3.8(b) that 𝑁 is a full diagonal subgroup of 𝐵 𝐴. In particular,
since 𝑋  𝑁 o 𝑇 with 𝑁  𝐴 ∈ {M24 , Alt(24), Sym(24)} and 𝑇  J4 , we have 𝑋 = 𝑁 × 𝑇.

   We now prove that 𝑇 = J4 is totally 2-closed.
Proposition 5.8. The Janko group J4 is totally 2-closed.
Proof. We use the notation fixed at the beginning of the section, so that 𝑇 = J4 , 𝐷 1  211 : M24
etc. Our task is to prove, using Strategy 4.5, that 𝑇 Ω = 𝑇 (2),Ω , where Ω = [𝑇 : 𝐻], for each proper
nontrivial subgroup 𝐻 of 𝑇. Since 𝑇 = Aut(𝑇) and 𝑇 has no 2-transitive representations, it follows
from Lemma 4.3(b)(i) that this holds for all maximal subgroups 𝐻. Thus we proceed to stage (2) of
Step 1 in Strategy 4.5: constructing the set S2 . By [9, Table 2], there are precisely three conjugacy
classes of maximal subgroups 𝑀 of 𝑇 such that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] has base size at least 3, with representatives
𝐷 1  211 : M24 , 𝐷 2  21+12 .3 : M22 .2, and 𝐷 3 = 210 : L5 (2) as defined at the beginning of the section.
Therefore according to Strategy 4.5, the set S2 consists of all non-maximal subgroups 𝐻 such that the
only maximal subgroups of 𝑇 containing 𝐻 are conjugate to 𝐷 1 , 𝐷 2 , or 𝐷 3 .
    We now move on to Strategy 4.5, Step 2, stage (1). We need to prove that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 2-closed for
all 𝐻 ∈ S2 with ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 2. Let 𝐻 ∈ S2 , and assume that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] ≠ 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝐻 ] . Let 𝑀 be a maximal
subgroup of 𝑇 containing 𝐻 so that, without loss of generality, 𝑀 = 𝐷 𝑖 , for some 𝑖 = 1, 2, 3 and 𝐻
is maximal in 𝑀. We use the rest of the notation in Notation 3.3, with 𝑇 = 𝐺. So Ω = [𝑇 : 𝐻],
Σ = [𝑇 : 𝑀], 𝐿 = 𝑇 Σ , 𝑀 = 𝑇Δ (with Δ ∈ Σ), 𝐻 = 𝑇𝜔 (with 𝜔 ∈ Δ), etc. Note that 𝐿 (2),Σ = 𝐿, by Step 1.
We also set 𝑋 = 𝑇 (2),Ω , so 𝑋 > 𝑇, and 𝑌 = 𝑋ΔΔ ≤ 𝑀 (2),Δ .
    Suppose first that 𝑖 = 1 or 3. Then 𝑀 = 𝐸 𝑖 o 𝐹𝑖 , where 𝐸 𝑖 is elementary abelian, and 𝐹𝑖 is a simple
group acting faithfully and irreducibly on 𝐸 𝑖 . Then, as mentioned in the proof of Proposition 5.6(1)(b),
since 𝐻 is maximal in 𝑀, either 𝐻  𝐹𝑖 or 𝐻 = 𝐸 𝑖 𝐼, where 𝐼 is a maximal subgroup of 𝐹𝑖 . It follows that
either 𝑀 [𝑀 :𝐻 ]  𝐸 𝑖 𝐹𝑖 is a primitive group of affine type, of degree |𝐸 𝑖 |; or 𝑀 [𝑀 :𝐻 ]  𝐹𝑖 is a primitive
almost simple group, of degree |𝐹𝑖 : 𝐼 |. Since 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is not 2-closed, it follows that the normal subgroup
𝐴 of 𝑌 ≤ 𝑀 (2),Δ from Proposition 3.10(2) is transitive. On the other hand, Proposition 3.10(2) and
Proposition 4.1 imply that the size of an 𝐴-orbit in Δ divides 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝑀), with 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝑀) as in Proposition
4.1(b), that is to say, |𝑀 : 𝐻| = |Δ| divides 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝑀). Now, by Proposition 4.1(b), 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝑀) divides
𝑔(𝑇, 𝑀), with 𝑔(𝑇, 𝑀) as in Table 1. In both cases 𝑔(𝑇, 𝑀) < |𝐸 𝑖 |, so 𝑀 [𝑀 :𝐻 ]  𝐹𝑖 is nonabelian
simple and primitive. If 𝑖 = 1 then 𝑔(𝑇, 𝑀) = 24 and it follows that |𝑀 : 𝐻| = 24 and 𝐼  M23 maximal
in 𝐹1  M24 ; however, by Proposition 5.7, 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 2-closed in this case, which is a contradiction.
Thus 𝑖 = 3, and by Proposition 4.1(b), 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝑀) ≤ 30. This means that |𝑀 : 𝐻| = |𝐹3 : 𝐼 | ≤ 30, which
is not possible for any maximal subgroup 𝐼 of 𝐹3  L5 (2). Thus 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 2-closed for all maximal
subgroups 𝐻 of 𝑀 ∈ {𝐷 1 , 𝐷 3 }.
    Next, assume that 𝐻 is maximal in 𝑀 = 𝐷 2 . Then, as mentioned in the proof of Proposition 5.5,
either 𝐻 is 𝑀-conjugate to a supplement 𝐹2  6.M22 : 2 for 𝐸 2 = 𝑂 2 (𝑀) in 𝑀, or 𝐻 = 𝐸 2 𝐼, for some
𝐼 < 𝐹2 maximal. Since 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is not 2-closed, it follows that the normal subgroup 𝐴 of the primitive
permutation group 𝑌 ≤ 𝑀 (2),Δ , from Proposition 3.10(2), is transitive. On the other hand, the size of
an 𝐴-orbit divides 2, by Proposition 4.1(b). Hence, we must have |𝑀 : 𝐻| = |Δ| = 2, and it follows that
38

𝐻 is the maximal subgroup [𝑀, 𝑀]  21+12 .3.M22 . By Proposition 3.10(1), for each Δ2 ∈ Σ \ {Δ}, the
stabiliser 𝑀2 = 𝑇Δ2 satisfies 𝑀 = (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2 )𝐻. We shall obtain a contradiction by proving that:

                for some Δ2 ∈ Σ \ {Δ}, the stabiliser 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2 = 𝑇Δ,Δ2 is contained in 𝐻.              (5.12)

We prove the claim using Magma and the 112-dimensional representation of 𝑇 over F2 . In particular,
we use the generating 112-dimensional matrices 𝑎 and 𝑏 of 𝑇 given in the Web Atlas [35], of orders 2
and 4, respectively. Using this notation, we have that 𝑀 is 𝑇-conjugate to 𝐶𝑇 (𝑎), so we may assume
that 𝑀 = 𝐶𝑇 (𝑎). Define
                                                                        2
                                      𝑡 := (𝑎𝑏 2 ) 4 ; 𝑐 := 𝑎𝑏; 𝑦 := 𝑡 𝑐 .

Using the excellent computations done in [6, Section 2], we have that

                𝑀 = h[𝑎, 𝑏] 5 (𝑎𝑏 2 ) 6 , 𝑏𝑎(𝑏 2 )𝑎𝑏[𝑎, 𝑏𝑎(𝑏 2 )𝑎𝑏] 5 𝑎𝑏𝑎𝑏𝑎𝑏[𝑎, 𝑎𝑏𝑎𝑏𝑎𝑏] 5 i.

Then the action of 𝑇 on the set of 𝑇-cosets of 𝑀 is permutation isomorphic to the action of 𝑇
on the set of 𝑇-conjugates of 𝑎. Thus, the 2-point stabilisers 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀2 in 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] are the groups
𝐶𝑇 (𝑎) ∩ 𝐶𝑇 (𝑎 𝑔 ), for 𝑔 ∈ 𝑇. Consider the 2-point stabiliser 𝐶 𝑀 (𝑎 𝑦 ) = 𝐶𝑇 (𝑎) ∩ 𝐶𝑇 (𝑎 𝑦 ). One can
quickly check using Magma [5] that (𝑎𝑎 𝑦 ) 6 is an element of 𝑀 of order 2, and that 𝐶 𝑀 ((𝑎𝑎 𝑦 ) 6 )
is contained in [𝑀, 𝑀] = 𝐻  21+12 .3.M22 . Hence, since 𝐶 𝑀 (𝑎 𝑦 ) ≤ 𝐶 𝑀 ((𝑎𝑎 𝑦 ) 6 ), we have that
𝐶𝑇 (𝑎) ∩ 𝐶𝑇 (𝑎 𝑦 ) = 𝐶 𝑀 (𝑎 𝑦 ) ≤ [𝑀, 𝑀] = 𝐻. Thus, (5.12) is proved, yielding a contradiction. We
conclude that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 2-closed for all maximal subgroups 𝐻 of 𝑀 = 𝐷 2 , and hence that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is
2-closed for all 𝐻 ∈ S2 with ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 2.
   This completes stage (1) of Step 2 of Strategy 4.5. For stage (2) of Step 2, we construct the set S3 .
By Proposition 5.6, we remove from S2 all (conjugates of) proper subgroups of 𝐷 1 , 𝐷 2 , and 𝐷 3 except
those (conjugates of) subgroups 𝐻 of 𝐷 2 such that ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) ≥ 3, and if 𝐻 < 𝐾 < 𝑇, then 𝐾 is conjugate
to one of the groups in
                                   {𝐷 2 , [𝐷 2 , 𝐷 2 ], 21+12 .3.L3 (4).2}.

The set S3 consists precisely of these remaining subgroups 𝐻.
   We now commence Strategy 4.5, Step 3, stage (1). We need to prove that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 2-closed for all
𝐻 ∈ S3 with ℓ𝑇 (𝐻) = 3. We may assume that such a subgroup 𝐻 is contained in 𝑀 := 𝐷 2 . Then
𝐻 must be a maximal subgroup in either [𝑀, 𝑀], or a subgroup of shape 21+12 .3.L3 (4).2. We listed
conjugacy class representatives for these subgroups in the proof of Proposition 5.6(1)(c), namely in
(5.9) and (5.10). We also showed that every maximal subgroup of [𝑀, 𝑀], apart from those conjugate
to 21+12 .3.Alt(7) or 21+12 .3.L3 (4), is contained in a maximal subgroup 𝐾 of 𝑀 with 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐾 ] of base size
2. Thus the subgroups 𝐻 which remain to be considered are the following:
  (i) the maximal subgroups 𝐻 of 21+12 .3.L3 (4).2 < 𝑀; and
 (ii) the subgroup 𝐻 := 21+12 .3.Alt(7) < [𝑀, 𝑀] < 𝑀.
Let 𝐻 be one of these subgroups, and let 𝐾 := 21+12 .3.L3 (4).2 in case (i), and 𝐾 = [𝑀, 𝑀] in case (ii),
so that 𝐻 is maximal in 𝐾. In either case the quantities 𝑔(𝑇, 𝐾) = 2 and 𝑑 (𝑇, 𝐾) ≤ 2 (see Table 1 and
Proposition 4.1(b)). Assume that 𝑇 (2), [𝑇 :𝐻 ] ≠ 𝑇. Then, by Proposition 3.10(2) applied to Σ = [𝑇 : 𝐾],
and Proposition 4.1(b), the usual argument shows that the only possibility is for 𝐾, 𝐻 as in case (i) with
𝐻 = [𝐾, 𝐾]  21+12 .3.L3 (4). So assume that we are in this case. Then by (5.12), there exists an element
𝑡 of 𝑇 such that 𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑡 ≤ [𝑀, 𝑀]. Hence, 𝐾 ∩ 𝐾 𝑡 ≤ 𝐾 ∩ [𝑀, 𝑀]  21+12 .3.L3 (4) = [𝐾, 𝐾]. It then
follows from Proposition 3.10(1) that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is 2-closed, which is a contradiction. This completes stage
(1) of Step 3. For stage (2) of Step 3, we simply note that the set S4 is empty, by Proposition 5.6(2).
Thus, it follows from Strategy 4.5 that 𝑇 = J4 is totally 2-closed.                                       

6. The exceptional groups
In this section, we prove that none of the finite simple exceptional groups of Lie type listed in Proposition
2.12(a) can be totally 2-closed. To do this, we assume throughout this section that

                      𝑇 ∈ {3 𝐷 4 (𝑞), 2 𝐹4 (𝑞) 0, 𝐹4 (𝑞), 2 𝐸 6 (𝑞), 𝐸 6 (𝑞), 𝐸 7 (𝑞), 𝐸 8 (𝑞)},
                      with 𝑞 = 𝑝 𝑓 , 𝑝 prime.                                                                                                 (6.1)

   Our aim is to prove the following.
Proposition 6.1. Let 𝑇 be one of the groups at (6.1). Then 𝑇 is not totally 2-closed.
   Recall that the subdegrees of a transitive permutation group are the orbit lengths of a point stabiliser.
Our first lemma collates the subdegrees of the minimal degree permutation representations of 𝑇, which
were determined in [30, Theorem 2] for 𝐹4 (𝑞), in [31, Theorems 1, 2 and 3] for 𝐸 6 (𝑞), 𝐸 7 (𝑞), 𝐸 8 (𝑞),
and in [32, Theorems 3, 4, 5 and 6] for 3 𝐷 4 (𝑞), 2 𝐸 6 (𝑞), 2 𝐹4 (𝑞) (𝑞 > 2), and 2 𝐹4 (2) 0, respectively.
Lemma 6.2. Let 𝑀 be a point stabiliser for 𝑇 in a minimal degree (necessarily primitive) permutation
representation. Then 𝑀 and the point stabilisers in 𝑀 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] are known, and 𝑀, the degree |𝑇 : 𝑀 |, the
rank, and the subdegrees are given in Table 2.

Proposition 6.3. Suppose that either 𝑇 is twisted; or 𝑇 is untwisted with 𝑓 > 1, where 𝑞 = 𝑝 𝑓 as in
(6.1). Let 𝑀 be a point stabilizer for 𝑇 in a minimal degree permutation representation, so 𝑀 is as in
Table 2. Then 𝑇 is not totally 2-closed.
Proof. By Lemma 6.2, the group 𝑀 is a maximal parabolic subgroup of 𝑇. More precisely, we write
𝑀 = 𝑃 𝐼 , where 𝐼 is a subset of the set of node-labels of the Dynkin diagram for 𝑇, and 𝑃 𝐼 is the
parabolic subgroup obtained by deleting the nodes with labels in 𝐼. In particular, in each case the group
𝐺 := 𝑇 𝑁Aut(𝑇 ) (𝑀) is strictly larger than 𝑇. Indeed, if 𝑇 is twisted, then 𝑇 has a non-trivial graph
automorphism which normalises 𝑀, while if 𝑇 is untwisted and 𝑓 > 1, then 𝑇 has a non-trivial field
40

automorphism which normalises 𝑀. See [16, Sections 2.5 and 2.6]. In particular, we use the definition
of graph, field, and graph-field automorphisms of 𝑇 given by [16, Definition 2.5.13].
    Now, since 𝑀 is maximal in 𝑇, we have 𝑀 = 𝑁𝑇 (𝑀). Hence, |𝐺 : 𝑁Aut(𝑇 ) (𝑀)| = |𝑇 : 𝑀 |, and
𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] is permutationally isomorphic to the permutation group 𝑇 [𝐺:𝑁Aut(𝑇 ) ( 𝑀 ) ] . By inspection of Table
2, we see that in each case, any two subdegrees of 𝑇 [𝐺:𝑁Aut(𝑇 ) ( 𝑀 ) ] involve different 𝑞-parts, and hence
the subdegrees are pairwise distinct. Thus 𝑇 and 𝐺 have the same orbits on ordered pairs of points from
[𝐺 : 𝑁Aut(𝑇 ) (𝑀)], and it follows from Theorem 2.4 that 𝐺 ≤ 𝑇 (2), [𝐺:𝑁Aut(𝑇 ) ( 𝑀 ) ] . Therefore 𝑇 is not
totally 2-closed.                                                                                            

   In proving Proposition 6.1, it is convenient to deal with the cases 𝐸 6 (2), 𝐸 7 (2) and 𝐸 8 (2) separately.
We do this in the next proposition, where we use the following labelling of the Dynkin diagrams for
these groups. This is consistent with the labelling in the computer algebra system Magma [5].

                                         𝐸6                                                         𝐸7
            1     3      4       5   6                                1    3   4       5   6    7

Proposition 6.4. The simple exceptional groups 𝐸 6 (2), 𝐸 7 (2), and 𝐸 8 (2), are not totally 2-closed.
Proof. Here 𝑇 = 𝐸 𝑚 (2) for some 𝑚 ∈ {6, 7, 8}. Let (𝐵, 𝑁) be a (𝐵, 𝑁)-pair for 𝑇. Since 𝑇 is defined
over a field of order 2, the group 𝑁 is isomorphic to the Weyl group 𝑊 of 𝑇, with respect to this
(𝐵, 𝑁)-pair. Let Φ be the associated root system for 𝑇, with fundamental roots Π := {𝑎 1 , . . . , 𝑎 𝑚 }. As
mentioned above, we label the roots and Dynkin diagram for 𝑇 as in Magma [5], see Figure 6.2. Let
𝑀 := 𝑃 𝑎3 be the maximal parabolic subgroup of 𝑇 obtained by deleting the node labelled by 3 in the
Dynkin diagram. Then 𝑀 = 𝑈 o 𝐿, where 𝑈 is the unipotent radical of 𝑀 and 𝐿 is a Levi subgroup.
    For each root 𝑎 𝑖 , we denote by Φ𝑖 the set of roots 𝑟 ∈ Φ with the property that the 𝑎 𝑖 -coordinate of 𝑟
is non-zero; and we set Φ¬ 𝑖 = Φ \ Φ𝑖 . For any subset Λ of Φ, we write Λ+ for the set of positive roots
in Λ. Finally, we write 𝑈𝑟 for the root subgroup of the unipotent radical 𝑈 associated with 𝑟.
    Then 𝑈 is the 2-group 𝑈 = h𝑈𝑟 : 𝑟 ∈ Φ+3 i, and we may take 𝐿 to be the standard Levi subgroup
𝐿 := h𝑈𝑟 : 𝑟 ∈ Φ¬ 3 i. It is clear from the Dynkin diagram, Figure 6.2, that

                      𝐿 = h𝑈±𝑎1 i × h𝑈±𝑎2 , 𝑈±𝑎4 , 𝑈±𝑎5 , . . . , 𝑈±𝑎𝑚 i  𝐴1 (2) × 𝐴𝑚−2 (2).            (6.3)

Let 𝜋1 : 𝐿 → 𝐴1 (2) and 𝜋2 : 𝐿 → 𝐴𝑚−2 (2) denote the canonical projections. Set 𝐻 = 𝑈 o [𝐿, 𝐿], so
that |𝑀 : 𝐻| = 2.
   Now a straightforward computation with Magma [5] shows that, for each 𝑤 ∈ 𝑊,

                                                  (Φ+3 ∪ Φ¬ 3 ) 𝑤 ∩ Φ¬ 3                                 (6.4)

contains a root 𝑟 𝑤 ∈ Φ with nonzero 𝑎 1 -coordinate (and zero 𝑎 3 -coordinate). Recall that 𝑁  𝑊, as
we noted above. Choose 𝑛 ∈ 𝑁, and suppose that 𝑛 corresponds to 𝑤 ∈ 𝑊. Let 𝑟 := 𝑟 𝑤 be a root in
the set in (6.4) (with nonzero 𝑎 1 -coordinate and zero 𝑎 3 -coordinate). Then it follows from (6.4) that
𝑀 𝑛 ∩ 𝐿 contains the root subgroup 𝑈𝑟 . Since 𝑈𝑟 has non-zero 𝑎 1 -coordinate, 𝜋1 (𝑈𝑟 ) contains a Sylow
2-subgroup of 𝐴1 (2)  Sym(3). Thus, 𝜋1 (𝑀 𝑛 ∩ 𝐿) contains a Sylow 2-subgroup of 𝐴1 (2), and hence
(𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑛 )𝐻 = 𝑀 for all 𝑛 ∈ 𝑁.
   Now, by Bruhat Normal Form [16, Theorem 2.3.5], we have 𝑇 = 𝐵𝑁 𝐵, so the element 𝑡 = 𝑥𝑛𝑦 for
some 𝑥, 𝑦 ∈ 𝐵 < 𝑀 and 𝑛 ∈ 𝑁. Then, noting that 𝑦 ∈ 𝑁𝑇 (𝐻) since |𝑀 : 𝐻| = 2, we have

                        (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑡 )𝐻 = (𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑛𝑦 )𝐻 = ((𝑀 ∩ 𝑀 𝑛 )𝐻) 𝑦 = 𝑀 𝑦 = 𝑀.
                                                                                                            41

It now follows from Proposition 3.10(1) applied with 𝐺, Ω, Σ, 𝑀, Δ and 𝐿 = 𝐿 (2),Σ being 𝑇, [𝑇 : 𝐻], [𝑇 :
𝑀], 𝑀, [𝑀 : 𝐻] and 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] , that at least one of 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝑀 ] or 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is not 2-closed. In either case 𝑇 is
not totally 2-closed.                                                                                        
   We are now ready to prove Proposition 6.1.
Proof of Proposition 6.1. By Proposition 6.3, we may assume that 𝑇 is untwisted and that 𝑞 =
𝑝 is prime. Thus, by Proposition 2.12(a) and Proposition 6.4, we may assume that 𝑇 ∈
{𝐹4 ( 𝑝), 𝐸 6 ( 𝑝), 𝐸 7 ( 𝑝), 𝐸 8 ( 𝑝)}, and that 𝑝 is an odd prime.
   Let 𝑆 be a maximally split torus in 𝑇, with (𝐵, 𝑁) a (𝐵, 𝑁)-pair for 𝑇, with respect to 𝑆. Then 𝐵 has
the form 𝐵 = 𝑈 o 𝑆, where 𝑈 is a Sylow 𝑝-subgroup of 𝑇. If 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐵] is not 2-closed there is nothing
further to prove for this group, so we may assume that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐵] is 2-closed. Since 𝑝 is odd, the group 𝑆
has even order, and hence has a subgroup 𝑅 of index 2. Let 𝐻 := 𝑈 𝑅. Then |𝐵 : 𝐻| = 2.
   For the permutation group 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐵] , the subgroup 𝐵 is the stabiliser of the ‘point’ 𝐵. Each 𝐵-orbit in
[𝑇 : 𝐵] \ {𝐵} is of the form {𝐵𝑎ℎ | ℎ ∈ 𝐵} for some 𝑎 ∈ 𝑇 \ 𝐵. Now, by Bruhat Normal Form [16,
Theorem 2.3.5], we have 𝑇 = 𝐵𝑁 𝐵, so 𝑎 = 𝑥𝑛𝑦 for some 𝑥, 𝑦 ∈ 𝐵 and 𝑛 ∈ 𝑁, and it follows that the
𝐵-orbit containing 𝐵𝑎 also contains 𝐵𝑎𝑦 −1 = 𝐵𝑛, and the stabiliser in 𝐵 of the point 𝐵𝑛 is 𝐵 ∩ 𝐵 𝑛 . Since
𝑁 = 𝑁𝑇 (𝑆), we have 𝑆 ≤ 𝐵 ∩ 𝐵 𝑛 , and it follows that 𝐵 = (𝐵 ∩ 𝐵 𝑛 )𝐻. This holds for all 𝑛 ∈ 𝑁.
   Finally, by again using the fact that 𝑇 = 𝐵𝑁 𝐵, and arguing in exactly the same way as in the final
paragraph of the proof of Proposition 6.4, we can see that (𝐵 ∩ 𝐵𝑡 )𝐻 = 𝐵 for all 𝑡 ∈ 𝑇, and hence, after
applying Proposition 3.10(1), that 𝑇 [𝑇 :𝐻 ] is not 2-closed. Hence, 𝑇 is not totally 2-closed.           

6.1. Proof of Theorem 1.1
By Proposition 2.12, together with our results in Sections 4, 5, and 6, on sporadic simple groups,
and Proposition 6.1 in this section for the exceptional groups, we know that each of the groups
J1 , J3 , J4 , Th, Ly, M is totally 2-closed, and that these are the only totally 2-closed simple groups. Thus
Theorem 1.1 is proved.


7. Direct products
In this section, our aim is to prove Theorem 1.2. For this reason, we assume throughout the section that
𝐺 is a non-trivial finite totally 2-closed group with 𝐹 (𝐺) = 1. By Theorem 2.5, the group 𝐺 must have
the form 𝐺 = 𝑇1 × . . . × 𝑇Î𝑟 where, for each 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟, 𝑇𝑖 is a finite totally 2-closed nonabelian simple group,
and 𝑇𝑖 is not a section of 𝑖≠ 𝑗 𝑇 𝑗 . Moreover, by Theorem 1.1, each of the 𝑇𝑖 lies in the set

                                           S := {J1 , J3 , J4 , Th, Ly, M}.

By inspection of the sections of these sporadic simple groups, we see that there exist distinct 𝑆, 𝑇 ∈ S
such that 𝑆 is isomorphic to a section of 𝑇 if and only if 𝑆 = Th and 𝑇 = M, see Remark 2.6. Thus not
both of the groups Th and M lie in {𝑇𝑖 : 1 ≤ 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟 }, and hence 𝑟 ≤ 5 and one of the conditions (3)(i) or
(3)(ii) of Theorem 1.2 holds. This proves that each of the assertions (1)–(3)Îof Theorem 1.2 holds.
   Thus to complete the proof of Theorem 1.2 we must show that, if 𝐺 = 𝑟𝑖=1 𝑇𝑖 with the 𝑇𝑖 pairwise
no-isomorphic, and if one of the conditions (3)(i) or (3)(ii) of Theorem 1.2 holds, then 𝐺 is totally 2-
closed. Since none of the groups in S admits a nontrivial factorisation (Corollary 2.3), it follows from
Proposition 2.10 that it is sufficient to prove that 𝜑(𝐺) is 2-closed for each permutation representation
𝜑 : 𝐺 → Sym(Ω) (faithful and non-faithful) with |Ω| > 1 and 𝜑(𝐺) transitive. With this in mind, we
introduce the following hypothesis and notation, which we will assume, for the remainder of the section:
Hypothesis 7.1. (a) The group 𝐺 = 𝑇1 × . . . × 𝑇𝑟 with the 𝑇𝑖 pairwise non-isomorphic, and either
  (i) 𝑇𝑖 ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Th, Ly} for each 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟; or
 (ii) 𝑇𝑖 ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly, M} for each 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟.
42

(b) We extend the notation for direct products introduced in Hypothesis 2.7. Namely, for a direct product
𝐺 1 × . . . × 𝐺 𝑠 of arbitrary finite groups 𝐺 𝑖 , and each subgroup 𝐿 𝑖 of 𝐺 𝑖 , we write

                   𝐿b𝑖 = {(𝑥1 , . . . , 𝑥 𝑠 ) : 𝑥𝑖 ∈ 𝐿 𝑖 , and 𝑥 𝑗 = 1 for 𝑗 ≠ 𝑖} ≤ 𝐺 1 × . . . × 𝐺 𝑠 .

(c) Seeking a contradiction, we assume that 𝐺 is not totally 2-closed, and that the number 𝑟 of simple
direct summands is minimal with respect to this property. Note that 𝑟 > 1 by Theorem 1.1, and
by Proposition 2.10, 𝐺 has a proper subgroup 𝐻 such that 𝐺 [𝐺:𝐻 ] is not 2-closed. Without loss of
generality we may assume that the proper subgroup 𝐻 is maximal by inclusion such that 𝐺 [𝐺:𝐻 ] is not
2-closed. By [33, Theorem 5.12 and Example 5.13], it follows that 𝐻 ≠ 1. Further, 𝐻 is core-free in 𝐺
(since otherwise 𝐺/Core𝐺 (𝐻)  𝐺 [𝐺:𝐻 ] is not totally 2-closed and is a direct product of less than 𝑟 of
the simple groups in (i) or (ii), contradicting the minimality of 𝑟).
(d) Next, write 𝜇𝑖 : 𝐺 → 𝑇𝑖 for the natural coordinate projection, for 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟. Note that 𝜇𝑖 (𝑇b𝑖 ∩𝐻) is normal
in 𝜇𝑖 (𝐻), but to avoid cumbersome notation, we will usually just say that 𝑇b𝑖 ∩ 𝐻 is normal in 𝜇𝑖 (𝐻).
(e) Our final piece of notation is defined with the minimality of 𝑟 in mind: we set 𝐺 1 := 𝑇1 , and
𝐺 2 := 𝑇2 × . . . × 𝑇𝑟 , so that both 𝐺 1 and 𝐺 2 are finite totally 2-closed groups (by the minimality of 𝑟).
We write the coordinate projections here as 𝜋1 : 𝐺 → 𝐺 1 and 𝜋2 : 𝐺 → 𝐺 2 (so in particular 𝜋1 = 𝜇1 ).
We also set 𝑀𝑖 := 𝜋𝑖 (𝐻) and 𝐻𝑖 = 𝐺      b𝑖 ∩ 𝐻, for 𝑖 ∈ {1, 2}, where 𝐺  b𝑖 is as defined in (b) relative to the
direct product 𝐺 1 × 𝐺 2 . Note that 𝐻 is a subdirect subgroup of 𝑀 := 𝑀1 × 𝑀2 ≤ 𝐺 and 𝜋𝑖 (𝐻𝑖 )  𝑀𝑖 for
each 𝑖. As in part (d), we often omit the 𝜋𝑖 , and just say that 𝐻𝑖  𝑀𝑖 . Since 𝐻 is a subdirect subgroup
of 𝑀 = 𝑀1 × 𝑀2 , it is important to note that 𝑀1 /𝐻1  𝑀2 /𝐻2 (Goursat’s Lemma, see [27, Theorem
4.8(i)]).
Remark 7.2. The final piece of notation in Hypothesis 7.1 is introduced for convenience only: there
will be nothing special about the labelling of the simple direct factors of 𝐺, and we will sometimes vary
the direct factor which is chosen to be 𝑇1 in our analysis. We warn the reader however, that the labelling
of the direct factors of 𝐺 changes in this way, then the group 𝑀 defined in Hypothesis 7.1(e) may also
change.
   In order to prove that each group 𝐺 satisfying Hypothesis 7.1 is totally 2-closed, we use the following
strategy:
Strategy 7.3. Let 𝐺, 𝑇𝑖 , 𝐻, etc be as in Hypothesis 7.1. We follow the four steps below.
Step 1: We prove (Lemma 7.4) that the subgroup 𝑀 = 𝑀1 × 𝑀2 in Hypothesis 7.1(e) is a proper
overgroup of 𝐻, that 𝑀 is core-free in 𝐺, and that 𝐺 [𝐺:𝑀 ] is 2-closed. This enables us to use the tools
developed in Section 3, (see Notation 3.3).
Step 2: The tools developed in Section 3 also require information concerning the transitive permutation
group 𝑀 [𝑀 :𝐻 ] with point stabiliser 𝐻 [𝑀 :𝐻 ] . Note that 𝐻 is a subdirect subgroup of 𝑀 = 𝑀1 × 𝑀2 .
Step 2 comprises two results (Lemmas 7.5 and 7.6) concerning subdirect subgroups of a direct product
of finite groups.
                                                                                                [𝑇 :𝜇𝑖 (𝐻 ) ]
Step 3: We prove (Lemma 7.7) that, for some 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟, the permutation group 𝑇𝑖 𝑖                                   has base size
greater than 2, and so, by Proposition 4.1, this pair (𝑇𝑖 , 𝜇𝑖 (𝐻)) lies in Table 1.
Step 4: For each pair (𝑇𝑖 , 𝜇𝑖 (𝐻)) in Table 1, we examine the structure of 𝑋 := 𝐺 (2), [𝐺:𝐻 ] using
Proposition 3.10(2), seeking a contradiction. We use the same notation as that introduced in Notation 3.3
with some small changes given in Notation 7.9.
     We begin with Step 1.
Lemma 7.4. Let 𝐺, 𝑟, 𝑇𝑖 , 𝐻, 𝑀 be as in Hypothesis 7.1. Then,
  (i) 𝜇𝑖 (𝐻) ≠ 𝑇𝑖 for any 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟, 𝑀 is core-free in 𝐺, 𝐺 [𝐺:𝑀 ] is 2-closed, and 𝐻 < 𝑀 < 𝐺; and
                                                                                                            43

 (ii) for each 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟, and each composition factor 𝑆 of 𝜇𝑖 (𝐻)/(𝑇b𝑖 ∩ 𝐻), there exists 𝑗 ≠ 𝑖 such that
      𝜇 𝑗 (𝐻) has a composition factor isomorphic to 𝑆.
Proof. (i) Note that Hypothesis 2.7 also holds for 𝐺 (with projection maps 𝐺 → 𝑇𝑖 now called 𝜇𝑖 ).
Hence, since 𝐻 is core-free in 𝐺 by Hypothesis 7.1(c), it follows from Lemma 2.8 that 𝜇𝑖 (𝐻) ≠ 𝑇𝑖 for
any 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟. Then, since 𝑀 ≤ 𝜇1 (𝐻) × . . . × 𝜇𝑟 (𝐻), the group 𝑀 does not contain 𝑇ˆ𝑖 , for any 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟, and
so 𝑀 is core-free in 𝐺. Also (see Hypothesis 7.1(e)), 𝑀 = 𝑀1 × 𝑀2 < 𝐺 1 × 𝐺 2 , and by the minimality
of 𝑟, 𝐺 𝑖[𝐺𝑖 :𝑀𝑖 ] is 2-closed for 𝑖 ∈ {1, 2}. Hence 𝐺 [𝐺:𝑀 ] is 2-closed, by [10, Theorem 5.1]. In particular,
since by assumption 𝐺 [𝐺:𝐻 ] is not 2-closed, we have 𝐻 < 𝑀 < 𝐺. This proves part (i).
(ii) In order to prove part (ii) we will prove the following claim:
   Claim: Let 𝑆 be a finite simple group, and let 𝑋1 , . . . , 𝑋𝑡 be finite groups (𝑡 ≥ 1) such that no 𝑋𝑖
has a section isomorphic to 𝑆. If 𝑋 is a subdirect subgroup of 𝑋1 × . . . × 𝑋𝑡 , then 𝑋 has no section
isomorphic to 𝑆.
     First we see that part (ii) follows from the claim. Indeed, assume that the claim holds, and that 𝑆 is a
composition factor of 𝜇𝑖 (𝐻)/(𝑇b𝑖 ∩ 𝐻), for some 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟. Without loss of generality assume that 𝑖 = 1, so 𝑆
is a composition factor of 𝜇1 (𝐻)/(𝑇b1 ∩ 𝐻) = 𝑀1 /𝐻1 . Since 𝐻 is a subdirect subgroup of 𝑀 = 𝑀1 × 𝑀2
(Hypothesis 7.1(e)), we have 𝑀1 /𝐻1  𝑀2 /𝐻2 , and hence 𝑆 is a composition factor of 𝑀2 . Then since
𝑀2 = 𝜋2 (𝐻) is a subdirect subgroup of 𝜇2 (𝐻) × . . . × 𝜇𝑟 (𝐻), it follows from the claim that 𝜇 𝑗 (𝐻) has
a composition factor isomorphic to 𝑆 for some 𝑗 ≥ 2.
Proof of the Claim: The proof is by induction on 𝑡. The case 𝑡 = 1 is trivially true, so assume that 𝑡 > 1
and that the claim holds for direct products of less than 𝑡 groups. Suppose that 𝑋 is a subdirect subgroup
of 𝑋1 × . . . × 𝑋𝑡 , that no 𝑋𝑖 has a section isomorphic to 𝑆, but that 𝑋 has a section isomorphic to 𝑆,
say 𝑆  𝑌 /𝑁 with 𝑁  𝑌 ≤ 𝑋. We will derive a contradiction. For each 𝑖 ≤ 𝑟, let 𝜈𝑖 : 𝑋 → 𝑋𝑖 be the
natural projection map and 𝑌𝑖 = 𝜈𝑖 (𝑌 ), so 𝑌 is a subdirect    subgroup of 𝑍 := 𝑌1 × · · · × 𝑌𝑡 and no 𝑌𝑖 has
a section isomorphic to 𝑆. Further let 𝜈𝑖0 : 𝑍 → 𝑗≠𝑖 𝑌 𝑗 be the natural projection map, for each 𝑖, and
                                                      Î
note that 𝜈10 (𝑌 ) is a subdirect subgroup of 𝑌2 × . . . × 𝑌𝑡 . Hence, if 𝜈10 (𝑌 ) has a section isomorphic to
𝑆, then by induction 𝑌𝑖 has a section isomorphic to 𝑆, for some 𝑖 ≥ 2, which is a contradiction. Hence
𝜈10 (𝑌 ) has no section isomorphic to 𝑆. Since 𝜈10 (𝑌 )/𝜈10 (𝑁) is isomorphic to a quotient of the simple
group 𝑌 /𝑁  𝑆, this implies that 𝜈10 (𝑁) = 𝜈10 (𝑌 ). Now the kernel of 𝜈10 |𝑌 is the group 𝐾 := 𝑌 ∩ 𝑌b1 , and
so 𝜈10 (𝑁) = 𝜈10 (𝑌 ) implies that 𝑌 = 𝑁𝐾, whence 𝐾/(𝑁 ∩ 𝐾)  𝑁𝐾/𝑁 = 𝑌 /𝑁  𝑆. Thus 𝑌b1  𝑌1 has a
section isomorphic to 𝑆, which is a contradiction. This completes the inductive proof of the claim, and
hence completes the proof of the lemma.                                                                      

   We now move to Step 2, and prove two lemmas concerning subdirect subgroups of direct products.
Lemma 7.5. Let 𝑋1 , . . . , 𝑋𝑡 be finite groups, and let 𝑋 be a subdirect subgroup of 𝑋1 × . . . × 𝑋𝑡 . Then
the following assertions hold.
                    b𝑖 ≤ 𝑋 for some 𝑖 ∈ {1, 2}, then 𝑋 = 𝑋1 × 𝑋2 .
  (i) If 𝑡 = 2, and 𝑋
 (ii) Let 𝑝 be a prime, and suppose that each group 𝑋𝑖 is a transitive permutation group of 𝑝-power
      degree. Then the Fitting subgroup 𝐹 (𝑋) is a (possibly trivial) 𝑝-group.
Proof. (i) This follows immediately from [27, Lemma 4.7].
    (ii) For each 𝑖 ≤ 𝑡, assume that 𝑋𝑖 is a transitive permutation group on a set Ω𝑖 with |Ω𝑖 | a power
of 𝑝, and let 𝜈𝑖 : 𝑋 → 𝑋𝑖 be the natural projection map. It is sufficient to show that 𝜈𝑖 (𝐹 (𝑋)) is a
𝑝-group for each 𝑖. Note that, for each 𝑖, 𝜈𝑖 (𝐹 (𝑋)) is a nilpotent normal subgroup of 𝜈𝑖 (𝑋) = 𝑋𝑖 (since
𝑋 is subdirect), and hence 𝜈𝑖 (𝐹 (𝑋)) ≤ 𝐹 (𝑋𝑖 ). If 𝜈𝑖 (𝐹 (𝑋)) = 1 there is nothing to prove so assume that
𝜈𝑖 (𝐹 (𝑋)) ≠ 1 and let 𝑞 be a prime dividing |𝜈𝑖 (𝐹 (𝑋))|. Then the unique (nontrivial) Sylow 𝑞-subgroup
𝑄 of 𝜈𝑖 (𝐹 (𝑋)) is characteristic in 𝜈𝑖 (𝐹 (𝑋)) and hence normal in 𝑋𝑖 . Since 𝑋𝑖 is transitive on Ω𝑖 , all
the orbits of its normal subgroup 𝑄 have the same size, say 𝑚. Thus 𝑚 divides |Ω𝑖 | which is a power
44

of 𝑝, and also 𝑚 divides |𝑄| which is a power of 𝑞. It follows that 𝑝 = 𝑞, and hence that 𝜈𝑖 (𝐹 (𝑋)) is a
𝑝-group. Thus part (ii) is proved.                                                                     

   We now move on to Step 4 of Strategy 7.3. We examine each possibility for (𝑇𝑖 , 𝜇𝑖 (𝐻)) from Table 1.
First we deal with the unique pair in Table 1 involving the Monster, namely (M, 2.B).
Lemma 7.8. For 𝑇𝑖 , 𝜇𝑖 , 𝐻 as in Hypothesis 7.1, no pair (𝑇𝑖 , 𝜇𝑖 (𝐻)) is equal to (M, 2.B).

Proof. Suppose to the contrary that (𝑇𝑖 , 𝜇𝑖 (𝐻)) = (M, 2.B), for some 𝑖. As discussed in Remark 7.2, we
may assume that 𝑖 = 1, so 𝑀1 = 2.B, and by Hypothesis 7.1, 𝑇 𝑗 ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly} for each 𝑗 ≥ 2. Now
𝐻 is a subdirect subgroup of 𝑀 = 𝑀1 × 𝑀2 , and by Lemma 7.4(i), 𝐻 is a proper subgroup of 𝑀. Thus,
by Lemma 7.5(i), 𝐻 does not contain 𝑀        b1 , so 𝐻1 = 𝑇b1 ∩ 𝐻 = 𝑀b1 ∩ 𝐻 is a proper normal subgroup of
𝑀1 = 2.B. It follows that B is a composition factor of 𝑀1 /𝐻1 , but this contradicts Lemma 7.4(ii) since,
for each 𝑗 ≥ 2, 𝑇 𝑗 ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly} and none of these simple groups has a section isomorphic to B. 

    Our strategy for proceeding is to prove that the parameter 𝑎 in Notation 7.9(e) divides a product of 𝑟
positive integers related to the simple groups 𝑇1 , . . . , 𝑇𝑟 (see Lemma 7.10). We then prove (see Lemma
7.11) that 𝑎 has the form 𝑎 = 𝑑1 𝑑2 , where the 𝑑𝑖 are orders of certain normal sections of 𝑀1 /𝐻1 . Finally,
in the proof of Theorem 1.2, we prove that in most cases, 𝑑1 𝑑2 cannot divide 𝑎, yielding a contradiction
in those cases.

     Next we prove Lemma 7.11 which provides a factorisation of the parameter 𝑎 = 𝑎(𝐺, 𝑀, 𝐻).
Lemma 7.11. Assume that the notation and conditions from Notation 7.9 hold, and recall that 𝑋 =
𝐺 (2),Ω . Then
  (i) there exist normal subgroups 𝑉 of the centre 𝑍 (𝑀1 /𝐻1 ), and 𝑈 of (𝑀1 /𝐻1 )/𝑍 (𝑀1 /𝐻1 ), such that

in part (i), each of 𝑈, 𝑉 is (isomorphic to) a normal section of 𝑀1 /𝐻1  𝑀2 /𝐻2 .

Proof. (i) By Notation 7.9(e), 𝐴  𝑌 = 𝑋ΔΔ , so the set of 𝐴-orbits in Δ is a 𝑌 -invariant partition of Δ
with parts of size 𝑎 > 1, and since 𝑀 Δ = 𝑅 ≤ 𝑌 (Notation 7.9(a)) this partition is also 𝑀 Δ -invariant.
By Notation 7.9(a), 𝐻 is the stabiliser in 𝑀 of a point 𝜔 ∈ Δ, and so the setwise stabiliser 𝐾 in 𝑀 of the
𝐴-orbit 𝜔 𝐴 satisfies 𝐻 < 𝐾 ≤ 𝑀 and |𝐾 : 𝐻| = 𝑎.

say. Now 𝑆 := 𝐻1 × 𝐻2  𝑀 = 𝑀1 × 𝑀2 and 𝑆 < 𝐻 < 𝑀, so the permutation groups induced on Δ

is the stabiliser of 𝜔 and 𝐾 = 𝐾/𝑆 is the setwise stabiliser of 𝜔 𝐴. In particular 𝑎 = |𝐾 : 𝐻|. Since 𝐻

power of 𝑝), and hence 𝐴 is a subdirect subgroup of 𝑋1 × · · · × 𝑋𝑡 with the 𝑋𝑖 satisfying the conditions
of Lemma 7.5(ii). Hence 𝐹 ( 𝐴) is a 𝑝-group, and therefore also 𝐹 (𝑋) is a 𝑝-group.                     

Remark 7.12. We make a preliminary remark about how we may exploit Lemma 7.11(ii) in the proof
of Theorem 1.2: suppose that, for a fixed pair (𝑇1 , 𝑀1 ), we have used Lemmas 7.10 and 7.11 to show
that 𝑎(𝐺, 𝑀, 𝐻) is a power of a prime 𝑝, and hence, by Lemma 7.11(ii) that 𝐹 (𝑋) is a 𝑝-group. Suppose
that we then consider a pair (𝑇 𝑗 , 𝜇 𝑗 (𝐻)) where 2 ≤ 𝑗 ≤ 𝑟. By changing the labelling, we can replace
(𝑇1 , 𝑀1 ) by (𝑇 𝑗 , 𝜇 𝑗 (𝐻)), but in doing this we change the overgroup 𝑀 of 𝐻, say to 𝑀.
                                                                                        e It may be possible
to use Lemmas 7.10 and 7.11 to show that 𝑎(𝐺, 𝑀,        e 𝐻) is a power of a prime 𝑠, with 𝑠 ≠ 𝑝, whence by
Lemma 7.11(ii), 𝐹 (𝑋) is an 𝑠-group, implying that 𝐹 (𝑋) = 1. This strategy proves to be very useful.
We emphasise that, when we change the labelling, even though the subgroup 𝑀 may change, the group
𝑋 = 𝐺 (2),Ω and its subgroup 𝐻 do not change.
   We are now ready to prove Theorem 1.2.

8. Concluding remarks: the general case
As a result of the work in this paper, the task of classifying all finite totally 2-closed groups 𝐺 can now
be reduced to the case where 𝐺 is insoluble and 𝐹 (𝐺) > 1 (see Question 1 in Section 1.1). We conclude
the paper with some remarks about this case, and a reduction theorem.
    We note first that a crucial step in our classification was the essential reduction to classifying those
finite groups (with trivial Fitting subgroup) which are 2-closed in all of their transitive permutation
representations (see Proposition 2.10). Although we weren’t able to reduce our study of arbitrary
finite totally 2-closed groups to transitive actions, the following theorem (and subsequent corollary)
significantly reduces the types of faithful actions that need to be examined. In order to state it, we need
some additional terminology: Permutation representations of a group 𝐺 on sets Γ and Γ0 are said to be
permutationally equivalent if there exists a bĳection 𝑓 : Γ → Γ0 such that, for all 𝛾 ∈ Γ and all 𝑔 ∈ 𝐺, the
image (𝛾 𝑔 ) 𝑓 = (𝛾 𝑓 ) 𝑔 . Note that 𝑓 induces a bĳection Γ × Γ → Γ0 × Γ0, namely 𝑓 : (𝛼, 𝛽) → (𝛼 𝑓 , 𝛽 𝑓 ),
and that this induced map sends 𝐺-orbits in Γ × Γ to 𝐺-orbits in Γ0 × Γ0.
    Our general reduction theorem can now be stated as follows.
Theorem 8.1. Let 𝐺 ≤ Sym(Ω), and suppose that Γ, Γ0 are distinct 𝐺-orbits on which the 𝐺-actions
are permutationally equivalent relative to a bĳection 𝑓 : Γ → Γ0. Let Ω0 := Ω \ Γ, so Ω = Ω0 ∪ Γ. Then
 (a) both 𝐺 and 𝐺 (2),Ω act faithfully on Ω0, and
                                           0
 (b) the restriction 𝐺 (2),Ω | Ω0 = 𝐺 (2),Ω .

 (c) If 𝐺 is finite, then 𝐺 = 𝐺 (2),Ω if and only if 𝐺 Ω = 𝐺 (2),Ω .
Proof. (a) Note first that since 𝐺 (2),Ω has the same orbits as 𝐺 in Ω, the set Ω0 is 𝐺 (2),Ω -invariant.
Also, 𝐺 ≤ 𝐺 (2),Ω . To prove (a), it is therefore sufficient to show that 𝐺 (2),Ω is faithful on Ω0. So assume
that 𝑥 ∈ 𝐺 (2),Ω such that 𝑥 fixes Ω0 pointwise, and let 𝛾 ∈ Γ. Then 𝛾 𝑓 ∈ Γ0 ⊆ Ω0, so (𝛾 𝑓 ) 𝑥 = 𝛾 𝑓 . By
Theorem 2.4, there exists 𝑔 ∈ 𝐺 such that 𝛾 𝑥 = 𝛾 𝑔 and (𝛾 𝑓 ) 𝑥 = (𝛾 𝑓 ) 𝑔 . Thus 𝛾 𝑓 = (𝛾 𝑓 ) 𝑔 , and by the
defining property of 𝑓 , (𝛾 𝑓 ) 𝑔 = (𝛾 𝑔 ) 𝑓 . This implies that 𝛾 𝑓 = (𝛾 𝑔 ) 𝑓 = (𝛾 𝑥 ) 𝑓 , and since 𝑓 is a bĳection
we deduce that 𝛾 = 𝛾 𝑥 . It follows that 𝑥 fixes Γ pointwise, and hence that 𝑥 = 1. This proves part (a).
